questions.explanation: Section 197 and the Third Schedule (Part II) of the 1999 Constitution establish a State Independent Electoral Commission (SIEC) in each state to conduct local government elections.

whyNot.B: INEC conducts federal and state elections, such as presidential, governorship and legislative elections, but not local government council elections in the states.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The elective principle was first introduced into Nigeria by the
questions.explanation: The Clifford Constitution of 1922 allowed four elected members in the Legislative Council: three from Lagos and one from Calabar. This encouraged the formation of the Nigerian National Democratic Party in 1923.

whyNot.B: The Richards Constitution of 1946 is known for introducing regionalism.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under the 1963 Republican Constitution of Nigeria, the President was
options: both head of state and head of government
the leader of the majority party in parliament
questions.explanation: Nigeria became a republic on 1 October 1963 but kept the parliamentary system. The President (Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe) was a ceremonial head of state, while executive power lay with the Prime Minister.

whyNot.B: An executive president combining both roles came with the 1979 Constitution.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The 'federal character' principle is provided for in which section of the 1999 Constitution?
questions.explanation: Section 14(3) requires that the composition of the Government of the Federation and its agencies reflect the federal character of Nigeria, so that no few states or ethnic or other sectional groups dominate. The Federal Character Commission enforces it.

whyNot.B: Section 6(6)(c) makes Chapter II non-justiciable.
whyNot.C: Section 153 lists the federal executive bodies such as INEC.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Nigeria was suspended from the Commonwealth in 1995 mainly because of
options: its refusal to pay Commonwealth subscriptions
a border war with a member state
the execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and other Ogoni activists under military rule
questions.explanation: After the military government executed Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other Ogoni activists in November 1995, the Commonwealth suspended Nigeria. It was restored to full membership after the return to civilian rule in 1999.

whyNot.B: Nigeria has never left ECOWAS; it is a founding member.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The ECOWAS Ceasefire Monitoring Group (ECOMOG) was first deployed in 1990 to
questions.explanation: ECOMOG, in which Nigeria played the leading role, was first deployed to Liberia in August 1990 to help end the civil war there. It later intervened in Sierra Leone in the late 1990s.

whyNot.C: ECOMOG went into Sierra Leone later, in the late 1990s.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Since independence, the centrepiece of Nigeria's foreign policy has been
questions.explanation: Nigerian governments have consistently made Africa the centrepiece of foreign policy, for example by supporting decolonisation, opposing apartheid and leading in ECOWAS and the OAU/AU.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Authority differs from power mainly because authority is
options: the ability to compel obedience by force
always backed by the armed forces
power that is recognised as legitimate
questions.explanation: Power is the ability to make others act as one wishes, even by force. Authority is power that people accept as rightful, for example because it comes from the constitution or tradition.

whyNot.A: The ability to compel by force describes power (or coercion), not authority.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A system of government in which rulers govern in the name of God or according to religious law is
questions.explanation: In a theocracy, religious leaders rule, or rulers claim to govern according to divine law. Some states have made religious law the basis of their constitution.

whyNot.A: A monarchy is headed by a king or queen; it is not necessarily religious.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A constitution that can be amended by the same procedure used for passing ordinary laws is said to be
questions.explanation: A flexible constitution can be changed by a simple majority of the legislature, like any ordinary law. The British constitution is the usual example.

whyNot.C: A rigid constitution needs a special amendment procedure.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which of the following countries is a classic example of a two-party system?
questions.explanation: In the USA, the Democratic and Republican parties have long dominated elections, making it the standard example of a two-party system.

whyNot.A: China is governed by a single ruling party.
whyNot.C: India has many national and regional parties, a multi-party system.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: How many local government areas (including the area councils of the FCT) are listed in the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria?
questions.explanation: The First Schedule lists 768 local government areas in the 36 states plus 6 area councils in the Federal Capital Territory, a total of 774.

whyNot.B: 768 is the number in the states alone, without the 6 FCT area councils.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) was founded on 25 May 1963 in
questions.explanation: African leaders signed the OAU Charter in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on 25 May 1963. Addis Ababa remains the headquarters of its successor, the African Union.

whyNot.B: Durban, South Africa, is where the African Union was launched in 2002.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The power of the President to veto a bill passed by the legislature is an example of
questions.explanation: Checks and balances allow each organ of government to limit the others. The executive's veto checks the legislature, which in turn can override the veto (section 58(5) of the 1999 Constitution).

whyNot.A: Judicial review is the courts' power to declare laws or actions unconstitutional, a check by the judiciary.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A state differs from a nation mainly because a state
options: has a government exercising sovereignty over a defined territory
always consists of a single ethnic group
is bound together by a common history and culture
is made up of people who share a common language
questions.explanation: A state is a political and legal entity with population, defined territory, government and sovereignty. A nation is a group of people bound by common identity such as language, culture or history, and may not have a state of its own.

whyNot.C: Common history and culture are features of a nation, not what defines a state.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A vote of no confidence is a feature of the
questions.explanation: In a parliamentary system, the executive depends on the support of parliament; if parliament passes a vote of no confidence, the prime minister and cabinet must resign or call an election.

whyNot.B: In a presidential system the president has a fixed term and is removed only by impeachment, not by a vote of no confidence.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: An official appointed to investigate complaints by citizens against maladministration by public officials is called
questions.explanation: The ombudsman investigates citizens' complaints against public officials. In Nigeria this role is performed by the Public Complaints Commission, established in 1975.

whyNot.C: The Auditor-General audits public accounts; he or she does not handle individual citizens' complaints.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The principle that civil servants should not be publicly praised or blamed for the policies they help to make is known as
questions.explanation: Under anonymity, civil servants remain in the background while ministers take public credit or blame for government policies.

whyNot.D: Permanence means civil servants keep their jobs when governments change.
whyNot.A: Neutrality means civil servants serve any government in power without party bias.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: An election held to fill a seat that becomes vacant through the death or resignation of a member is a
questions.explanation: A by-election fills a single vacancy that arises between general elections, for example when a legislator dies or resigns.

whyNot.C: A primary election is held within a party to choose its candidates.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC)?
questions.explanation: The Third Schedule of the 1999 Constitution gives INEC powers to organise federal and state elections, register political parties, monitor their finances and register voters.

whyNot.D: Interpreting the Constitution is the work of the courts.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC), formed in 1944, was led at its founding by
options: Ahmadu Bello and Abubakar Tafawa Balewa
questions.explanation: The NCNC was formed in August 1944 with Herbert Macaulay as its first president and Nnamdi Azikiwe as general secretary; Azikiwe became its leader after Macaulay died in 1946.

whyNot.B: Awolowo and Akintola were leaders of the Action Group (AG).
whyNot.A: Ahmadu Bello and Tafawa Balewa were leaders of the Northern People's Congress (NPC).

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Federalism was formally introduced into Nigeria by the
questions.explanation: The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954 made Nigeria a federation of three regions and the federal territory of Lagos, dividing powers between the federal and regional governments.

whyNot.A: The Richards Constitution of 1946 introduced regionalism, which prepared the ground for federalism.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Nigeria's four regions were replaced by twelve states on 27 May 1967 by the government of
questions.explanation: General Yakubu Gowon created twelve states by decree on 27 May 1967, shortly before the civil war (1967–70). General Murtala Mohammed later increased the number to 19 in 1976.

whyNot.D: Murtala Mohammed's government created 19 states in 1976.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under section 143 of the 1999 Constitution, the President is removed from office through impeachment when the report of the investigating panel is adopted by
options: not less than two-thirds of all the members of each House of the National Assembly
a simple majority of the Senate only
questions.explanation: Section 143 requires a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds majority of all the members of each House to adopt the panel's report, after which the President stands removed from office.

whyNot.D: Section 143(10) excludes the courts from impeachment proceedings.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Nigeria became a member of the United Nations in
questions.explanation: Nigeria was admitted to the UN on 7 October 1960, a week after independence on 1 October 1960, as its 99th member.

whyNot.C: 1945 is when the UN itself was founded.
whyNot.A: 1963 is the year Nigeria became a republic and the OAU was founded.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The principal judicial organ of the United Nations is the
questions.explanation: The International Court of Justice, which sits at The Hague in the Netherlands, settles legal disputes between states and gives advisory opinions.

whyNot.D: The Security Council is responsible for maintaining international peace and security, not for judging cases.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The diplomatic representative of one Commonwealth country in another Commonwealth country is known as a
questions.explanation: Commonwealth members exchange High Commissioners rather than ambassadors. A Nigerian envoy in Ghana or the UK is therefore a High Commissioner.

whyNot.B: The Secretary-General heads the Commonwealth Secretariat in London; he or she is not a country's envoy.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In Aristotle's classification of governments, the corrupt form of aristocracy is
questions.explanation: Aristotle saw oligarchy as the perversion of aristocracy, where the few rule for their own interest. Tyranny is the corrupt form of monarchy and democracy (mob rule) the corrupt form of polity.

whyNot.D: Tyranny is the corrupt form of monarchy (rule by one).

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
When the national grid failed for the third week running, the residents of Sabon Gari in Kano stopped complaining and started looking for Musa.

Two years earlier, Musa had been a secondary-school leaver with no money for university and a head full of questions about the solar panels he saw on the roofs of the rich. Instead of waiting for admission, he attached himself to an electrician on Bello Road who was willing to teach him in exchange for free labour. For eleven months he carried ladders, swept the shop and watched. He learned to test a battery, to read the small print on an inverter and, most of all, to tell a customer the truth about what a system could and could not do.

Now his own shop, painted bright yellow, was the busiest on the street. Customers liked that he never sold them more panels than they needed. "A small house does not need a big system," he would say. "It needs a careful owner." Some of his rivals called this bad business. Musa called it the reason people came back.

His mother, who had once begged him to find "a proper job", now kept his accounts.
questions.stem: Why did the residents of Sabon Gari start looking for Musa?
options: Their electricity from the national grid had failed for weeks
His shop had moved to a new street
They wanted him to teach them how to install panels
They wanted to complain about his prices
questions.explanation: The first sentence links the two events: the national grid had failed for the third week running, so people turned to Musa, who installs and repairs solar systems.

whyNot.C: Nothing in the passage says the residents wanted to learn the trade themselves.
whyNot.D: The passage says customers liked him because he did not oversell; there is no complaint about prices.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how did Musa learn his trade?
options: By working without pay for an electrician who taught him
By reading the instructions printed on inverters
By watching his rivals install solar panels
By studying electrical engineering at a university
questions.explanation: Musa had no money for university, so he worked for an electrician on Bello Road "in exchange for free labour" for eleven months, learning as he carried ladders, swept and watched.

whyNot.D: The passage says he had no money for university and did not wait for admission.
whyNot.B: Reading the small print on an inverter was one thing he learned, not how he learned the trade.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, "attached himself to" an electrician means that Musa
options: followed the electrician around without permission
was employed by the electrician on a good salary
joined the electrician as a helper in order to learn
questions.explanation: The rest of the sentence explains the phrase: the electrician taught him "in exchange for free labour". Musa joined him as an unpaid helper, which is an apprenticeship.

whyNot.C: A partner shares ownership; Musa only carried ladders and swept the shop.
whyNot.B: He worked for free labour, so he earned no salary.

questions.stem: Musa's rivals called his way of working "bad business" because he
options: charged more than other shops on the street
painted his shop a bright colour to attract attention
refused to repair systems he had not installed
sold customers fewer panels than he could have sold them
questions.explanation: The sentence just before says Musa "never sold them more panels than they needed". To rivals, turning down extra sales looked like lost profit, so they called it bad business.

whyNot.A: Prices are not mentioned anywhere in the passage.
whyNot.B: The yellow paint is a detail of description; the rivals' comment follows the point about not overselling.

questions.stem: What does the last sentence of the passage suggest about Musa's mother?
options: She has come to accept and support the work she once doubted
She was the one who taught him to keep accounts
She still wishes he had found a proper job
She has taken over the running of his shop
questions.explanation: She once begged him to find "a proper job", but now she keeps his accounts. The contrast shows that she has changed her mind and now takes part in his business.

whyNot.C: Keeping his accounts shows the opposite: she now treats his work as a proper job.
whyNot.D: Keeping the accounts is one task; the passage does not say she runs the shop.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
Every rainy season, the same scene plays out in many Nigerian cities. A heavy downpour lasts an hour, and by evening roads have become rivers, cars are abandoned and traders are bailing water out of their shops with buckets. It is tempting to blame the rain alone. Yet the rain is only part of the story.

Engineers who study urban flooding point to two other causes. The first is the steady loss of open ground. When swamps are filled and gardens are paved over, rainwater that once soaked into the soil has nowhere to go but the streets. The second cause is more embarrassing because it is entirely within our control: the drains are blocked. Plastic bottles, nylon bags and food packs thrown carelessly into gutters collect at narrow points and form dams. Water that should flow to the lagoon backs up instead.

Government can dredge canals and build wider channels, and it must. But no channel is wide enough to carry a city's rubbish as well as its rain. The monthly sanitation exercises of the past were unpopular, but they reminded every household that the gutter in front of its gate was its own responsibility. Until that sense of ownership returns, each new drain will simply be a bigger place to throw waste.
questions.stem: Which cause of flooding does the writer describe as "entirely within our control"?
questions.explanation: In paragraph 2 the writer says the second cause "is entirely within our control: the drains are blocked" by bottles, nylon bags and food packs.

whyNot.D: The writer says rain is only part of the story; nobody controls rainfall.
whyNot.A: The filling of swamps is the first cause (loss of open ground), not the one called "entirely within our control".

questions.context:

questions.stem: According to the passage, paving over gardens leads to flooding because
options: paved roads slope towards the lagoon
rainwater can no longer soak into the soil
the paving stones block the drains
questions.explanation: The passage says that when gardens are paved over, rainwater "that once soaked into the soil has nowhere to go but the streets". Less open ground means more water on the roads.

whyNot.D: Blocked drains are a separate cause, caused by rubbish, not by paving.
whyNot.B: Rubbish is linked to the drains, not to paved surfaces.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, to "dredge" canals means to
options: cover them so that rubbish cannot enter
build new walls along their sides
fill them in to create dry land
remove mud and waste from their beds to deepen them
questions.explanation: To dredge a canal is to dig out the mud, sand and waste that have settled at the bottom, so that water can flow freely. It sits beside "build wider channels" as a way to carry more water.

whyNot.C: Filling in canals would reduce drainage, the opposite of what the writer wants government to do.
whyNot.A: Covering channels is not what dredging means.

questions.stem: In the sentence "Government can dredge canals and build wider channels, and it must", the words "it must" mean that government
options: must stop households from throwing waste
must bring back the monthly sanitation exercise
must blame the rain for the floods
has a duty to dredge canals and build wider channels
questions.explanation: "It must" is short for "it must dredge canals and build wider channels". The writer agrees that this work is government's duty, before adding that it is not enough on its own.

whyNot.A: Stopping households from dumping waste is the writer's later point, not what "it must" refers to.
whyNot.B: The sanitation exercise is mentioned in the next sentences, but the writer does not say government must bring it back.

questions.context:

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the writer's main point?
options: New drains will not stop floods unless people stop dumping waste in them
Monthly sanitation exercises should be made compulsory again
Heavy rain is the main cause of urban flooding
Government alone is to blame for flooding in Nigerian cities
questions.explanation: The passage builds to its last sentence: until households take ownership of their gutters, "each new drain will simply be a bigger place to throw waste". Government work is needed, but people's habits must change too.

whyNot.D: The writer says government "must" act but places much of the blame on careless dumping.
whyNot.C: The writer says rain is "only part of the story".
whyNot.B: The writer says the exercises reminded people of their duty, but does not argue they should be compulsory again.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The principal commended the students for their DILIGENT preparation for the examination.
questions.explanation: Diligent means showing steady care and effort in one's work. The students were praised (commended), which fits hard-working preparation.

whyNot.D: Careless is close to the opposite of diligent.
whyNot.A: Hurried preparation would not usually be praised, and it does not mean diligent.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The new manager was praised for being FRUGAL with the company's funds.
questions.explanation: Frugal means using money carefully and avoiding waste. Its opposite is extravagant: spending far more than is necessary.

whyNot.B: Sparing is a synonym of frugal, not its opposite.
whyNot.D: Careful is close in meaning to frugal.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Neither the teacher nor the students ___ aware of the change in the timetable.
questions.explanation: With "neither … nor", the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it (the rule of proximity). The nearer subject is "the students", which is plural, so the verb is "were".

whyNot.A: "Was" would agree with "the teacher", but the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "the students".
whyNot.D: "Is" is singular and also in the wrong tense for this past-tense sentence.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: By the time the police arrived, the robbers ___.
questions.explanation: Two past actions are compared: the escape happened before the police arrived. The earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect tense, "had escaped".

whyNot.D: "Have escaped" is present perfect and does not fit with the past "arrived".
whyNot.C: "Will have escaped" is future perfect and points to the future, not the past.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Bola is married ___ a doctor who works at the teaching hospital.
questions.explanation: In standard English, a person is married to someone. "Married with" is a common error.

whyNot.B: "Married with" is a common error; the correct preposition is "to".

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: After failing the test, Emeka decided to BURN THE MIDNIGHT OIL before the resit. This means that Emeka decided to
questions.explanation: To burn the midnight oil is an idiom meaning to work or study until very late at night. It comes from the days when people studied by oil lamps.

whyNot.B: This takes the idiom literally; no real oil is involved.
whyNot.A: Studying late is the opposite of giving up.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words is spelt correctly? The school has no ___ for visiting athletes.
questions.explanation: Accommodation has a double c and a double m: ac-com-mo-da-tion.

whyNot.A: This has only one m; the word needs a double m.
whyNot.D: This has only one c; the word needs a double c.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following sentences uses "its" and "it's" correctly?
options: Its time the school repaired its gate.
It's time the school repaired its gate.
It's time the school repaired it's gate.
Its time the school repaired it's gate.
questions.explanation: "It's" is short for "it is", so "It's time" needs the apostrophe. "Its" is the possessive (the gate belonging to the school) and never takes an apostrophe.

whyNot.C: "It's gate" would mean "it is gate"; the possessive "its" has no apostrophe.
whyNot.A: "Its time" needs an apostrophe because it means "it is time".

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: "Had Ngozi known about the test, she would have prepared for it." This sentence means that Ngozi
options: knew about the test and prepared well
prepared even though she did not know about the test
did not know about the test, so she did not prepare
knew about the test but did not prepare
questions.explanation: "Had Ngozi known" is a past (third) conditional, the same as "If Ngozi had known". It describes something that did not happen: she did not know, and so she did not prepare.

whyNot.D: The conditional tells us she did not know about the test.
whyNot.A: "Would have prepared" shows that the preparation did not actually happen.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Everybody was at the meeting, ___?
questions.explanation: "Everybody" takes a singular verb ("was"), but in the question tag it is referred to with "they", and "they" needs "were". The main clause is positive, so the tag is negative: "weren't they?"

whyNot.A: "Everybody" includes men and women, so the tag uses "they", not "he".
whyNot.C: The main verb is "was", so the tag repeats the verb "be", not "do".

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words contains the vowel sound /ɪ/, as in "ship"?
questions.explanation: "Busy" is pronounced /ˈbɪzi/: although it is spelt with u, its stressed vowel is /ɪ/, the same as in "ship".

whyNot.D: "Sheep" has the long vowel /iː/.
whyNot.B: "Shape" has the diphthong /eɪ/.
whyNot.C: "Shop" has the vowel /ɒ/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words has the vowel sound /ɔː/, as in "caught"?
questions.explanation: In British RP, "court" is pronounced /kɔːt/, exactly like "caught". The r is not pronounced before a consonant.

whyNot.B: "Coat" has the diphthong /əʊ/.
whyNot.C: "Cot" has the short vowel /ɒ/.
whyNot.A: "Cut" has the vowel /ʌ/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words contains the diphthong /aɪ/?
questions.explanation: "Height" is pronounced /haɪt/, with the diphthong /aɪ/ as in "high". The spelling -eigh- is misleading: in the other words it gives different sounds.

whyNot.A: "Weight" is /weɪt/, with the diphthong /eɪ/.
whyNot.C: "Receipt" is /rɪˈsiːt/, with the long vowel /iː/ (and a silent p).
whyNot.D: "Eight" is /eɪt/, with /eɪ/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words begins with the consonant sound /dʒ/?
questions.explanation: "Gentle" is pronounced /ˈdʒentl/: the g before e is soft, giving /dʒ/ as in "judge".

whyNot.A: "Guest" begins with the hard /ɡ/.
whyNot.D: "Yacht" begins with /j/.
whyNot.C: "Chorus" begins with /k/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words ends with the sound /t/ when spoken?
questions.explanation: The past tense ending -ed is said as /t/ after a voiceless sound. "Look" ends in voiceless /k/, so "looked" is /lʊkt/.

whyNot.D: "Played" ends in a vowel sound, so -ed is /d/: /pleɪd/.
whyNot.A: After /t/ or /d/, -ed is /ɪd/: "wanted" is /ˈwɒntɪd/.
whyNot.C: "Beg" ends in voiced /ɡ/, so -ed is /d/: /beɡd/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: In which of the following words is the sound /ʃ/ heard?
questions.explanation: In "machine" (/məˈʃiːn/), the letters ch stand for /ʃ/, the sound in "shoe". This happens in several words borrowed from French.

whyNot.B: In "chemist", ch is said as /k/.
whyNot.D: "Cereal" begins with /s/.
whyNot.A: "Measure" has the voiced sound /ʒ/, not /ʃ/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words is stressed on the second syllable?
questions.explanation: "Examine" is pronounced ex-AM-ine, /ɪɡˈzæmɪn/, with the stress on the second syllable.

whyNot.B: "Comfort" is stressed on the first syllable: COM-fort.
whyNot.A: "Jealous" is stressed on the first syllable: JEA-lous.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words is stressed on the third syllable?
questions.explanation: "Education" is ed-u-CA-tion, /ˌedʒuˈkeɪʃn/. Words ending in -tion are stressed on the syllable just before the ending, which here is the third.

whyNot.A: "Photography" is stressed on the second syllable: pho-TOG-ra-phy.
whyNot.D: "Necessary" is stressed on the first syllable: NE-ces-sa-ry.
whyNot.B: "Comfortable" is stressed on the first syllable: COM-for-ta-ble.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem:
In the sentence below, the word in capitals carries the emphatic stress. Which question does the sentence answer?
MUSA bought the car yesterday.
options: When did Musa buy the car?
Did Musa sell the car yesterday?
questions.explanation: Emphatic stress falls on the word that carries the new or important information. Stressing MUSA answers a question about the person: who bought the car.

whyNot.C: This question would need the stress on CAR.
whyNot.A: This question would need the stress on YESTERDAY.
whyNot.B: This question would need the stress on BOUGHT, to contrast it with "sell".

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: "Where are you going?" Which intonation tune is normally used when this question is asked simply to get information?
questions.explanation: Questions that begin with a wh-word (who, what, where, when, why, how) normally take a falling tune (Tune 1) in RP when they simply ask for information. Yes/no questions are the ones that normally rise.

whyNot.B: A rising tune is normal for yes/no questions, or for a wh-question said with surprise or to ask for a repeat.
whyNot.C: A level tune is not the normal pattern for questions in English.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
Chiamaka noticed the purse only when the bus jerked to a stop at Ogui Junction in Enugu. It had slipped down between the seat and the window: a brown leather purse, heavy with something. The woman who had been sitting beside her, a trader with a basket of tomatoes, was already crossing the road.

Chiamaka hesitated. Inside, she could see a thick bundle of notes and an identity card. Her own school fees were three weeks overdue; her father had been promising to pay "by month end" for two months now. For a moment the purse felt less like a burden than an answer.

Then she remembered the trader's face: tired, sunburnt, the kind of face she saw every evening on her own mother. She jumped down from the bus, ignoring the conductor's shout, and ran. When she caught up with the woman at the edge of the market, the trader stared at the purse, then at her, and burst into tears. The money, she explained, was for her son's hospital bill.

The woman tried to press a note into Chiamaka's hand. Chiamaka refused it, but she accepted a single tomato, which she ate slowly on the long walk home.
questions.stem: Where did Chiamaka find the purse?
options: In the trader's basket of tomatoes
At the edge of the market
Between the seat and the window of the bus
On the road at Ogui Junction
questions.explanation: The passage says the purse "had slipped down between the seat and the window" of the bus.

whyNot.D: Ogui Junction is where the bus stopped, not where the purse was.
whyNot.B: The edge of the market is where Chiamaka caught up with the trader.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
Chiamaka noticed the purse only when the bus jerked to a stop at Ogui Junction in Enugu. It had slipped down between the seat and the window: a brown leather purse, heavy with something. The woman who had been sitting beside her, a trader with a basket of tomatoes, was already crossing the road.

Chiamaka hesitated. Inside, she could see a thick bundle of notes and an identity card. Her own school fees were three weeks overdue; her father had been promising to pay "by month end" for two months now. For a moment the purse felt less like a burden than an answer.

Then she remembered the trader's face: tired, sunburnt, the kind of face she saw every evening on her own mother. She jumped down from the bus, ignoring the conductor's shout, and ran. When she caught up with the woman at the edge of the market, the trader stared at the purse, then at her, and burst into tears. The money, she explained, was for her son's hospital bill.

The woman tried to press a note into Chiamaka's hand. Chiamaka refused it, but she accepted a single tomato, which she ate slowly on the long walk home.
questions.stem: "For a moment the purse felt less like a burden than an answer." This sentence shows that Chiamaka
options: knew the answer to a question in her school work
found the purse too heavy to carry
was briefly tempted to use the money to pay her school fees
wanted to give the purse to the conductor
questions.explanation: The sentence comes straight after we learn that her fees are overdue. For a moment, the money looked like an "answer" to her problem of unpaid fees, so she was tempted to keep it.

whyNot.B: "Burden" here means a troubling responsibility, not physical weight.
whyNot.A: "Answer" is used figuratively: a solution to her money problem, not to school work.

questions.stem: What finally made Chiamaka decide to return the purse?
options: The bus conductor shouted at her to return it
She was afraid that someone had seen her take it
The trader's face reminded her of her own mother
She saw the trader's identity card
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 begins "Then she remembered the trader's face" and describes it as "the kind of face she saw every evening on her own mother". This thought made her run after the woman.

whyNot.A: The conductor shouted because she jumped down from the bus; she ignored him.
whyNot.B: The passage does not mention any fear of being seen.

questions.stem: Why did the trader burst into tears?
options: She was angry that Chiamaka had opened the purse
Her tomatoes had been spoilt on the bus
Chiamaka had refused to give back the purse
The money she thought she had lost was for her son's hospital bill
questions.explanation: She explained that the money was for her son's hospital bill. Getting back money that important, after losing it, moved her to tears of relief.

whyNot.C: Chiamaka did give back the purse; that is why the trader cried.
whyNot.A: Nothing suggests anger; she tried to reward Chiamaka.

questions.stem: Chiamaka refused the money but accepted a single tomato. This suggests that she
options: was too hungry to refuse any food
wanted to sell the tomato later
did not want payment for being honest but accepted a small sign of thanks
thought the note offered was too small
questions.explanation: Taking money would have turned her honesty into a paid service. A single tomato is a small token of gratitude, and accepting it lets the trader say thank you without Chiamaka being rewarded.

whyNot.A: Nothing in the passage says she was hungry; the tomato matters as a token of thanks, not as food.
whyNot.D: She refused the note completely; she did not ask for more.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.context:
Ask a class of secondary-school students in Nigeria what they want to become, and you will hear "doctor", "engineer", "lawyer", perhaps "content creator". Very few will say "farmer". For many young people, farming means a cutlass, a hoe and a lifetime of poverty: the life their grandparents worked hard to escape.

This picture is understandable, but it is out of date. Across the country, a new kind of farmer is appearing. In Ogun State, a graduate raises catfish in tanks behind her house and sells them smoked to supermarkets. In Benue, a group of young men use a mobile phone app to learn when to plant and where to get the best price for their yams. These farmers are not escaping technology; they are using it.

None of this means farming is easy. Loans are hard to get, the roads to markets are poor, and storage is a constant worry: many of the tomatoes grown in the North rot before they reach southern cities. But these are problems to be solved, not reasons to stay away. A country that imports food it could grow is not short of opportunities; it is short of people willing to see them.
questions.stem: According to the passage, why do very few students say they want to be farmers?
options: They link farming with hard manual work and poverty
Their teachers discourage them from farming
There is no land available for young people
Farming is not taught in secondary schools
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says that for many young people "farming means a cutlass, a hoe and a lifetime of poverty", the life their grandparents tried to escape.

whyNot.C: Lack of land is not mentioned in the passage.
whyNot.B: The passage says nothing about teachers' views.

questions.stem: When the writer says "This picture is understandable, but it is out of date", the writer means that
options: photographs of farms in textbooks are old
farming was easier in the past than it is today
the old image of farming no longer matches how farming is changing
young people's career choices are understandable and correct
questions.explanation: "This picture" refers to the image of farming as cutlass, hoe and poverty. The writer accepts why people think so, but says it no longer describes the new kind of farmer described next.

whyNot.A: "Picture" is used figuratively to mean an idea or image in people's minds, not a photograph.
whyNot.D: The writer understands their view but argues it is mistaken.

questions.stem: The writer mentions the catfish farmer in Ogun State and the yam farmers in Benue to show that
options: farming is only possible in some states
fish farming pays better than yam farming
young people are farming successfully with modern methods
questions.explanation: Both examples support the claim that "a new kind of farmer is appearing": a graduate with fish tanks selling to supermarkets, and young men using a phone app. They "are not escaping technology; they are using it".

whyNot.C: The passage does not compare the profits of different kinds of farming.
whyNot.B: The example of the graduate suggests the opposite.

questions.stem: Which of the following problems facing farmers is NOT mentioned in the passage?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists three problems: loans are hard to get, roads to markets are poor, and storage is a constant worry. Rainfall is not mentioned.

whyNot.B: "Loans are hard to get" is in paragraph 3.
whyNot.C: "Storage is a constant worry" is in paragraph 3, with the example of rotting tomatoes.

questions.stem: "A country that imports food it could grow is not short of opportunities; it is short of people willing to see them." The writer is suggesting that
options: Nigeria has farming opportunities that people are failing to take
Nigeria should stop importing all food at once
only foreigners can see the opportunities in farming
Nigeria does not have enough land to grow its own food
questions.explanation: If a country imports food it could grow itself, there is room for local farmers to supply that food. The writer says the opportunity exists; what is missing is people willing to take it up.

whyNot.B: The writer criticises importing food that could be grown, but does not call for an immediate ban.
whyNot.D: "Food it could grow" means the country is able to grow it.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The witness gave a LUCID account of the accident at the junction.
questions.explanation: Lucid means clearly expressed and easy to understand. A lucid account is one that is clear.

whyNot.C: Confused is the opposite of lucid.
whyNot.A: A lucid account may be long or short; lucid is about clarity, not length.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: Halima's response to the scholarship offer was ENTHUSIASTIC.
questions.explanation: Enthusiastic means showing great interest and excitement. The opposite is indifferent: showing no interest or concern.

whyNot.D: Eager is close in meaning to enthusiastic.
whyNot.A: Grateful is a different feeling, not the opposite of enthusiastic.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: The committee ___ submitted its report to the principal.
questions.explanation: A collective noun takes a singular verb when the group acts as one unit. The pronoun "its" shows the committee is treated as one body, so the verb must be singular: "has submitted".

whyNot.D: "Have" would treat the committee as separate members, which clashes with the singular "its".
whyNot.C: "Are submitted" is not a correct verb form here, and "are" is plural.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Mathematics ___ my favourite subject.
questions.explanation: Although it ends in -s, "mathematics" is the name of one subject and takes a singular verb: "Mathematics is…". Physics, economics and news behave the same way.

whyNot.B: "Are" treats mathematics as plural because of the -s ending.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: If I ___ you, I would accept the offer.
questions.explanation: This is an imaginary (second) conditional: I am not you. Formal English uses "were" for all persons in this kind of condition: "If I were you, I would…".

whyNot.C: "Am" is used for real present conditions and does not go with "would".
whyNot.D: "Had been" belongs to the past (third) conditional, which needs "would have accepted".

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: Candidates were warned to abstain ___ examination malpractice.
questions.explanation: The verb "abstain" always takes the preposition "from": to abstain from something is to keep yourself from doing it.

whyNot.A: We warn against something, but we abstain from it.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: When Tola asked to travel to Lagos alone, her father PUT HIS FOOT DOWN. This means that her father
questions.explanation: To put one's foot down is an idiom meaning to insist firmly on something, usually by refusing to allow it.

whyNot.C: This takes the idiom literally.
whyNot.B: Agreeing is the opposite of what the idiom means.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Choose the correct spelling to complete the sentence: Please do not ___ your sister in front of her friends.
questions.explanation: Embarrass has a double r and a double s: em-bar-rass.

whyNot.A: This has only one r; the word needs a double r.
whyNot.C: This has only one s at the end; the word needs a double s.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: "Scarcely had we entered the hall when the lights went off." This sentence means that
options: the lights went off just after we entered the hall
the lights went off before we entered the hall
we entered the hall long after the lights went off
questions.explanation: "Scarcely … when" shows that one action happened immediately after another. We had only just entered when the lights went off.

whyNot.C: We were already inside when the lights went off.
whyNot.A: "Scarcely" here means "only just", not "rarely".

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: "The man who lives next door is a doctor." The words "who lives next door" form
questions.explanation: "Who lives next door" has its own verb (lives), so it is a clause. It describes the noun "man", telling us which man, so it does the work of an adjective: an adjectival (relative) clause.

whyNot.C: A noun clause would act as subject or object of the sentence; this one describes a noun.
whyNot.A: It identifies the man rather than telling us where an action happened.
whyNot.D: It cannot stand alone; the main clause is "The man is a doctor".

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words contains the vowel sound /ʊ/, as in "put"?
questions.explanation: "Woman" is pronounced /ˈwʊmən/: the o in the first syllable is said as the short /ʊ/ in "put".

whyNot.A: "Moon" has the long vowel /uː/.
whyNot.D: "Mud" has the vowel /ʌ/.
whyNot.C: "Mould" has the diphthong /əʊ/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words contains the vowel sound /ʌ/, as in "cup"?
questions.explanation: "Country" is pronounced /ˈkʌntri/: the ou spelling here gives /ʌ/, as in "cup".

whyNot.C: "County" is /ˈkaʊnti/, with the diphthong /aʊ/.
whyNot.B: "Court" has /ɔː/.
whyNot.A: "Cart" has /ɑː/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words has the same vowel sound as "hair"?
questions.explanation: "Hair" is /heə/ and "their" is /ðeə/: both have the diphthong /eə/.

whyNot.D: "Here" has the diphthong /ɪə/.
whyNot.A: "Hire" has /aɪə/.
whyNot.B: "Her" has the long vowel /ɜː/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words contains the vowel sound /ɑː/?
questions.explanation: "Heart" is pronounced /hɑːt/, with the long open vowel /ɑː/ as in "car". In RP the r is silent.

whyNot.B: "Hurt" has /ɜː/.
whyNot.A: "Hat" has the short /æ/.
whyNot.C: "Hot" has /ɒ/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words contains the consonant sound /ð/?
questions.explanation: "Breathe" (the verb) is /briːð/ and ends in the voiced /ð/, as in "this". The noun "breath" ends in the voiceless /θ/.

whyNot.A: "Breath" (the noun) is /breθ/, with voiceless /θ/.
whyNot.D: "Thank" begins with voiceless /θ/.
whyNot.B: "Teeth" ends with voiceless /θ/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: In which of the following words is the letter "b" silent?
questions.explanation: "Debt" is pronounced /det/: the b is not sounded. The same is true of "doubt", "climb" and "thumb".

whyNot.C: In "rubber" the b is sounded: /ˈrʌbə/.
whyNot.A: Both b's in "bulb" are sounded.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words is stressed on the first syllable?
questions.explanation: "Colleague" is pronounced COL-league, /ˈkɒliːɡ/, with the stress on the first syllable.

whyNot.D: "Career" is stressed on the second syllable: ca-REER.
whyNot.B: "Canal" is stressed on the second syllable: ca-NAL.
whyNot.C: "Cement" is stressed on the second syllable: ce-MENT.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: In which of the following words does the main stress fall on the second syllable?
questions.explanation: "Photographer" is pho-TOG-ra-pher, /fəˈtɒɡrəfə/. Adding -er moves the stress from the first syllable of "photograph" to the second.

whyNot.B: "Photograph" is stressed on the first syllable: PHO-to-graph.
whyNot.A: "Photographic" is stressed on the third syllable: pho-to-GRAPH-ic.
whyNot.C: "Telephone" is stressed on the first syllable: TE-le-phone.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: Which of the following words rhymes with "flood"?
questions.explanation: "Flood" is /flʌd/ and "mud" is /mʌd/: both end in /ʌd/, so they rhyme, even though the spellings differ.

whyNot.B: "Food" is /fuːd/, with the long vowel /uː/.
whyNot.D: "Good" is /ɡʊd/, with /ʊ/.

questions.subject: english-language
questions.stem: "Is the library open today?" Which intonation tune is normally used when this question is asked simply to get a yes or no answer?
questions.explanation: Questions that can be answered with yes or no normally end with a rising tune (Tune 2) in RP. Wh-questions and statements normally take a falling tune.

whyNot.A: A falling tune is normal for statements and wh-questions, not neutral yes/no questions.
whyNot.C: A level tune is not the normal pattern for questions in English.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Convert 43 (base ten) to a number in base two.
questions.explanation: Divide by 2 repeatedly and read the remainders from the bottom up: 43 ÷ 2 = 21 r 1, 21 ÷ 2 = 10 r 1, 10 ÷ 2 = 5 r 0, 5 ÷ 2 = 2 r 1, 2 ÷ 2 = 1 r 0, 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r 1. Reading upwards gives 101011₂ (32 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 43).

whyNot.A: 110101₂ is the correct digits read in the wrong order (top to bottom); it equals 53.
whyNot.D: 101101₂ equals 45, not 43.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Express 72 as a product of its prime factors in index form.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Evaluate log₂ 32 + log₃ 27 − log₅ 25.
questions.explanation: Write each number as a power of its base: 32 = 2⁵, so log₂ 32 = 5; 27 = 3³, so log₃ 27 = 3; 25 = 5², so log₅ 25 = 2. The value is 5 + 3 − 2 = 6.

whyNot.A: 10 comes from adding all three logarithms instead of subtracting the last one.
whyNot.D: 4 comes from subtracting log₃ 27 and adding log₅ 25 (mixing up the signs).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Simplify √50 − √18 + √8.

whyNot.C: 2√2 comes from subtracting √8 as well instead of adding it.
whyNot.B: Surds cannot be added by adding the numbers under the root sign: √50 − √18 + √8 is not √(50 − 18 + 8).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Mrs Okafor saves ₦50,000 in a bank at 8% per annum compound interest. Find the interest earned after 2 years.

whyNot.B: ₦8,000 is simple interest (50,000 × 8 × 2 ÷ 100); compound interest also earns interest on the first year's interest.
whyNot.D: ₦58,320 is the total amount in the account, not the interest.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Find the value of x if 23ₓ = 32₅.
questions.explanation: Change both sides to base ten. 32₅ = 3 × 5 + 2 = 17. 23ₓ = 2 × x + 3 = 2x + 3. So 2x + 3 = 17, giving 2x = 14 and x = 7. Check: 23₇ = 14 + 3 = 17.

whyNot.B: With x = 6, 23₆ = 15, not 17.
whyNot.C: x cannot be 5: then 23₅ = 13, and 32₅ is 17.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Solve the equation 5(x − 2) = 3x + 4.
questions.explanation: Expand the bracket: 5x − 10 = 3x + 4. Collect like terms: 5x − 3x = 4 + 10, so 2x = 14 and x = 7. Check: 5(7 − 2) = 25 and 3(7) + 4 = 25.

whyNot.A: x = 3 comes from multiplying only the x by 5 (5x − 2 = 3x + 4).
whyNot.D: x = −3 comes from a sign error when moving −10 across the equals sign.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Solve the simultaneous equations 2x + 3y = 12 and x − y = 1.
questions.explanation: From x − y = 1, x = y + 1. Substitute into the first equation: 2(y + 1) + 3y = 12, so 5y + 2 = 12, 5y = 10 and y = 2. Then x = 2 + 1 = 3. Check: 2(3) + 3(2) = 12 and 3 − 2 = 1.

whyNot.C: x = 2, y = 3 gives 2(2) + 3(3) = 13 and x − y = −1; the values are swapped.
whyNot.B: x = 4, y = 3 satisfies x − y = 1 but gives 2(4) + 3(3) = 17, not 12.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: y varies inversely as the square of x. When x = 3, y = 8. Find y when x = 6.

whyNot.A: 4 treats y as varying inversely as x (not x²): doubling x would only halve y.
whyNot.D: 32 treats y as varying directly as x².

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Find the range of values of x for which −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 9.
questions.explanation: Subtract 1 from all three parts: −4 < 2x ≤ 8. Divide all three parts by 2 (a positive number, so the signs stay the same): −2 < x ≤ 4.

whyNot.A: −1 < x ≤ 5 comes from adding 1 instead of subtracting it.
whyNot.D: The inequality signs must stay as they were: < on the left and ≤ on the right.
whyNot.C: −4 < x ≤ 8 stops before dividing by 2.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Find the sum of the first five terms of the geometric progression 2, 6, 18, …

whyNot.C: 162 is the fifth term (2 × 3⁴), not the sum of five terms.
whyNot.B: 486 is 2 × 3⁵, the sixth term of the progression.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Find the positive value of k for which the equation x² + kx + 16 = 0 has equal roots.
questions.explanation: A quadratic ax² + bx + c = 0 has equal roots when b² − 4ac = 0. Here k² − 4(1)(16) = 0, so k² = 64 and k = ±8. The positive value is 8. Check: x² + 8x + 16 = (x + 4)².

whyNot.D: 4 is √16; it comes from forgetting the factor 4 in b² − 4ac.
whyNot.C: 64 is k², not k.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Find the area of a sector of a circle of radius 14 cm which subtends an angle of 45° at the centre. (Take π = 22/7.)

whyNot.D: 154 cm² is the area for a 90° sector (a quarter of the circle).
whyNot.B: 11 cm is the arc length of the sector, (45/360) × 2πr, not its area.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: An overhead water tank in Kano is a cuboid 2 m long, 1.5 m wide and 1 m deep. How many litres of water does it hold when full? (1 m³ = 1000 litres)
questions.explanation: Volume = length × width × depth = 2 × 1.5 × 1 = 3 m³. Since 1 m³ = 1000 litres, the tank holds 3 × 1000 = 3 000 litres.

whyNot.A: 300 litres comes from multiplying by 100 instead of 1000.
whyNot.B: 4 500 litres multiplies the 3 m³ by 1.5 a second time.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Find the length of the arc of a sector of radius 7 cm whose angle at the centre is 120°. (Take π = 22/7.)

whyNot.C: 29⅓ cm uses the diameter in place of the radius, doubling the answer.
whyNot.B: 51⅓ cm² is the area of the sector, (1/3) × πr², not the arc length.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Find the total surface area of a closed cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. (Take π = 22/7.)
questions.explanation: Total surface area = curved surface + two circular ends = 2πrh + 2πr² = 2πr(h + r) = 2 × (22/7) × 7 × (10 + 7) = 44 × 17 = 748 cm².

whyNot.D: 440 cm² is only the curved surface (2πrh).
whyNot.A: 594 cm² counts only one circular end; a closed cylinder has two.
whyNot.C: 1540 cm³ is the volume, πr²h.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: A solid sphere has radius 21 cm. Find its volume. (Take π = 22/7.)

whyNot.D: 5 544 cm² is the surface area, 4πr², not the volume.
whyNot.C: 9 702 cm³ is (1/3)πr³: the factor 4 has been left out.
whyNot.B: 29 106 cm³ is πr³: the whole factor 4/3 has been left out.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: A sector of a circle of radius 10 cm with angle 216° at the centre is folded to form a cone, with the two straight edges joined. Find the radius of the base of the cone.
questions.explanation: The arc of the sector becomes the circumference of the cone's base. Arc length = (216/360) × 2π × 10 = 12π cm. So 2πr = 12π, giving r = 6 cm. (The radius of the sector, 10 cm, becomes the slant height.)

whyNot.B: 8 cm is the vertical height of the cone, √(10² − 6²), not the base radius.
whyNot.D: 3.6 cm comes from dividing 216 by 60 instead of using the arc-length formula.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Find the size of each interior angle of a regular octagon.
questions.explanation: The sum of interior angles of an n-sided polygon is (n − 2) × 180°. For an octagon, (8 − 2) × 180° = 1080°. Each of the 8 equal angles is 1080° ÷ 8 = 135°. (Or: exterior angle = 360° ÷ 8 = 45°, so interior = 180° − 45° = 135°.)

whyNot.B: 45° is each exterior angle of a regular octagon.
whyNot.A: 120° is the interior angle of a regular hexagon.
whyNot.C: 1080° is the sum of all eight interior angles.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: In a circle with centre O, an arc PQ subtends an angle of 110° at O. R is a point on the major arc. Find angle PRQ.
questions.explanation: The angle which an arc subtends at the centre is twice the angle it subtends at any point on the remaining part of the circumference. So angle PRQ = 110° ÷ 2 = 55°.

whyNot.B: 110° is the angle at the centre, not at the circumference.
whyNot.A: 125° (180° − 55°) is the angle at a point on the minor arc.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: The bearing of village P from village Q is 065°. What is the bearing of Q from P?
questions.explanation: The back bearing differs from the bearing by 180°. Since 065° is less than 180°, add 180°: 065° + 180° = 245°.

whyNot.B: 115° is 180° − 065°; back bearings are found by adding or subtracting 180°, not subtracting from 180°.
whyNot.D: 295° is 360° − 065°, which reflects the direction instead of reversing it.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral. Angle PQR = 3x and angle PSR = x + 40°. Find x.
questions.explanation: Q and S are opposite vertices of the cyclic quadrilateral, so their angles add up to 180°: 3x + x + 40° = 180°. Then 4x = 140° and x = 35°. (Angle PQR = 105° and angle PSR = 75°.)

whyNot.D: 20° comes from setting the two angles equal (3x = x + 40°); opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, not equal.
whyNot.C: 45° comes from forgetting the 40° (4x = 180°).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: From the top of a vertical cliff 40 m high, the angle of depression of a boat on the sea is 30°. How far is the boat from the foot of the cliff?
questions.explanation: The angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation of the top from the boat, 30°. In the right-angled triangle, tan 30° = 40 / d, so d = 40 / tan 30° = 40 ÷ (1/√3) = 40√3 m (about 69.3 m).

whyNot.C: (40√3)/3 m comes from multiplying 40 by tan 30° instead of dividing by it.
whyNot.A: 20 m is 40 sin 30°, which uses the wrong ratio.
whyNot.B: 80 m is 40 ÷ sin 30°, the line-of-sight distance from the top of the cliff to the boat.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: In triangle ABC, a = 3 cm, b = 5 cm and angle C = 120°. Find the length of side c.
questions.explanation: Use the cosine rule: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C = 9 + 25 − 2(3)(5)cos 120°. Since cos 120° = −½, c² = 34 − 30(−½) = 34 + 15 = 49, so c = 7 cm.

whyNot.C: √19 cm comes from taking cos 120° as +½ instead of −½.
whyNot.D: √34 cm leaves out the −2ab cos C term, as if the angle were 90°.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: A letter is chosen at random from the word MATHEMATICS. What is the probability that it is M?
questions.explanation: MATHEMATICS has 11 letters, and M appears twice. Probability = number of Ms ÷ total letters = 2/11.

whyNot.A: 1/11 counts only one M; the word has two.
whyNot.B: 1/4 = 2/8 divides by the 8 different letters instead of all 11 letters in the word.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: In a pie chart showing the monthly spending of a family in Ibadan, food is represented by a sector of 135°. If the family spends ₦80,000 a month in all, how much is spent on food?
questions.explanation: The whole pie chart (360°) stands for ₦80,000. The food sector is 135/360 of it: (135/360) × 80,000 = (3/8) × 80,000 = ₦30,000.

whyNot.D: ₦13,500 multiplies 135 by 100 and does not use the total of ₦80,000.
whyNot.C: ₦27,000 divides by 400 instead of 360.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: The mean of the numbers 12, 15, 9, 18 and x is 13. Find x.
questions.explanation: Mean = sum ÷ number of values, so the sum of the five numbers is 13 × 5 = 65. The known numbers add up to 12 + 15 + 9 + 18 = 54. So x = 65 − 54 = 11.

whyNot.D: 13 is the mean itself; x does not have to equal the mean.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Two fair dice are thrown together. What is the probability that the sum of the two numbers is 7?
questions.explanation: There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes. A sum of 7 comes from (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2) and (6,1): 6 outcomes. Probability = 6/36 = 1/6.

whyNot.C: 7/36 assumes the number of ways equals the sum; there are only 6 ways to get 7.
whyNot.A: 1/12 counts (1,6) and (6,1) and so on as the same outcome, giving only 3 ways.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.context:
The scores of 20 pupils in a short quiz are shown in the table.
Score: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Number of pupils: 3, 5, 7, 4, 1
questions.stem: Find the median score.
questions.explanation: There are 20 scores, so the median is the average of the 10th and 11th scores in order. The cumulative frequencies are 3, 8, 15, 19, 20. The 9th to 15th scores are all 3, so the 10th and 11th are both 3 and the median is 3.

whyNot.A: 2.75 is the mean score (55 ÷ 20), not the median.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: A bag contains 5 red and 3 green balls. Two balls are taken out one after the other without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.explanation: P(first red) = 5/8. One red ball has gone, so 4 red remain out of 7: P(second red) = 4/7. P(both red) = 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14.

whyNot.A: 25/64 = (5/8)² treats the draws as with replacement.
whyNot.C: 15/28 is the probability of one red and one green (in either order).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Convert 1213₄ to a number in base ten.
questions.explanation: Multiply each digit by its place value in base four: 1 × 4³ + 2 × 4² + 1 × 4 + 3 × 1 = 64 + 32 + 4 + 3 = 103.

whyNot.C: 183 treats the number as base five (125 + 50 + 5 + 3).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Evaluate 3⁻² × 9^½.

whyNot.D: 3 is 9^½ alone; the factor 3⁻² = 1/9 has been ignored.
whyNot.B: 1/27 takes 9^½ as 1/3 instead of 3.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Chinedu measured the length of a rod as 4.8 cm. The actual length is 5.0 cm. Find the percentage error in his measurement.
questions.explanation: Error = 5.0 − 4.8 = 0.2 cm. Percentage error = (error ÷ actual value) × 100% = (0.2 ÷ 5.0) × 100% = 4%.

whyNot.D: 4.17% divides the error by the measured value (4.8) instead of the actual value (5.0).
whyNot.C: 0.2 is the error in cm, not the percentage error.
whyNot.A: 96% is the measured value as a percentage of the actual value.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: At what rate of simple interest per annum will ₦15,000 earn ₦3,600 interest in 4 years?

whyNot.D: 24% is the total interest over 4 years as a percentage of ₦15,000; it must be divided by 4 to get the yearly rate.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Solve log₁₀(x + 2) + log₁₀ 5 = 2.
questions.explanation: Use log a + log b = log ab: log₁₀ 5(x + 2) = 2. So 5(x + 2) = 10² = 100, x + 2 = 20 and x = 18.

whyNot.B: 20 is the value of x + 2, not x.
whyNot.A: 98 comes from ignoring log₁₀ 5 and solving x + 2 = 100.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Rationalise the denominator of 6/(√5 − √2).

whyNot.A: The conjugate of √5 − √2 is √5 + √2, so the numerator becomes 6(√5 + √2), not 6(√5 − √2).
whyNot.C: 6√5 + 6√2 forgets to divide by 5 − 2 = 3.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Simplify (x² − 9)/(x + 3).
questions.explanation: x² − 9 is a difference of two squares: x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3). Then (x − 3)(x + 3)/(x + 3) = x − 3 (for x ≠ −3).

whyNot.D: Cancelling (x + 3) leaves the other factor, x − 3, not x + 3.
whyNot.C: x − 9 wrongly cancels x² with x and 3 with 3 term by term.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: If x = 2 is a root of the equation x² + px − 10 = 0, find the value of p.
questions.explanation: Substitute x = 2: 2² + 2p − 10 = 0, so 4 + 2p − 10 = 0, 2p = 6 and p = 3. Check: x² + 3x − 10 = (x + 5)(x − 2), which has root 2.

whyNot.B: −3 comes from a sign error when moving −6 across the equals sign.
whyNot.D: 7 comes from taking 4 + 10 = 2p, treating −10 as +10.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Solve the equation 3x² − 5x − 2 = 0.
questions.explanation: Factorise: 3x² − 5x − 2 = 3x² − 6x + x − 2 = 3x(x − 2) + 1(x − 2) = (3x + 1)(x − 2). So 3x + 1 = 0 or x − 2 = 0, giving x = −1/3 or x = 2.

whyNot.C: x = −2 or x = 1/3 has both signs wrong; these are the roots of 3x² + 5x − 2 = 0.
whyNot.B: The product of the roots is c/a = −2/3, so one root must be negative.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: The 3rd term of an arithmetic progression is 11 and the 7th term is 27. Find the 10th term.
questions.explanation: Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d. So a + 2d = 11 and a + 6d = 27. Subtracting, 4d = 16 and d = 4; then a = 11 − 8 = 3. T₁₀ = a + 9d = 3 + 36 = 39.

whyNot.C: 43 uses a + 10d instead of a + 9d.
whyNot.B: 35 is the 9th term, a + 8d.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: P varies directly as Q and inversely as R. When Q = 4 and R = 2, P = 6. Find P when Q = 9 and R = 3.
questions.explanation: P = kQ/R. Using P = 6, Q = 4, R = 2: 6 = 4k/2 = 2k, so k = 3. Then P = 3 × 9/3 = 9.

whyNot.A: 4 comes from taking P as varying directly as R and inversely as Q (P = kR/Q), the reverse of the statement.
whyNot.C: 27 forgets to divide by R = 3.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: If x + y = 5 and xy = 6, find the value of x² + y².
questions.explanation: (x + y)² = x² + 2xy + y², so x² + y² = (x + y)² − 2xy = 5² − 2(6) = 25 − 12 = 13. (Check: x = 2, y = 3 gives 4 + 9 = 13.)

whyNot.C: 25 is (x + y)²; (x + y)² is not equal to x² + y².
whyNot.A: 37 adds 2xy instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Find the circumference of a circular tray of diameter 14 cm. (Take π = 22/7.)
questions.explanation: Circumference = πd = (22/7) × 14 = 44 cm. (Equivalently 2πr with r = 7 cm.)

whyNot.B: 88 cm uses 2π × 14, treating the diameter as the radius.
whyNot.C: 154 cm² is the area of the tray, πr², not its circumference.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: A square-based pyramid has base edge 6 cm and vertical height 10 cm. Find its volume.
questions.explanation: Volume of a pyramid = ⅓ × base area × height = ⅓ × (6 × 6) × 10 = ⅓ × 360 = 120 cm³.

whyNot.C: 360 cm³ is the volume of a cuboid on the same base; the ⅓ has been left out.
whyNot.A: 180 cm³ uses ½ instead of ⅓.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Find the area of triangle PQR in which PQ = 8 cm, PR = 10 cm and angle QPR = 30°.
questions.explanation: Area = ½ × PQ × PR × sin P = ½ × 8 × 10 × sin 30° = ½ × 80 × ½ = 20 cm².

whyNot.A: 40 cm² leaves out the ½ in the formula.
whyNot.D: 20√3 cm² uses cos 30° (or sin 60°) instead of sin 30°.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Find the volume of a hemisphere of radius 3 cm. Leave your answer in terms of π.
questions.explanation: A hemisphere is half a sphere: V = ½ × (4/3)πr³ = (2/3)πr³ = (2/3) × π × 27 = 18π cm³.

whyNot.A: 36π cm³ is the volume of the whole sphere.
whyNot.D: 27π cm³ is πr³, leaving out the fraction 2/3.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: A cone has base radius 6 cm and vertical height 8 cm. Find its curved surface area. Leave your answer in terms of π.
questions.explanation: First find the slant height: l = √(r² + h²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 cm. Curved surface area = πrl = π × 6 × 10 = 60π cm².

whyNot.B: 48π cm² uses the vertical height (π × 6 × 8) instead of the slant height.
whyNot.D: 96π cm² is the total surface area, which adds the base area 36π.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: A chord of a circle of radius 14 cm subtends an angle of 90° at the centre. Find the area of the minor segment cut off by the chord. (Take π = 22/7.)
questions.explanation: Area of segment = area of sector − area of triangle. Sector = (90/360) × (22/7) × 14² = ¼ × 616 = 154 cm². Triangle = ½ × 14 × 14 × sin 90° = 98 cm². Segment = 154 − 98 = 56 cm².

whyNot.D: 154 cm² is the area of the whole sector, before the triangle is taken away.
whyNot.A: 98 cm² is the area of the triangle formed by the chord and the two radii.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. Find the largest angle.
questions.explanation: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. The ratio has 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 parts, so one part is 180° ÷ 9 = 20°. The largest angle is 4 × 20° = 80°.

whyNot.A: 60° is the middle angle (3 parts).
whyNot.D: 40° is the smallest angle (2 parts).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: If cos θ = 5/13 and θ is an acute angle, find sin θ.
questions.explanation: Draw a right-angled triangle with adjacent side 5 and hypotenuse 13. The opposite side is √(13² − 5²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12. So sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse = 12/13.

whyNot.A: 5/12 is adjacent/opposite, which is cot θ.
whyNot.C: 12/5 is opposite/adjacent, which is tan θ.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: A point is 30 m from the foot of a vertical mast on level ground. The angle of elevation of the top of the mast from the point is 30°. Find the height of the mast.

whyNot.D: 30√3 m divides 30 by tan 30° instead of multiplying.
whyNot.B: 15 m uses sin 30° instead of tan 30°.
whyNot.C: 15√3 m uses cos 30° and also treats 30 m as the slant distance.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: A and B are points on a circle with centre O. The tangent to the circle at A makes an angle of 58° with the chord AB. Find angle AOB, where AOB is the angle at the centre facing the minor arc AB.
questions.explanation: The radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent, so angle OAB = 90° − 58° = 32°. Triangle OAB is isosceles (OA = OB), so angle OBA = 32° too. Angle AOB = 180° − 32° − 32° = 116°. (This agrees with the alternate segment theorem: the angle at the circumference is 58°, and the angle at the centre is twice that.)

whyNot.B: 58° is the angle subtended by AB at the circumference in the alternate segment, not at the centre.
whyNot.D: 122° is 180° − 58°, which is not a rule for the angle at the centre.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: In triangle ABC, angle A = 30°, angle B = 45° and side a = 8 cm. Find side b.
questions.explanation: Use the sine rule: a/sin A = b/sin B. So b = a sin B / sin A = 8 × sin 45° ÷ sin 30° = 8 × (√2/2) ÷ (1/2) = 8√2 cm (about 11.3 cm).

whyNot.C: 4√2 cm multiplies by sin 45° but forgets to divide by sin 30°.
whyNot.D: 16 cm divides 8 by sin 30° but forgets to multiply by sin 45°.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Emeka walks 5 km due north from a junction and then 12 km due east. Find the bearing of his final position from the junction, correct to the nearest degree.
questions.explanation: The bearing is measured clockwise from north. In the right-angled triangle, tan θ = east distance ÷ north distance = 12/5 = 2.4, so θ = 67.4° ≈ 67°. The bearing is 067°. (He is 13 km from the junction.)

whyNot.D: 023° uses tan θ = 5/12, measuring the angle from east instead of from north.
whyNot.B: 247° is the bearing of the junction from his final position (the back bearing).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: The probability that it rains in Jos on a particular day is 0.35. What is the probability that it does not rain on that day?
questions.explanation: An event and its complement have probabilities that add up to 1. P(no rain) = 1 − P(rain) = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65.

whyNot.C: 0.75 is a subtraction slip: 1 − 0.35 is 0.65.
whyNot.B: A probability can never be greater than 1; 1.35 adds instead of subtracting.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: The ages, in years, of six pupils are 11, 13, 12, 14, 13 and 15. Find their mean age.
questions.explanation: Mean = sum ÷ number of pupils = (11 + 13 + 12 + 14 + 13 + 15) ÷ 6 = 78 ÷ 6 = 13 years.

whyNot.A: 15.6 years divides the total 78 by 5 instead of by the 6 pupils.
whyNot.D: 4 years is the range (15 − 11), a measure of spread, not the mean.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: The mean of five numbers is 13. When a sixth number is added, the mean becomes 14. Find the sixth number.
questions.explanation: The five numbers add up to 5 × 13 = 65. The six numbers add up to 6 × 14 = 84. So the sixth number is 84 − 65 = 19.

whyNot.C: 14 is the new mean; the added number must be larger than 14 to pull the mean up by 1.
whyNot.D: 1 is the change in the mean, not the new number.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Thirty cards are numbered 1 to 30. One card is picked at random. What is the probability that the number on it is a prime number?
questions.explanation: The prime numbers from 1 to 30 are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 and 29: there are 10 of them. Probability = 10/30 = 1/3.

whyNot.D: 11/30 wrongly counts 1 as a prime number; a prime has exactly two factors, and 1 has only one.
whyNot.A: 3/10 misses one prime, usually 2 (the only even prime).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: Find the standard deviation of the numbers 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.
questions.explanation: Mean = 30 ÷ 5 = 6. Deviations from the mean: −4, −2, 0, 2, 4; their squares: 16, 4, 0, 4, 16, which add up to 40. Variance = 40 ÷ 5 = 8. Standard deviation = √8 = 2√2 (about 2.83).

whyNot.C: 8 is the variance; the standard deviation is its square root.
whyNot.B: √10 divides the sum of squares by 4 (n − 1) instead of by n = 5.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.stem: The probability that Ada passes an examination is 2/3 and the probability that Bola passes it is 3/5. The two events are independent. Find the probability that only one of them passes.
questions.explanation: Only one passes means (Ada passes and Bola fails) or (Ada fails and Bola passes). P = (2/3)(2/5) + (1/3)(3/5) = 4/15 + 3/15 = 7/15.

whyNot.B: 2/5 = (2/3)(3/5) is the probability that both pass.
whyNot.A: 13/15 is the probability that at least one passes (1 − 2/15).
whyNot.D: 2/15 = (1/3)(2/5) is the probability that neither passes.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A micrometer screw gauge has a thimble scale on which each division is 0.01 mm. The sleeve (main scale) reading is 5.5 mm and the 23rd thimble division lines up with the reference line. What is the reading of the gauge?
questions.explanation: Reading = sleeve reading + (thimble division × value of one division). Thimble part = 23 × 0.01 mm = 0.23 mm. Reading = 5.5 mm + 0.23 mm = 5.73 mm.

whyNot.A: 5.523 mm treats each thimble division as 0.001 mm instead of 0.01 mm.
whyNot.C: 5.23 mm drops the half-millimetre shown on the sleeve; the sleeve reads 5.5 mm, not 5.0 mm.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A ripe mango falls from rest from a branch 5 m above the ground. How long does it take to reach the ground? (g = 10 m s⁻², ignore air resistance)
questions.explanation: The mango starts from rest, so h = ½gt². Then t² = 2h ÷ g = (2 × 5) ÷ 10 = 1, so t = 1.0 s.

whyNot.B: 0.5 s is h ÷ g with the square root also left out; the correct working is t = √(2h/g).
whyNot.C: 0.71 s is √(h/g); it forgets the 2 that comes from the ½ in h = ½gt².

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A woman whose weight is 600 N stands on the heel of one shoe. The area of the heel in contact with the floor is 2 cm². What pressure does she exert on the floor?
questions.explanation: Pressure = force ÷ area. Convert the area to m²: 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m², so 2 cm² = 2 × 10⁻⁴ m². Pressure = 600 ÷ (2 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.0 × 10⁶ Pa.

whyNot.B: 3.0 × 10⁴ Pa comes from converting 2 cm² to 2 × 10⁻² m²; since 1 cm = 10⁻² m, 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m².
whyNot.D: 300 Pa divides 600 by 2 without converting cm² to m².
whyNot.C: 1.2 × 10³ multiplies force by area; pressure is force divided by area.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A bus moves at a steady 20 m s⁻¹ for 10 s. The driver then brakes and the bus slows down uniformly, coming to rest 4 s later. What total distance does the bus cover?
questions.explanation: Distance = area under the velocity–time graph. Steady part: 20 × 10 = 200 m. Braking part (a triangle): ½ × 20 × 4 = 40 m. Total = 200 + 40 = 240 m.

whyNot.D: 280 m treats the braking part as a rectangle (20 × 4 = 80 m); the speed falls to zero, so the area is a triangle.
whyNot.A: 200 m counts only the steady part and leaves out the distance covered while braking.
whyNot.C: 40 m is only the braking distance.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A box of mass 5 kg rests on a rough horizontal floor. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the box and the floor is 0.4. A horizontal force of 30 N pulls the box along the floor. What is the acceleration of the box? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation: Normal reaction R = mg = 5 × 10 = 50 N. Friction F = μR = 0.4 × 50 = 20 N. Net force = 30 − 20 = 10 N. Acceleration a = net force ÷ mass = 10 ÷ 5 = 2.0 m s⁻².

whyNot.D: 6.0 m s⁻² is 30 ÷ 5; it ignores friction, which opposes the motion.
whyNot.B: 4.0 m s⁻² is 20 ÷ 5; it uses the friction force as if it were the net force.
whyNot.C: 10 m s⁻² adds friction to the pull; friction acts against the motion, so it must be subtracted.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A solid object weighs 50 N in air and 30 N when it is completely immersed in water. What is the relative density of the material of the object?
questions.explanation: Upthrust = loss in weight = 50 − 30 = 20 N, which equals the weight of water displaced (an equal volume of water). Relative density = weight in air ÷ weight of equal volume of water = 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5.

whyNot.C: 1.7 is 50 ÷ 30; you must divide by the loss in weight (the upthrust), not by the weight in water.
whyNot.B: 0.6 is 30 ÷ 50; it is upside down, and a solid that sinks in water must have a relative density greater than 1.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Metals are much better conductors of heat than wood mainly because metals
options: expand more than wood when heated
have higher melting points than wood
contain free electrons that carry energy quickly through them
questions.explanation: In a metal, some electrons are free to move through the whole lattice. When one end is heated these free electrons gain kinetic energy and quickly carry it to cooler parts, in addition to the slower passing on of vibrations between atoms. Wood has no free electrons, so it conducts heat poorly.

whyNot.A: Density does not decide conduction; some dense non-metals are poor conductors.
whyNot.C: A high melting point does not make a material conduct heat well; many ceramics melt at very high temperatures but are insulators.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: The mercury thread of an unmarked thermometer is 4.0 cm long when the bulb is in melting ice and 24.0 cm long in steam above water boiling at standard pressure. When the bulb is placed in a liquid, the thread is 12.0 cm long. What is the temperature of the liquid?
questions.explanation: θ = (L − L₀) ÷ (L₁₀₀ − L₀) × 100 °C, where L₀ is the length at the ice point and L₁₀₀ at the steam point. θ = (12.0 − 4.0) ÷ (24.0 − 4.0) × 100 = 8 ÷ 20 × 100 = 40 °C.

whyNot.C: 50 °C is 12 ÷ 24 × 100; it forgets that the thread is already 4.0 cm long at 0 °C.
whyNot.A: 60 °C measures down from the steam point, (24 − 12) ÷ 20 × 100, instead of up from the ice point.
whyNot.B: 33 °C is 8 ÷ 24 × 100; the fundamental interval is 24 − 4 = 20 cm, not 24 cm.

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: 2000 J of heat is supplied to a 0.5 kg block of copper. By how much does its temperature rise? (specific heat capacity of copper = 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)

whyNot.C: 5 K is 2000 ÷ 400; it leaves out the mass of the block.
