the age of the mother at the time of fertilisation
whether the sperm that fertilises the egg carries an X or a Y chromosome
questions.explanation: A woman is XX, so every egg carries an X chromosome. A man is XY, so half his sperm carry X and half carry Y. An X sperm gives a girl (XX) and a Y sperm gives a boy (XY).

whyNot.B: Eggs always carry an X chromosome; they never carry a Y.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The forelimbs of a human, a bat and a whale are used for different jobs, yet they have the same basic arrangement of bones. Which kind of evidence for evolution does this provide?
questions.explanation: Comparing body structures of different organisms is comparative anatomy. Limbs built on the same plan but used for different purposes are homologous structures, suggesting that these animals came from a common ancestor.

whyNot.C: Fossil records are remains of organisms preserved in rocks, not the comparison of living animals' bones.
whyNot.B: Comparative embryology compares how embryos develop, not adult limb bones.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A child with Down's syndrome has 47 chromosomes in each body cell instead of 46. What causes this?
options: A change in the gene for haemoglobin
Two copies of a recessive allele from the parents
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome is a chromosome mutation. When chromosome 21 fails to separate during meiosis, a gamete gets an extra copy, so the child has three copies of chromosome 21 and 47 chromosomes in all.

whyNot.C: A missing X chromosome would give 45 chromosomes (Turner's syndrome), not 47.
whyNot.B: Inheriting two recessive alleles does not change the number of chromosomes.
whyNot.A: A change in the haemoglobin gene causes sickle-cell anaemia, with a normal chromosome number.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant over dwarf (t). A tall plant of unknown genotype is crossed with a dwarf plant, and all 120 offspring are tall. What is the genotype of the tall parent?
options: Either TT or Tt, as the result cannot tell them apart
questions.explanation: This is a test cross. The dwarf parent (tt) can only give t. If the tall parent were Tt, about half the offspring would be dwarf (tt). Since all 120 are tall, the tall parent can only give T, so it is homozygous TT.

whyNot.B: Tt × tt would give about 60 tall and 60 dwarf offspring.
whyNot.D: A tt plant would be dwarf, not tall.
whyNot.C: With 120 offspring and not one dwarf, Tt is ruled out, so the cross does tell them apart.

questions.subject: biology
questions.context: A specimen collected from under a rock in a school garden has a body in two parts: a joined head and thorax (cephalothorax) and an abdomen. It has four pairs of jointed walking legs and no antennae.
questions.stem: To which class of arthropods does the specimen belong?
questions.explanation: Two body parts (cephalothorax and abdomen), four pairs of legs and no antennae are the features of arachnids, such as spiders and scorpions.

whyNot.B: Insects have three body parts, three pairs of legs and one pair of antennae.
whyNot.A: Crustaceans such as crabs and prawns have two pairs of antennae.
whyNot.D: Myriapods such as millipedes have many body segments, each with legs.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: What is the function of the lateral line found along each side of a fish such as tilapia?
options: Controlling the fish's depth in the water
Detecting vibrations and pressure changes in the water
questions.explanation: The lateral line is a sense organ: a canal with sensory cells that detect vibrations and pressure changes in the water. It helps the fish sense prey, predators and obstacles, even in muddy water.

whyNot.D: Oxygen is absorbed by the gills.
whyNot.B: Depth is controlled mainly by the swim bladder.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which of the following organisms is prokaryotic, with no true nucleus?
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes: their DNA lies free in the cytoplasm and is not enclosed by a nuclear membrane. Amoeba, yeast and Spirogyra are all eukaryotes with a true nucleus.

whyNot.C: Yeast is a fungus, and fungi are eukaryotes with a true nucleus.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In a fern, the familiar leafy plant whose fronds carry brown spore-producing sori on their lower surface is the
questions.explanation: Ferns show alternation of generations. The large leafy fern plant is the diploid sporophyte; its sori make spores. A spore grows into a small heart-shaped prothallus, which is the gametophyte that makes the gametes.

whyNot.A: The gametophyte in ferns is the small prothallus, not the leafy plant.
whyNot.D: The prothallus is the gametophyte; it does not bear sori.
whyNot.C: A protonema is the thread-like early stage of a moss, not part of a fern.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which pair of features is found only in mammals?
options: Hair on the skin and mammary glands
A constant body temperature and lungs
questions.explanation: Only mammals have hair and mammary glands that make milk to feed their young. The other features are also found in other groups, such as birds and reptiles.

whyNot.C: Birds also have a four-chambered heart and lungs.
whyNot.B: Reptiles and birds also have internal fertilisation and a backbone.
whyNot.D: Birds also keep a constant body temperature and breathe with lungs.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In the scientific name of the human being, Homo sapiens, the word Homo is the name of the
questions.explanation: In binomial nomenclature, the first name (written with a capital letter) is the genus and the second (small letter) is the specific name. Together they name the species.

whyNot.D: The species is named by both words together; sapiens alone is the specific name.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In which organelle of a green plant cell does photosynthesis take place?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll, which traps light energy. They use this energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.

whyNot.C: The mitochondrion releases energy by respiration; it does not make food.
whyNot.D: Ribosomes make proteins.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The cell membrane is described as partially (selectively) permeable. This means that it
options: lets no molecules pass through at all
lets substances pass in but not out
lets some molecules pass through but not others
lets all molecules pass through freely
questions.explanation: A partially permeable membrane allows small molecules such as water and oxygen to pass through, but holds back larger molecules such as proteins. This lets the cell control what enters and leaves.

whyNot.D: A fully permeable barrier, like the cellulose cell wall, lets most substances through.
whyNot.B: Substances such as carbon dioxide and urea also pass out of cells through the membrane.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which event takes place in meiosis but not in mitosis?
questions.explanation: In the first division of meiosis, homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange pieces in crossing over. This mixes alleles and gives variation. DNA replication, spindle formation and separation of chromatids happen in both kinds of division.

whyNot.B: DNA is copied before mitosis as well as before meiosis.
whyNot.C: Sister chromatids separate in anaphase of mitosis and also in the second division of meiosis.
whyNot.D: A spindle forms in both mitosis and meiosis.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A student heats a sample of pawpaw juice with Benedict's solution, and a brick-red precipitate forms. What does this show?
options: A reducing sugar such as glucose is present
questions.explanation: Benedict's solution is blue. When heated with a reducing sugar such as glucose or fructose, it changes through green and yellow to a brick-red precipitate.

whyNot.B: Starch is tested with iodine solution, which turns blue-black.
whyNot.C: Protein is tested with the biuret test, which turns purple.
whyNot.D: Fat is tested with the ethanol (emulsion) test or the grease-spot test.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A single cell in a laboratory culture divides by mitosis every 20 minutes, and every new cell does the same. How many cells will there be after 2 hours?
questions.explanation: 2 hours = 120 minutes, which is 120 ÷ 20 = 6 divisions. The number doubles at each division: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32 → 64, that is 2⁶ = 64 cells.

whyNot.C: 12 is 6 × 2; the cell number doubles each time, so it must be 2⁶, not 6 × 2.
whyNot.D: 32 is the number after only 5 divisions (100 minutes).
whyNot.B: 128 would need 7 divisions (140 minutes).

questions.subject: biology
questions.context: An electron micrograph of an animal cell is described as follows. A large round body near the centre is surrounded by a double membrane with pores. Inside this body is a smaller, darker, round region labelled Q, which has no membrane of its own.
questions.stem: What is the main function of the region labelled Q?
questions.explanation: The large body with a double, porous membrane is the nucleus, and the small dark region inside it is the nucleolus. The nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosomes, which then pass out through the nuclear pores.

whyNot.D: Respiration happens in mitochondria, which lie in the cytoplasm.
whyNot.A: Digestion of worn-out organelles is done by lysosomes.
whyNot.B: Packaging proteins for secretion is the job of the Golgi body.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The elbow joint lets the forearm move up and down in one plane only. What type of joint is it?
questions.explanation: A hinge joint, like the hinge of a door, allows movement in one plane only. The elbow and the knee are hinge joints.

whyNot.B: A ball and socket joint, such as the shoulder, allows movement in many directions.
whyNot.C: A pivot joint allows rotation, as between the first two vertebrae of the neck.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. What is its main role in digestion?
options: It breaks large fat droplets into tiny droplets (emulsification)
It digests proteins into amino acids
It absorbs digested fat into the blood
questions.explanation: Bile contains bile salts but no digestive enzymes. The bile salts break fats into tiny droplets, giving a much larger surface area for lipase to act on. Bile is also alkaline, which helps neutralise acid from the stomach.

whyNot.C: Protein digestion is done by enzymes such as pepsin and trypsin.
whyNot.A: Starch is digested by amylase.
whyNot.D: Digested fat is absorbed into the lacteals of the villi, not by bile.

questions.subject: biology
questions.context: A diagram of a section through the human eye shows a layer at the back of the eye, labelled P, that contains rods and cones. Part of the back of the eye, labelled Q, is the point where the optic nerve leaves the eyeball; Q has no rods or cones.
questions.stem: What is the part labelled Q?
questions.explanation: The point where the optic nerve leaves the eye has no light-sensitive cells, so an image falling on it cannot be seen. It is called the blind spot. P is the retina.

whyNot.B: The yellow spot (fovea) is packed with cones and gives the sharpest vision.
whyNot.A: The choroid is the dark layer behind the retina that supplies blood and stops reflection.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: During photosynthesis in a cassava leaf, what is the source of the oxygen gas that is released?
questions.explanation: In the light stage, light energy absorbed by chlorophyll splits water molecules (photolysis) into hydrogen and oxygen. The oxygen is released as a by-product, while the hydrogen is used to reduce carbon dioxide to sugar.

whyNot.A: The oxygen from carbon dioxide ends up in the glucose that is made, not in the oxygen gas.
whyNot.B: Chlorophyll absorbs light; it is not broken down to give oxygen.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: A student at rest breathes in 500 cm³ of air at each breath and takes 16 breaths per minute. What volume of air does he breathe in per minute?
questions.explanation: Volume per minute = volume per breath × breaths per minute = 500 cm³ × 16 = 8 000 cm³. Since 1 dm³ = 1 000 cm³, this is 8 dm³.

whyNot.D: 0.8 dm³ is a unit slip: 8 000 cm³ is 8 dm³.
whyNot.B: 516 cm³ is 500 + 16; the two values must be multiplied.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which hormone, released by the pituitary gland, causes a mature follicle in the ovary to release an egg (ovulation)?
questions.explanation: Around the middle of the menstrual cycle there is a sharp rise in luteinising hormone (LH) from the pituitary gland. This surge causes the follicle to burst and release the egg.

whyNot.A: Progesterone is made by the corpus luteum after ovulation and keeps the uterus lining ready.
whyNot.D: Oestrogen repairs the uterus lining and helps trigger the LH surge, but LH itself causes ovulation.

questions.subject: biology
questions.context:
Part of a food web in the Nigerian savanna:
• Grass is eaten by grasshoppers, grasscutters and antelopes.
• Grasshoppers are eaten by lizards.
• Lizards are eaten by snakes.
• Grasscutters are eaten by snakes.
• Antelopes are eaten by lions.
questions.stem: Which organism in this food web is both a secondary consumer and a tertiary consumer?
questions.explanation: When the snake eats a grasscutter (a primary consumer), it is a secondary consumer. When it eats a lizard (itself a secondary consumer), the snake is a tertiary consumer. So it feeds at two levels.

whyNot.B: The lizard eats only grasshoppers, so it is only a secondary consumer.
whyNot.A: The lion eats only antelopes, so it is only a secondary consumer.
whyNot.C: The grasscutter eats grass, so it is a primary consumer.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In the nitrogen cycle, the conversion of nitrates in the soil into nitrogen gas by some bacteria is called
questions.explanation: Denitrifying bacteria, which thrive in waterlogged soils with little oxygen, break down nitrates and release nitrogen gas back into the air. This makes the soil less fertile.

whyNot.D: Nitrification is the change of ammonium compounds to nitrites and then nitrates.
whyNot.A: Nitrogen fixation turns nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds, the opposite direction.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which vegetation zone of Nigeria is found in the far north-east around Lake Chad, with the lowest rainfall in the country and short, scattered grasses and thorny shrubs?
questions.explanation: The Sahel savanna lies in the extreme north-east of Nigeria near Lake Chad. It has a very long dry season and little rain, so the plants are short, sparse grasses and drought-resistant thorny shrubs.

whyNot.D: The Guinea savanna has tall grasses and lies in the Middle Belt, with much more rain.
whyNot.C: The rainforest is in the wet south of the country.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which instrument is used to measure wind speed in an ecological study?
questions.explanation: An anemometer has small cups that spin in the wind; the faster they spin, the greater the wind speed.

whyNot.B: A wind vane shows the direction of the wind, not its speed.
whyNot.D: A hygrometer measures relative humidity.
whyNot.C: A Secchi disc measures how clear (turbid) water is.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Large trees such as the silk-cotton tree in Nigeria's rainforest often have broad buttress roots spreading out from the base of the trunk. What is the main advantage of these roots?
options: They take in oxygen from waterlogged mud
They support the tall tree in shallow forest soil
They store water for the dry season
They protect the trunk from bush fires
questions.explanation: Rainforest soils are often shallow, and the trees are very tall. Buttress roots spread wide around the base of the trunk and act like props, keeping the tree steady in strong winds.

whyNot.C: Water storage is an adaptation of plants in dry areas, such as the baobab.
whyNot.A: Taking in oxygen from mud is done by the breathing roots (pneumatophores) of mangroves.
whyNot.D: Fire protection by thick bark is an adaptation of savanna trees.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Sulphur dioxide released when fossil fuels are burned dissolves in rainwater. This form of pollution is known as
questions.explanation: Sulphur dioxide (and oxides of nitrogen) dissolve in rainwater to form acids. This acid rain damages leaves, makes soils and lakes acidic, harms aquatic life and corrodes buildings.

whyNot.A: Eutrophication is caused by excess nutrients, such as fertiliser, entering water.
whyNot.D: Thermal pollution is the release of hot water, for example from factories, into rivers.
whyNot.C: Ozone depletion is caused mainly by CFCs, not by sulphur dioxide.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In some cattle, red coat (RR) and white coat (WW) are codominant, so heterozygous (RW) cattle are roan, with mixed red and white hairs. If roan cattle are mated with roan cattle and 80 calves are born, how many of the calves are expected to be roan?
questions.explanation: RW × RW gives RR : RW : WW in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1. With codominance each genotype has its own appearance: 1 red : 2 roan : 1 white. Roan = 2/4 = 1/2 of 80 = 40.

whyNot.D: 20 is the expected number of red calves, or of white calves (1/4 of 80).
whyNot.A: 60 would be the 3/4 expected if one colour were dominant, but here neither allele is dominant.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Why is the sickle-cell allele (HbS) more common in people in malaria areas such as Nigeria than in places with no malaria?
options: People with genotype HbSS are fully protected from malaria and are healthy
Mosquitoes bite people with the HbS allele less often
Malaria parasites change the HbA allele into the HbS allele
People with genotype HbAS are more resistant to severe malaria, so they survive and pass on the allele
questions.explanation: Carriers (HbAS) are healthy and are more likely to survive severe malaria than HbAA people. More of them live to have children, so natural selection keeps the HbS allele common where malaria is common. This is called heterozygote advantage.

whyNot.C: Mutations are not caused by malaria parasites; the allele is inherited.
whyNot.A: HbSS people have sickle-cell anaemia, a serious illness.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which of the following conditions is inherited as a sex-linked trait in humans?
questions.explanation: The gene for a blood-clotting factor lies on the X chromosome, so haemophilia is sex-linked. It is much more common in males, who have only one X chromosome.

whyNot.A: The sickle-cell gene lies on an autosome, not on a sex chromosome.
whyNot.D: Albinism is controlled by an allele on an autosome.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: In a sample of double-stranded DNA, 30% of the bases are adenine. What percentage of the bases are guanine?
questions.explanation: Adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine, so A = T and G = C. A = 30%, so T = 30%, making 60%. The remaining 40% is shared equally between G and C, so guanine = 20%.

whyNot.C: 30% is the percentage of thymine, which pairs with adenine.
whyNot.B: 40% is guanine and cytosine together.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Remains or traces of organisms that lived long ago, preserved in rocks, are called
questions.explanation: Fossils such as bones, shells, footprints and leaf prints preserved in rock layers show how living things have changed over time. They are an important evidence of evolution.

whyNot.A: Vestigial organs are reduced organs in living organisms, such as the human appendix.
whyNot.D: Homologous structures are organs with the same basic plan in living organisms.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Which of these human characteristics shows discontinuous variation?
questions.explanation: Discontinuous variation puts people into a few clear groups with no in-between forms. A person is blood group A, B, AB or O, nothing in between. Height, mass and skin colour vary gradually across a range.

whyNot.C: Height varies continuously over a range of values.
whyNot.B: Skin colour shows many shades, so it is continuous variation.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: An earthworm has a long body divided into many ring-like segments, with a swollen band called the clitellum. To which phylum does it belong?
questions.explanation: Annelids are segmented worms. The earthworm's body is made of many similar segments, and the clitellum is used in reproduction.

whyNot.A: Nematodes (roundworms) such as Ascaris are not segmented.
whyNot.C: Platyhelminthes are flatworms such as tapeworms and liver flukes.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: The giant African land snail, often eaten in southern Nigeria, belongs to the phylum
questions.explanation: Snails are molluscs: they have a soft, unsegmented body, a muscular foot for movement and usually a hard shell.

whyNot.B: Arthropods have jointed legs and an exoskeleton, which snails lack.
whyNot.C: Echinoderms such as starfish live only in the sea and have spiny skin.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Rhizopus (black bread mould) grows on stale bread. How does it reproduce asexually?
questions.explanation: Rhizopus grows upright hyphae with round heads called sporangia. Many spores form inside each sporangium; when it bursts, the light spores are carried by air to new food, where they germinate.

whyNot.B: Budding is the usual asexual method in yeast.
whyNot.D: Binary fission is how bacteria and Amoeba reproduce.

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Birds such as the hornbill have hollow bones containing air spaces. How does this help them?
options: It keeps the body warm at night
It helps the bird float on water
It stores food for the breeding season
It makes the skeleton light for flight
questions.explanation: Hollow bones with air spaces are strong but light. A light body needs less energy to lift into the air, which is an adaptation for flight.

whyNot.A: Body warmth is kept mainly by feathers, which trap air.

questions.subject: biology
questions.context:
A dichotomous key to four animals:
1a. Legs absent ........................ Python
1b. Legs present ........................ go to 2
2a. Body covered with feathers ........ Hornbill
2b. Body not covered with feathers .... go to 3
3a. Skin dry and covered with scales .. Agama lizard
3b. Skin moist, without scales ........ Toad
questions.stem: A student catches an animal on the school farm. It has four legs, no feathers, and moist skin without scales. Using the key, which animal is it?
questions.explanation: Start at 1: legs are present, so go to 2. At 2 the body has no feathers, so go to 3. At 3 the skin is moist without scales, so the key leads to the toad.

whyNot.A: The agama lizard has dry, scaly skin (3a).
whyNot.D: The hornbill is covered with feathers (2a).

questions.subject: biology
questions.stem: Viruses are often said to be on the border between living and non-living things. Which observation best supports this?
options: They are made of many cells, but they cannot move
They can reproduce only inside living cells, but outside them they can be crystallised like chemicals
They have a nucleus, but no cell membrane
They make their own food, but they do not respire
questions.explanation: Inside a host cell a virus uses the cell to make copies of itself, a feature of living things. Outside cells it shows no life processes at all and can even be crystallised and stored like a chemical.

whyNot.A: Viruses are not made of cells at all.
whyNot.D: Viruses cannot make food; they depend on host cells.
whyNot.C: Viruses have no nucleus; they are just nucleic acid in a protein coat.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following factors of production is a free gift of nature?
questions.explanation: Land covers all natural resources (soil, minerals, rivers, forests) that are not made by man. It is called a free gift of nature, and its reward is rent.

whyNot.A: Capital is man-made, such as machines and buildings.
whyNot.D: Labour is human effort, physical or mental, not a gift of nature.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A list of a person's unsatisfied wants arranged in order of importance is called a
questions.explanation: Because resources are scarce, a rational person ranks wants from the most pressing to the least. This ranking is the scale of preference, and it guides choice.

whyNot.B: A demand schedule shows quantities demanded at different prices, not a ranking of wants.
whyNot.C: A budget line shows combinations of goods a given income can buy.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A provision seller in Ibadan recorded her sales for five days as ₦4,000, ₦6,000, ₦5,000, ₦7,000 and ₦8,000. What were her mean daily sales?

whyNot.A: ₦5,000 is the middle figure as written (the third day), not the mean.
whyNot.D: ₦30,000 is the total for five days, not the daily mean.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Chinedu, a trained tailor, leaves tailoring to become a secondary school teacher. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Occupational mobility of labour is the ease with which a worker moves from one job or occupation to another. Chinedu changed his occupation, not his location.

whyNot.A: Geographical mobility is moving from one place to another, for example from Kano to Lagos.
whyNot.C: Division of labour is splitting a production process into separate tasks.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A production possibility curve that is concave (bowed outward) to the origin shows that
options: the economy has some unemployed resources
the opportunity cost of both goods is constant
the opportunity cost of a good rises as more of it is produced
resources are equally suited to producing both goods
questions.explanation: Resources are not equally suited to every use. As more of one good is produced, resources less suited to it must be moved over, so ever larger amounts of the other good are given up. This rising opportunity cost bends the curve outward.

whyNot.B: Constant opportunity cost gives a straight-line curve.
whyNot.D: If resources were equally suited to both goods, the opportunity cost would be constant and the curve straight.
whyNot.A: Unemployed resources are shown by a point inside the curve, not by its shape.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A major disadvantage of a centrally planned (command) economy is that
options: prices are set entirely by market forces
income is very unequally distributed by private profit
consumers have little freedom of choice
there is too much competition among firms
questions.explanation: In a command economy the state decides what, how and for whom to produce. Consumers must largely accept what the planners provide, so their freedom of choice is limited, and planning often becomes slow and bureaucratic.

whyNot.D: Heavy competition is a feature of a free-market economy, not a planned one.
whyNot.A: Prices in a command economy are fixed by the planning authority, not by market forces.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A fall in the price of a commodity itself, other things being equal, leads to
options: an extension of demand along the same demand curve
an outward shift of the demand curve
an inward shift of the demand curve
a contraction of demand along the same demand curve
questions.explanation: A change in the commodity's own price causes a movement along the demand curve. A fall in price raises quantity demanded, which is called an extension of demand. Shifts of the curve are caused by other factors such as income or tastes.

whyNot.B: An outward shift comes from changes in factors other than the good's own price, such as higher income.
whyNot.D: A contraction of demand follows a rise in price, not a fall.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Goods that are demanded together to satisfy a single want, such as a car and petrol, are said to be in
questions.explanation: Joint (complementary) demand exists when two goods are used together, so a change in the price of one affects the demand for the other in the opposite direction.

whyNot.A: Competitive demand applies to substitutes, such as beef and fish.
whyNot.B: Derived demand is demand for something because of the demand for another product it helps to make, such as labour for building.
whyNot.C: Composite demand is when one good is demanded for several different uses.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: When a household's monthly income rises from ₦20,000 to ₦25,000, its demand for rice rises from 40 kg to 60 kg. What is the income elasticity of demand for rice?
questions.explanation: Income elasticity = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income. % change in quantity = 20 ÷ 40 × 100 = 50%. % change in income = 5,000 ÷ 20,000 × 100 = 25%. Income elasticity = 50 ÷ 25 = 2. It is positive, so rice is a normal good for this household.

whyNot.B: 0.5 comes from dividing the % change in income by the % change in quantity (the formula upside down).
whyNot.A: 20 is the change in quantity in kg, not an elasticity.

questions.subject: economics
questions.context:
The table shows the market demand and supply schedules for a commodity.
Price (₦) | Quantity demanded | Quantity supplied
100 | 900 | 100
200 | 700 | 300
300 | 500 | 500
400 | 300 | 700
500 | 100 | 900
questions.stem: If the government fixes a maximum price of ₦200 for the commodity, what is the resulting shortage?
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is at ₦300, where 500 units are demanded and supplied. A maximum price of ₦200 is below equilibrium, so at ₦200 quantity demanded is 700 and quantity supplied is 300. Shortage = 700 − 300 = 400 units.

whyNot.A: 200 units is the fall in quantity supplied from equilibrium (500 − 300), only part of the gap.
whyNot.C: 700 units is the quantity demanded at ₦200, not the shortage.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following would shift the supply curve of tomatoes to the left?
options: An improvement in the method of growing tomatoes
A fall in the cost of fertiliser
A pest attack that destroys many tomato farms
A rise in the price of tomatoes
questions.explanation: A leftward shift means less is supplied at every price. A pest attack reduces the amount farmers can offer at any price, so supply decreases and the curve shifts left.

whyNot.D: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the supply curve, not a shift.
whyNot.A: Better methods raise supply, shifting the curve to the right.
whyNot.B: Cheaper fertiliser lowers costs and raises supply, shifting the curve to the right.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A shoe seller cuts the price of a pair of slippers from ₦200 to ₦150, and her weekly sales rise from 100 to 160 pairs. What is the price elasticity of demand (using the original price and quantity), and what happens to her total revenue?
questions.explanation: % change in quantity = 60 ÷ 100 × 100 = 60%. % change in price = 50 ÷ 200 × 100 = 25%. Elasticity = 60 ÷ 25 = 2.4 (elastic). Total revenue before = 200 × 100 = ₦20,000; after = 150 × 160 = ₦24,000. Because demand is elastic, the price cut raises total revenue by ₦4,000.

whyNot.A: With elastic demand a price cut raises total revenue; here it goes from ₦20,000 to ₦24,000.
whyNot.D: 0.42 is the formula upside down (25 ÷ 60).
whyNot.B: 0.6 is only the proportional change in quantity, not divided by the change in price.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A cost that changes directly with the level of a firm's output is called
questions.explanation: Variable costs, such as raw materials and wages of casual workers, rise when output rises and fall when output falls. They are zero when nothing is produced.

whyNot.C: Fixed costs, such as rent, stay the same whatever the output in the short run.
whyNot.D: Overhead cost is another name for fixed (indirect) cost.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A pure water producer in Enugu sells 200 bags a day at ₦50 per bag. Her total cost for the day is ₦7,500. What is her profit for the day?
questions.explanation: Total revenue = price × quantity = 50 × 200 = ₦10,000. Profit = total revenue − total cost = 10,000 − 7,500 = ₦2,500.

whyNot.A: ₦10,000 is total revenue, before cost is taken away.
whyNot.B: ₦12,500 comes from adding cost to revenue instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: economics
questions.context:
The table shows a firm's short-run total cost (TC) at different levels of output.
Output (units) | TC (₦)
0 | 100
1 | 150
2 | 190
3 | 220
4 | 260
5 | 320
questions.stem: What is the firm's average fixed cost when it produces 4 units?
questions.explanation: Total fixed cost is the cost at zero output, ₦100, because nothing variable is used then. Average fixed cost = TFC ÷ output = 100 ÷ 4 = ₦25.

whyNot.D: ₦65 is average total cost at 4 units (260 ÷ 4).
whyNot.B: ₦40 is the marginal cost of the 4th unit (260 − 220), and also the average variable cost (160 ÷ 4).
whyNot.C: ₦100 is total fixed cost, not the average per unit.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The extent to which division of labour can be practised is limited mainly by the
questions.explanation: Splitting production into many specialised tasks pays only when output is large. If the market for the product is small, a firm cannot sell enough to justify a high degree of specialisation.

whyNot.B: The number of owners does not decide how far tasks can be split.
whyNot.C: Interest rates affect borrowing costs, not the scope for specialisation.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: When a firm grows so large that management becomes difficult and its long-run average cost begins to rise, it is experiencing
options: diminishing returns in the short run
questions.explanation: Diseconomies of scale are the disadvantages of growing too large, such as poor coordination and slow decisions. They make long-run average cost rise as the scale of production increases.

whyNot.A: Economies of scale make long-run average cost fall, not rise.
whyNot.B: Diminishing returns are a short-run idea, with at least one factor fixed; this question is about the scale of the whole firm.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A monopolist can practise price discrimination successfully only if
options: the product has many close substitutes
the markets can be kept separate and have different elasticities of demand
the goods can easily be resold from the cheap market to the dear one
buyers in all markets have the same elasticity of demand
questions.explanation: Price discrimination means charging different prices for the same product. It works only if buyers cannot resell between markets (the markets are separated) and demand elasticities differ, so the firm can charge more where demand is less elastic.

whyNot.A: With many close substitutes the firm is not a monopolist and cannot raise price in any market.
whyNot.D: With identical elasticities there is no gain from charging different prices.
whyNot.C: Easy resale would let buyers in the cheap market sell to the dear market, ending the price difference.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The function of money that allows a trader to buy goods now and pay for them later is
questions.explanation: As a standard of deferred payment, money is used to state and settle debts that will be paid in the future, so credit transactions become possible.

whyNot.D: Medium of exchange refers to money being accepted in payment at the time of purchase.
whyNot.C: Unit of account means money measures the value of goods.
whyNot.B: Store of value means money can be saved to keep wealth over time.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: In Nigeria, the body mainly responsible for regulating and developing the capital market is the
questions.explanation: The SEC is the apex regulator of Nigeria's capital market. It registers securities and market operators, supervises exchanges and protects investors.

whyNot.D: The NDIC insures bank deposits and supervises banks alongside the CBN; it does not regulate the capital market.
whyNot.C: The CBN regulates banks and the money supply, not the capital market.
whyNot.A: FIRS collects federal taxes.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Using the quantity theory of money MV = PT, if the money supply is ₦4,000, the price level is ₦8 and the volume of transactions is 2,500, what is the velocity of circulation?
questions.explanation: From MV = PT, V = PT ÷ M. PT = 8 × 2,500 = 20,000. V = 20,000 ÷ 4,000 = 5. Each naira changes hands five times in the period.

whyNot.D: 0.2 is M ÷ PT, the formula upside down.
whyNot.C: 500 comes from dividing M by P (4,000 ÷ 8) and ignores T.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A fresh cash deposit of ₦10,000 enters the banking system. If the Central Bank of Nigeria raises the cash reserve ratio from 10% to 20%, the maximum total deposits that can be created from this deposit
questions.explanation: Maximum total deposits = initial deposit ÷ cash reserve ratio. At 10%: 10,000 ÷ 0.10 = ₦100,000. At 20%: 10,000 ÷ 0.20 = ₦50,000. A higher reserve ratio reduces banks' ability to create credit.

whyNot.C: A higher reserve ratio reduces, not increases, credit creation.
whyNot.A: ₦90,000 and ₦40,000 are the new loans (total deposits minus the initial ₦10,000), not total deposits.
whyNot.D: ₦80,000 wrongly treats the reserve ratio as a simple deduction of 20% from ₦100,000.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A sharp rise in the pump price of diesel raises transport and production costs, and firms pass these on as higher prices. This is
questions.explanation: Cost-push inflation occurs when rising costs of production (fuel, wages, raw materials) push up the general price level, even without a rise in demand.

whyNot.B: Demand-pull inflation comes from too much spending (demand) chasing too few goods, not from higher costs.
whyNot.D: Deflation is a persistent fall in the general price level.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A Treasury bill issued by the Central Bank of Nigeria on behalf of the Federal Government is
options: a cheque drawn on the Treasury's account
a bank note used to pay government workers
a long-term company share traded on the stock exchange
a short-term government security traded in the money market
questions.explanation: A Treasury bill is a short-term (usually up to one year) debt instrument through which government borrows. It is bought and sold in the money market, where short-term funds are lent and borrowed.

whyNot.C: Company shares are long-term securities dealt with in the capital market.
whyNot.B: A Treasury bill is a borrowing instrument, not currency.

questions.subject: economics
questions.context:
Expenditure figures for a country in one year (₦ billion):
Consumption (C) | 500
Investment (I) | 150
Government spending (G) | 200
Exports (X) | 120
Imports (M) | 170
questions.stem: Using the expenditure approach, what is the country's GDP?
questions.explanation: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M) = 500 + 150 + 200 + (120 − 170) = 850 − 50 = ₦800 billion. Imports are subtracted because they are spending on goods produced abroad.

whyNot.D: ₦970 billion adds exports but forgets to subtract imports.
whyNot.B: ₦1,140 billion adds imports instead of subtracting them.
whyNot.C: ₦850 billion leaves out net exports altogether.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Compared with a base year, a country's index of export prices is now 110 and its index of import prices is 88. What are its terms of trade, and are they favourable?
questions.explanation: Terms of trade = (index of export prices ÷ index of import prices) × 100 = 110 ÷ 88 × 100 = 125. A figure above 100 means each unit of exports now buys more imports than in the base year, so the terms of trade are favourable.

whyNot.C: 80 is the import index divided by the export index, the formula upside down.
whyNot.A: A value above 100 is favourable, not unfavourable.
whyNot.D: 22 is the difference between the indices, not their ratio.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Nigeria is a member of OPEC. The members of this organisation are
options: countries of the West African sub-region
questions.explanation: OPEC (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) is made up of oil-exporting countries that coordinate their petroleum policies, including production levels. Nigeria is a member because crude oil is its main export.

whyNot.A: The West African grouping is ECOWAS, not OPEC.
whyNot.C: Former British colonies belong to the Commonwealth.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The balance of trade of a country is the difference between the value of its
options: total receipts and total payments abroad
questions.explanation: The balance of trade covers only goods (visible items). It is visible exports minus visible imports. Services and other items are added to give the wider balance of payments.

whyNot.D: Invisible items (services) are part of the current account but not the balance of trade.
whyNot.A: All receipts and payments abroad make up the balance of payments, not just the balance of trade.
whyNot.C: Capital flows are recorded in the capital (financial) account.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: If the naira is devalued, the most likely immediate effect is that Nigeria's
options: exports become cheaper to foreign buyers and imports dearer at home
imports and exports both become cheaper in naira
terms of trade improve and imports rise
exports become dearer to foreign buyers and imports cheaper at home
questions.explanation: Devaluation lowers the value of the naira against other currencies. Foreign buyers need less of their own currency to buy Nigerian goods, so exports become cheaper to them, while Nigerians must pay more naira for imports.

whyNot.D: This describes a rise (revaluation) in the naira's value, the opposite of devaluation.
whyNot.C: Devaluation usually worsens the terms of trade and is meant to reduce imports, not raise them.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A farmer sells wheat to a miller for ₦100. The miller makes flour and sells it to a baker for ₦250. The baker sells the bread to consumers for ₦400. Using the value-added method, how much does this chain add to national output?
questions.explanation: Value added at each stage = sales − cost of inputs bought from other firms. Farmer: 100 − 0 = 100. Miller: 250 − 100 = 150. Baker: 400 − 250 = 150. Total = 100 + 150 + 150 = ₦400, the value of the final product. This avoids double counting.

whyNot.A: ₦750 adds all the sales together, which counts the wheat and flour more than once (double counting).
whyNot.B: ₦650 adds the miller's and baker's sales, still double counting the flour.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Economic goods are goods that
options: are scarce and therefore command a price
are provided free by nature in unlimited amounts
are consumed only by the rich
are produced only by the government
questions.explanation: An economic good is limited in supply relative to the demand for it, so people must pay to obtain it. Its scarcity is what gives it a price.

whyNot.B: Goods available in unlimited amounts without payment, like air, are free goods.
whyNot.D: Economic goods can be produced by private firms as well as by government.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The reward for labour as a factor of production is
questions.explanation: Each factor of production earns a reward: land earns rent, labour earns wages (or salaries), capital earns interest and the entrepreneur earns profit.

whyNot.A: Rent is the reward for land.
whyNot.D: Interest is the reward for capital.
whyNot.C: Profit is the reward for the entrepreneur.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The numbers of cartons of eggs sold by a poultry farm on six days were 12, 7, 15, 9, 10 and 18. What is the median?
questions.explanation: Arrange the data in order: 7, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18. With six (an even number of) items, the median is the average of the 3rd and 4th: (10 + 12) ÷ 2 = 11.

whyNot.D: 12 is the average of the two middle numbers in the unsorted list (15 and 9); the data must be arranged in order first.
whyNot.B: About 11.8 is the mean (71 ÷ 6), not the median.
whyNot.C: 10 is only the 3rd item; with an even number of items you average the two middle ones.

questions.subject: economics
questions.context:
Production possibilities of a small economy:
Combination | Rice (bags) | Beans (bags)
A | 0 | 40
B | 10 | 36
C | 20 | 28
D | 30 | 16
E | 40 | 0
questions.stem: What is the opportunity cost of each extra bag of rice when the economy moves from combination B to combination C?
questions.explanation: Moving from B to C, rice rises by 20 − 10 = 10 bags and beans fall by 36 − 28 = 8 bags. Opportunity cost per extra bag of rice = 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8 bag of beans.

whyNot.C: 1.25 is 10 ÷ 8, the cost of a bag of beans measured in rice, the wrong way round.
whyNot.D: 8 bags is the total beans given up for 10 bags of rice, not the cost per bag.
whyNot.A: 2.8 is 28 ÷ 10, using the level of beans at C instead of the change.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to raise the efficiency of labour in a factory?
questions.explanation: Efficiency of labour is the output a worker can produce in a given time. Training improves skill, so each worker produces more and better output.

whyNot.A: Long hours without rest cause fatigue, which lowers efficiency.
whyNot.B: Lower wages tend to reduce morale and effort.
whyNot.C: Old machines usually lower, not raise, output per worker.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: In economics, capital as a factor of production refers to
options: money kept in a savings account
natural resources such as land and minerals
man-made goods used to produce other goods
the skill of the owner of a business
questions.explanation: Capital means produced means of production, such as machines, tools, vehicles and buildings, which are used to make other goods and services. Its reward is interest.

whyNot.A: Money saved is a financial asset; in economics, capital means real goods used in production.
whyNot.B: Natural resources are land.
whyNot.D: Organising skill is entrepreneurship.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Supply in economics is best defined as the quantity of a commodity that sellers are
options: able to produce in a year
willing and able to offer for sale at a given price and time
questions.explanation: Supply is not the total stock. It is the amount producers are willing and able to offer for sale at a particular price over a particular period.

whyNot.D: Goods held in a warehouse are stock; not all of it may be offered for sale.
whyNot.A: Productive capacity is not the same as the amount offered at a given price.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A rise in the price of beef leads to an increase in the demand for fish. Beef and fish are
questions.explanation: Substitutes (goods in competitive demand) can replace each other. When beef becomes dearer, consumers switch to fish, so the demand for fish rises.

whyNot.B: For complements, a rise in the price of one reduces demand for the other.
whyNot.D: Inferior goods are those whose demand falls when income rises; this case is about prices of related goods.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: When the price of a bag of cement rises from ₦400 to ₦500, the quantity demanded in a town falls from 1,000 to 900 bags. What is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: % change in quantity = 100 ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 10%. % change in price = 100 ÷ 400 × 100 = 25%. Elasticity = 10 ÷ 25 = 0.4 (ignoring the minus sign). Since 0.4 is less than 1, demand is inelastic.

whyNot.C: 2.5 is 25 ÷ 10, the formula upside down.
whyNot.A: 0.1 is only the proportional change in quantity.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Before a tax, a commodity sold at ₦100. The government then places a tax of ₦20 per unit on it, and the market price rises to ₦115. How much of the tax per unit is borne by producers?
questions.explanation: Consumers now pay ₦15 more per unit (115 − 100), so they bear ₦15 of the tax. The rest, 20 − 15 = ₦5, comes out of what producers receive, so producers bear ₦5 per unit.

whyNot.D: ₦15 is the consumers' share, shown by the rise in price.
whyNot.C: ₦20 is the whole tax; producers bear all of it only if the price does not rise at all.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The demand for bricklayers rises when more houses are being built. The demand for bricklayers is an example of
questions.explanation: Derived demand is demand for a factor or input that comes from the demand for the final product it helps to produce. Bricklayers are wanted because houses are wanted.

whyNot.B: Joint demand is for goods used together, such as cars and petrol.
whyNot.D: Composite demand is for a good with several uses, such as cassava for garri and for starch.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: If both the demand for and the supply of a commodity increase at the same time, the equilibrium
options: quantity will rise, but the change in price cannot be known without more information
price will fall and quantity will remain the same
price and quantity will both rise
price will rise and quantity will fall
questions.explanation: An increase in demand raises both price and quantity; an increase in supply raises quantity but lowers price. Together they surely raise quantity, but price may rise, fall or stay the same depending on which shift is larger.

whyNot.C: Price rises only if the increase in demand is larger than the increase in supply.
whyNot.D: Both shifts push quantity up, so quantity cannot fall.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of tertiary production?
questions.explanation: Tertiary production is the provision of services, including commercial services like banking, insurance and transport, and direct services like teaching.

whyNot.A: Fishing is primary production (extracting from nature).
whyNot.C: Mining is primary production.
whyNot.B: Baking turns raw materials into finished goods, which is secondary production.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A market in which there is only one seller of a product that has no close substitute is called
questions.explanation: A monopoly is a market with a single seller, a product with no close substitutes and barriers that keep other firms out.

whyNot.C: Perfect competition has many sellers of an identical product.
whyNot.A: Oligopoly has a few large sellers.

questions.subject: economics
questions.context:
Total product of a farm as more workers are added to a fixed plot of land:
Workers | Total product (bags)
1 | 8
2 | 20
3 | 36
4 | 48
5 | 56
6 | 60
questions.stem: With the employment of which worker do diminishing marginal returns begin?
questions.explanation: Marginal product = change in total product. MPs are 8, 12, 16, 12, 8 and 4. MP rises up to the 3rd worker (16), then falls to 12 with the 4th worker, so diminishing marginal returns begin with the 4th worker.

whyNot.A: The 3rd worker has the highest marginal product (16); returns are still increasing there.
whyNot.B: Total product is still rising with the 6th worker; diminishing returns had already started earlier.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A firm can sell 10 units at ₦60 each, but to sell 11 units it must lower the price of every unit to ₦58. What is the marginal revenue of the 11th unit?
questions.explanation: Marginal revenue = change in total revenue. TR at 10 units = 10 × 60 = ₦600. TR at 11 units = 11 × 58 = ₦638. MR = 638 − 600 = ₦38. It is less than the price because the price was cut on all the earlier units too.

whyNot.B: ₦58 is the price (average revenue) of the 11th unit, not the addition to total revenue.
whyNot.A: ₦2 is the fall in price per unit.
whyNot.D: ₦638 is total revenue at 11 units.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A small soap factory has total fixed costs of ₦12,000. It sells each bar of soap at ₦50, and its average variable cost is a constant ₦30 per bar. How many bars must it sell to break even?
questions.explanation: At break-even, total revenue = total cost. Each bar contributes 50 − 30 = ₦20 towards fixed costs. Break-even output = 12,000 ÷ 20 = 600 bars.

whyNot.A: 240 bars is 12,000 ÷ 50, which ignores variable cost.
whyNot.C: 400 bars is 12,000 ÷ 30, dividing by the variable cost instead of the contribution.
whyNot.B: 150 bars is 12,000 ÷ (50 + 30), adding instead of subtracting.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Several garment firms located in the same industrial estate all benefit from good roads, a pool of skilled workers and nearby suppliers. These benefits are
options: increasing returns to a variable factor
questions.explanation: External economies of scale are cost advantages a firm gets from the growth or concentration of the whole industry in an area, not from its own size.

whyNot.C: Internal economies come from the growth of the firm itself, such as bulk buying.
whyNot.B: Diseconomies of scale raise average cost; these benefits lower it.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The most important quality that anything must have to serve as money is
questions.explanation: Whatever is used as money must be generally accepted in payment for goods and services and in settling debts. Without acceptability, the other qualities do not make it money.

whyNot.D: Durability is a useful quality, but a durable item that nobody accepts cannot be money.
whyNot.B: Portability makes money convenient but does not by itself make people accept it.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Which of the following is an instrument of monetary policy used by the Central Bank of Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Monetary policy controls the money supply and credit. Its instruments include the cash reserve ratio, open market operations and the monetary policy rate, all operated by the CBN.

whyNot.A: Tax rates are tools of fiscal policy, set by government.
whyNot.B: Government spending is fiscal policy.
whyNot.D: Customs duties are taxes on trade, part of fiscal and trade policy.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The Nigerian Exchange (NGX), formerly the Nigerian Stock Exchange, is best described as a market where
options: foreign currencies are exchanged at the official rate
existing shares and bonds are bought and sold
the Central Bank lends to commercial banks
short-term loans are given to farmers
questions.explanation: The NGX is a stock exchange, part of the capital market. It provides a place where long-term securities such as shares and bonds can be bought and sold, making it easier for companies to raise funds and for investors to sell their holdings.

whyNot.D: Short-term loans belong to the money market and to banks, not the stock exchange.
whyNot.C: Central bank lending to banks is part of the money market, not the stock exchange.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Commercial banks create money mainly by
options: granting loans and overdrafts to customers
questions.explanation: When a commercial bank grants a loan, it credits the borrower's account, creating a new deposit. Deposits are money, so lending increases the money supply.

whyNot.B: Notes are issued only by the Central Bank of Nigeria.
whyNot.A: The monetary policy rate is set by the CBN, not by commercial banks.

questions.subject: economics
questions.context:
Monetary data for a country (₦ trillion):
Currency outside banks | 3
Demand deposits | 12
Savings and time deposits | 20
questions.stem: Narrow money (M1) is currency outside banks plus demand deposits. Using the data, what is narrow money?
questions.explanation: M1 = currency outside banks + demand deposits = 3 + 12 = ₦15 trillion. Savings and time deposits are not included in narrow money; adding them gives broad money (35).

whyNot.B: ₦35 trillion adds savings and time deposits, which gives broad money, not narrow money.
whyNot.C: ₦32 trillion adds demand deposits to savings and time deposits but leaves out currency.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A country's consumer price index rose from 120 last year to 150 this year. What was the rate of inflation?
questions.explanation: Rate of inflation = (change in index ÷ old index) × 100 = (150 − 120) ÷ 120 × 100 = 30 ÷ 120 × 100 = 25%.

whyNot.A: 30% is the change in points, not the percentage change.
whyNot.D: 20% divides by the new index (150) instead of the old one.
whyNot.B: 125% is the new index as a percentage of the old one, not the rate of increase.

questions.subject: economics
questions.context:
Income data for a country in one year (₦ billion):
Wages and salaries | 400
Rent | 60
Interest | 50
Profits | 140
Pensions and other transfer payments | 30
questions.stem: Using the income approach, what is the national income?
questions.explanation: The income approach adds the rewards of the factors of production: 400 + 60 + 50 + 140 = ₦650 billion. Transfer payments such as pensions are left out because they are not payments for current production.

whyNot.D: ₦680 billion wrongly includes the transfer payments.
whyNot.A: ₦590 billion leaves out rent.
whyNot.C: ₦510 billion leaves out profits.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: The headquarters of the ECOWAS Commission is located in
questions.explanation: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) has its Commission, the main executive body, in Abuja, Nigeria.

whyNot.D: Lomé hosts the ECOWAS Bank for Investment and Development, not the Commission.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: Over a period, a country's export prices rose by 26% while its import prices fell by 10%. Taking the base-year index for both as 100, what are its terms of trade now?
questions.explanation: Export price index = 126 and import price index = 90. Terms of trade = (126 ÷ 90) × 100 = 140. The figure is above 100, so the terms of trade are favourable.

whyNot.A: 116 adds the 26% rise and subtracts the 10% fall (100 + 26 − 10), which is not the formula.
whyNot.C: 71.4 is 90 ÷ 126 × 100, the formula upside down.
whyNot.D: 136 simply adds the two percentage changes to 100.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A country's national income at current prices is ₦600 billion and the price index is 120 (base year = 100). What is its national income at base-year (constant) prices?
questions.explanation: Real national income = money national income ÷ price index × 100 = 600 ÷ 120 × 100 = ₦500 billion. Deflating removes the effect of the 20% rise in prices.

whyNot.A: ₦720 billion multiplies by the index instead of dividing, inflating the figure further.
whyNot.D: ₦480 billion subtracts 20% of ₦600 billion, which is not the same as dividing by 1.2.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A foreign firm sells textiles in Nigeria at prices below what it charges in its home market, in order to capture the Nigerian market. This practice is called
questions.explanation: Dumping is selling goods abroad at prices lower than in the home market (often below cost). It can harm local industries, and countries protect themselves against it with anti-dumping duties.

whyNot.C: Devaluation is a deliberate lowering of the value of a country's currency.
whyNot.A: An embargo is a ban on trade in certain goods or with a country.
whyNot.B: Import substitution is producing at home goods that were formerly imported.

questions.subject: economics
questions.stem: A group of countries removes tariffs on trade among themselves, but each member keeps its own separate tariffs on goods from non-members. This form of economic integration is a
questions.explanation: In a free trade area, members trade freely with one another but each sets its own tariffs on outsiders. A customs union adds a common external tariff, and a common market adds free movement of labour and capital.

whyNot.C: A customs union has a common external tariff, not separate ones.
whyNot.B: A common market also has a common external tariff plus free movement of factors.
whyNot.D: A monetary union shares a common currency.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which of the following is an essential feature of every state?
questions.explanation: Every state must have four elements: a population, a defined territory, a government and sovereignty. A written constitution, several parties or an elected head of state are found in some states but not in all of them.

whyNot.C: The United Kingdom is a state but has no single written constitution.
whyNot.D: Monarchies such as Saudi Arabia are states even though their heads of state are not elected.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The theory that the state came into being when people agreed to give up some of their natural rights to a ruler in return for protection is the
questions.explanation: The social contract theory, linked with Thomas Hobbes, John Locke and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, holds that the state arose from an agreement among people who left the 'state of nature' and accepted a government to secure order and protect their rights.

whyNot.D: The divine right theory says the state and its rulers were created by God, not by agreement among the people.
whyNot.A: The force theory says the state was created when the strong conquered the weak.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A system in which all the citizens meet in person to debate and make laws, as was done in ancient Athens, is known as
questions.explanation: In direct democracy, citizens take decisions themselves instead of electing representatives. It worked in small Greek city-states such as Athens, where citizens gathered in the Assembly. Large modern states use representative democracy instead.

whyNot.D: In representative democracy citizens elect representatives who make laws on their behalf; they do not all meet in person.
whyNot.C: Oligarchy is rule by a small group, the opposite of all citizens taking part.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Fascism as a political ideology is most closely associated with
questions.explanation: Fascism developed in Italy under Benito Mussolini, who came to power in 1922. It glorifies the nation and the state, rejects liberal democracy and opposes communism, and it is ruled by a single party under a strong leader.

whyNot.A: Lenin led the 1917 Russian Revolution and is associated with communism, which fascism opposed.
whyNot.C: Nyerere is associated with African socialism (Ujamaa) in Tanzania.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In a capitalist economic system, the means of production are owned mainly by
questions.explanation: Capitalism rests on private ownership of land, factories and other means of production, with prices and output decided largely by market forces and the profit motive.

whyNot.C: State ownership of the means of production is a feature of socialism and communism.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation on the rule of law in Nigeria?
options: The right of an accused person to a fair hearing
The equality of all citizens before the law
The immunity of the President and Governors from civil and criminal proceedings while in office
questions.explanation: The rule of law requires that everyone be equal before the law. Section 308 of the 1999 Constitution protects the President, Vice-President, Governors and Deputy Governors from civil and criminal proceedings while in office, so they cannot be tried like ordinary citizens during their tenure. This limits the rule of law.

whyNot.D: An independent judiciary supports the rule of law; it does not limit it.
whyNot.A: Fair hearing is one of the principles of the rule of law, not a limitation on it.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A legislature that is made up of two chambers or houses is described as
questions.explanation: A bicameral legislature has two houses, such as Nigeria's National Assembly, made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives. A unicameral legislature has only one house, such as a State House of Assembly in Nigeria.

whyNot.D: Unicameral means a single chamber.
whyNot.A: Bipartisan describes cooperation between two political parties, not the number of chambers.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The power of the courts to declare a law or an executive action void because it conflicts with the constitution is called
questions.explanation: Judicial review lets the courts test laws and government actions against the constitution and strike down those that are inconsistent with it. It is one of the main ways the judiciary checks the legislature and the executive.

whyNot.A: Judicial precedent is the practice of courts following earlier decisions of higher courts.
whyNot.D: Delegated legislation is law made by bodies other than the legislature, not a power to cancel laws.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Rules, regulations and bye-laws made by ministers, local councils or public bodies under powers given to them by an Act of the legislature are known as
questions.explanation: The legislature cannot make every detailed rule itself, so a parent Act gives power to ministers, local governments or agencies to make rules. These rules are called delegated (or subsidiary) legislation, and they must stay within the powers granted.

whyNot.B: Conventions are unwritten customs of the constitution, not rules made under an Act.
whyNot.C: A private member's bill is a bill introduced in the legislature by an ordinary member, not a rule made outside it.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Unwritten rules of political practice that are not laws but are obeyed as binding, such as the British monarch always giving assent to bills passed by Parliament, are called
questions.explanation: Constitutional conventions are customs and practices that have grown up over time. No court enforces them, yet politicians follow them as if they were law. They are a major source of the British constitution.

whyNot.D: Statutes are written laws passed by the legislature.
whyNot.B: Decrees are written laws made by a military government.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Fusion of powers is a feature of the parliamentary system mainly because
options: judges are appointed by the head of state
the legislature cannot remove the cabinet
the head of state is also head of government
ministers are also members of the legislature
questions.explanation: In a parliamentary system the prime minister and other ministers are drawn from parliament and keep their seats there. The same people therefore take part in both making and carrying out laws, so legislative and executive powers are fused rather than separated.

whyNot.C: In a parliamentary system the two roles are separate: a ceremonial head of state and a prime minister as head of government.
whyNot.B: Parliament can remove the cabinet through a vote of no confidence.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A major advantage of a unitary system of government is that
options: the component units may leave the union whenever they wish
it gives each ethnic group its own government with guaranteed powers
powers are divided by the constitution between two levels of government
it allows uniform laws and quick decisions across the whole country
questions.explanation: In a unitary state, power is concentrated in one central government, which can pass one set of laws for the whole country and take decisions quickly without negotiating with regional governments. Britain is a common example.

whyNot.B: Separate governments with guaranteed powers for groups are a feature of federalism.
whyNot.A: The right of units to leave is a feature of a confederation.
whyNot.C: Division of powers between levels of government describes a federal system.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The method of voting that ensures that no one else can know how a voter cast his or her vote is
questions.explanation: Under the secret ballot, each voter marks the ballot paper privately, for example in a polling booth, and drops it in a box. This protects voters from intimidation and bribery and makes elections freer.

whyNot.A: In an open ballot others can see how a person votes, for example by queuing behind a candidate.
whyNot.C: Proportional representation is a way of allocating seats, not a method of casting votes.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) is best described as
questions.explanation: The NLC is the umbrella body of trade unions in Nigeria. It seeks to influence government policy on wages and workers' welfare, through negotiations and strikes, but it does not contest elections to form a government, which makes it a pressure (interest) group.

whyNot.D: A political party sponsors candidates for elections to control government; the NLC does not.
whyNot.C: The NLC is a voluntary association of workers, not part of government.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The first political party in Nigeria, the Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP), was founded in 1923 by
questions.explanation: Herbert Macaulay formed the NNDP in 1923 to contest the elective seats for Lagos created by the Clifford Constitution of 1922. It won all three Lagos seats in the 1923 election.

whyNot.A: Azikiwe later led the NCNC, which was formed in 1944.
whyNot.D: Awolowo founded the Action Group in 1951.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The Action Group (AG), formed in 1951 under the leadership of Obafemi Awolowo, grew out of the cultural organisation known as
questions.explanation: Egbe Omo Oduduwa was a Yoruba cultural association founded by Awolowo and others. Its leaders transformed it into the Action Group in 1951 to contest elections under the Macpherson Constitution, with its main base in the Western Region.

whyNot.C: Jam'iyyar Mutanen Arewa was the northern cultural body that gave rise to the Northern People's Congress (NPC).
whyNot.D: The Nigerian Youth Movement was a nationalist political organisation of the 1930s, not the cultural body behind the AG.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The Northern People's Congress (NPC) was led by
options: Sir Ahmadu Bello, the Sardauna of Sokoto
questions.explanation: Sir Ahmadu Bello, the Sardauna of Sokoto, led the NPC and became Premier of the Northern Region. His deputy in the party, Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, became Prime Minister of the Federation.

whyNot.B: Aminu Kano led the Northern Elements Progressive Union (NEPU), a rival of the NPC in the North.
whyNot.D: Awolowo led the Action Group.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under section 134 of the 1999 Constitution, a candidate is declared elected President at the first ballot if he or she has the highest number of votes and also
options: a majority of the votes in every one of the 36 states
at least one-quarter of the votes cast in each of at least two-thirds of all the states and the FCT
the support of two-thirds of the members of the National Assembly
more than half of all the votes cast in the country
questions.explanation: Section 134(2) requires two things: the highest number of votes cast, and not less than one-quarter of the votes cast in each of at least two-thirds of all the states and the Federal Capital Territory. This spread requirement is meant to make sure the President has support across the country, not just in one area.

whyNot.D: An overall majority of more than half is not required; the highest number of votes plus the spread is enough.
whyNot.C: The President is elected directly by the people, not by the National Assembly.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The constitution that first set up a Council of Ministers that included Nigerian ministers from the regions was the
questions.explanation: The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 created a central Council of Ministers made up of official members and twelve Nigerian ministers, four from each region. It also created a central House of Representatives.

whyNot.B: The Clifford Constitution is known for introducing the elective principle.
whyNot.C: The Richards Constitution is known for introducing regionalism.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Lagos was separated from the Western Region and made a federal territory under the
questions.explanation: The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954, which made Nigeria a federation, also made Lagos a separate federal territory, removing it from the Western Region.

whyNot.A: Under the Macpherson Constitution Lagos was still part of the Western Region.
whyNot.D: Lagos was already a federal territory long before the Republican Constitution of 1963.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The presidential system of government was introduced into Nigeria by the
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution replaced the Westminster-style parliamentary system with an executive presidential system modelled on that of the USA, in which the President is both head of state and head of government.

whyNot.D: The 1960 Constitution kept a parliamentary system with a Prime Minister.
whyNot.A: The 1963 Constitution made Nigeria a republic but kept the parliamentary system with a ceremonial President.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A major result of the 1976 Local Government Reform in Nigeria was the introduction of
options: elections of local councils by the State Houses of Assembly
the abolition of local government councils
native authorities headed by emirs and chiefs
a uniform single-tier system of local government throughout the country
questions.explanation: The 1976 reform under the military government made local government a distinct third tier of government and gave the whole country one uniform, single-tier system with elected councils and defined functions.

whyNot.B: The reform strengthened local government councils; it did not abolish them.
whyNot.C: Native authorities under traditional rulers belonged to the colonial system of indirect rule, which the reform replaced.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under the 1999 Constitution, the highest court in Nigeria is the
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court, headed by the Chief Justice of Nigeria, is the final court of appeal. Its decisions bind all other courts in the country.

whyNot.A: The Court of Appeal hears appeals from the high courts, but its decisions can be appealed to the Supreme Court.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under section 58 of the 1999 Constitution, if the President withholds assent to a bill, the bill can still become law without assent if it is passed again by
options: a two-thirds majority of each House of the National Assembly
a simple majority of the Senate alone
the Supreme Court in an advisory opinion
a majority of the State Houses of Assembly
questions.explanation: Section 58(5) provides that where the President withholds assent and the bill is again passed by each House of the National Assembly by a two-thirds majority, it becomes law and the President's assent is no longer required. This is the legislature's check on the executive veto.

whyNot.B: Both Houses must act, and a simple majority is not enough to override the veto.
whyNot.D: Approval by State Houses of Assembly is part of the procedure for amending the Constitution, not for overriding a veto.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The two heads of state who took the lead in the formation of ECOWAS were
options: Léopold Senghor of Senegal and Félix Houphouët-Boigny of Côte d'Ivoire
Murtala Mohammed of Nigeria and Siaka Stevens of Sierra Leone
Yakubu Gowon of Nigeria and Gnassingbé Eyadéma of Togo
Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana and Sékou Touré of Guinea
questions.explanation: General Yakubu Gowon of Nigeria and General Gnassingbé Eyadéma of Togo championed the idea of a West African economic community, which led to the signing of the ECOWAS Treaty in Lagos in May 1975.

whyNot.D: Nkrumah and Touré were associated with the Ghana–Guinea Union of 1958, long before ECOWAS.
whyNot.B: Murtala Mohammed came to power in July 1975, after the treaty had already been signed in May.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The Secretariat of the Commonwealth of Nations has its headquarters in
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth Secretariat, set up in 1965, is based at Marlborough House in London. It organises meetings of Commonwealth heads of government and carries out the association's programmes.

whyNot.B: Abuja is the headquarters of ECOWAS, not of the Commonwealth.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Nigeria became a member of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) in
questions.explanation: OPEC was founded in Baghdad in 1960 by five countries. Nigeria, whose oil production grew fast after the civil war, joined in 1971.

whyNot.B: 1960 is the year OPEC was founded (and the year of Nigeria's independence), not the year Nigeria joined.
whyNot.C: 1975 is the year ECOWAS was formed.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The Charter of the United Nations was signed in June 1945 at a conference held in
questions.explanation: Delegates of 50 countries signed the UN Charter in San Francisco on 26 June 1945, and the UN came into existence on 24 October 1945. New York later became the site of its permanent headquarters.

whyNot.D: New York is the UN's headquarters, but the Charter was signed in San Francisco.
whyNot.B: Geneva was the headquarters of the League of Nations.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Nigeria's policy of not joining either the Western bloc or the Eastern (communist) bloc during the Cold War is known as
questions.explanation: Non-alignment meant that Nigeria judged each international issue on its merits instead of automatically siding with the USA-led West or the Soviet-led East. Nigeria was a member of the Non-Aligned Movement.

whyNot.D: Isolationism means withdrawing from world affairs; Nigeria remained active in international organisations.
whyNot.B: Apartheid was South Africa's policy of racial segregation, which Nigeria opposed.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: In 1979 the Nigerian government nationalised the assets of British Petroleum (BP) in Nigeria mainly in order to
options: pressure Britain over majority rule in Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe)
force Britain to leave the Commonwealth
protest against British nuclear tests in the Sahara
questions.explanation: In 1979 the Obasanjo government took over BP's Nigerian interests to pressure Britain to support black majority rule in Rhodesia, and over concern that oil was reaching apartheid South Africa. Zimbabwe became independent in 1980. The action showed Nigeria using its oil wealth in its Africa-centred foreign policy.

whyNot.B: Britain supported the Federal Government, not Biafra, during the civil war.
whyNot.D: The atomic tests in the Sahara were carried out by France, which led Nigeria to break relations with France in 1961.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: The theory which holds that kings receive their authority from God and are answerable only to God is the
questions.explanation: The divine right of kings teaches that a monarch's power comes directly from God, so subjects must obey and only God can judge the king. King James I of England was a well-known supporter of this view.
