whyNot.D: A cultivator loosens soil and removes weeds between crop rows.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A tractor pulls a plough of working width 1.5 m at 5 km/h with a field efficiency of 80%. What is its effective field capacity?
questions.explanation: Area covered per hour = width × distance = 1.5 m × 5,000 m = 7,500 m² = 0.75 ha. Allowing for 80% efficiency: 0.75 × 0.8 = 0.6 ha per hour.

whyNot.B: 0.75 ha per hour is the theoretical capacity, before the 80% efficiency is applied.
whyNot.C: 7.5 ha per hour comes from dividing 7,500 m² by 1,000 instead of 10,000 (a unit slip).

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which method of irrigation wastes the least water by delivering it slowly to the root zone of each plant?
questions.explanation: Drip irrigation releases water drop by drop through emitters near each plant, so little is lost to evaporation, run-off or deep drainage. It is suited to vegetables and orchards where water is scarce.

whyNot.C: Flood irrigation covers the whole surface and loses much water by evaporation and seepage.
whyNot.B: Sprinklers wet leaves and the whole surface, and water drifts and evaporates in the air.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A narrow, raised structure with walls of wire mesh or slats, used for drying and storing maize cobs, is called a
questions.explanation: A maize crib is narrow and well ventilated so air passes through the cobs and dries them. It is raised on posts fitted with rat guards to keep out rodents.

whyNot.B: A silo is a tall airtight structure for bulk grain or silage, not an open, ventilated crib.
whyNot.D: A rhumbu is a traditional mud-and-thatch granary used in northern Nigeria.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A rectangular farm measures 250 m by 160 m. What is its area in hectares?
questions.explanation: Area = 250 m × 160 m = 40,000 m². Since 1 ha = 10,000 m², the area is 40,000 ÷ 10,000 = 4 ha.

whyNot.C: 40 ha comes from dividing by 1,000 instead of 10,000.
whyNot.D: 410 comes from adding the two sides instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In a four-stroke tractor engine, during which stroke are both valves closed while the piston moves up the cylinder?
questions.explanation: The four strokes are induction (inlet valve open, piston down), compression (both valves closed, piston up), power (both closed, piston forced down) and exhaust (exhaust valve open, piston up). Both valves closed with the piston rising is compression.

whyNot.D: In the power stroke both valves are closed but the piston moves down.
whyNot.B: In the exhaust stroke the piston moves up but the exhaust valve is open.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The deliberate growing of trees together with crops and/or livestock on the same piece of land is called
questions.explanation: Agroforestry combines trees with crops or animals on the same land. The trees can protect the soil, add organic matter, provide shade and yield timber, fruit or fodder.

whyNot.D: Monocropping is growing only one crop on a piece of land.
whyNot.A: Pastoralism is rearing livestock by grazing, often moving with the herd.
whyNot.B: Horticulture is the growing of fruits, vegetables and flowers.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which of the following is a biotic factor that affects crop production?
questions.explanation: Biotic factors are living things, such as pests, diseases, weeds and soil organisms. Rainfall, temperature and soil pH are abiotic (non-living) factors.

whyNot.C: Rainfall is a climatic, abiotic factor.
whyNot.D: Soil pH is an edaphic (soil), abiotic factor.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A community in Sokoto State plants rows of neem and acacia on bare land that has not had forest cover in living memory, to check desert encroachment. This is best described as
questions.explanation: Afforestation is establishing trees on land that was not previously forest. Reafforestation is replanting where an existing forest has been cut down.

whyNot.B: Reafforestation replaces trees on land that recently carried forest.
whyNot.D: Deforestation is the removal of trees, the opposite.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A major advantage of mixed farming (keeping crops and livestock on the same farm) is that
options: animal dung fertilises the crops and crop residues feed the animals
the farmer can sell the produce only at harvest
pests and diseases cannot attack the farm
the farmer needs no labour for either enterprise
questions.explanation: In mixed farming each enterprise supports the other: manure from the animals improves soil fertility, and crop by-products such as maize stover and groundnut haulms are fed to the animals. It also spreads risk.

whyNot.D: Mixed farming actually needs more labour and management skill.
whyNot.C: Pests and diseases can still attack both crops and animals.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The Green Revolution Programme, launched in 1980 to boost food production, was introduced by the government of
questions.explanation: The Green Revolution was launched in 1980 by President Shehu Shagari's civilian government. It followed Operation Feed the Nation (1976) and aimed at self-sufficiency in food.

whyNot.D: Obasanjo's military government launched Operation Feed the Nation in 1976.
whyNot.B: Buhari's military government came to power in December 1983, after the programme started.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Large quantities of tomatoes rot in markets in Kano during the peak harvest season. The main cause is
options: low rainfall during the growing season
too many extension agents in the state
questions.explanation: Tomatoes are highly perishable. Without cold storage, processing factories and good transport, the glut at harvest cannot be kept or converted to paste, so much of it spoils (post-harvest loss).

whyNot.A: Low rainfall would reduce the harvest, not cause a glut that rots.
whyNot.D: Improved varieties raise yields; the losses come from poor handling after harvest.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which of the following is a typical feature of commercial agriculture?
options: Production is mainly for sale and profit
Only family labour is used on the farm
Many crops are grown together on tiny plots
Simple tools such as hoes and cutlasses are used
questions.explanation: Commercial agriculture produces mainly for the market. It is usually large-scale, specialised, uses hired labour and machines, and aims at profit.

whyNot.B: Relying only on family labour is typical of subsistence farming.
whyNot.C: Many crops on tiny plots (mixed cropping on small holdings) is typical of subsistence farming.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which research institute in Ibadan has the national mandate for research on cocoa, kola, coffee, cashew and tea?
options: Nigerian Institute for Oil Palm Research (NIFOR)
questions.explanation: CRIN, located in Ibadan, Oyo State, researches cocoa, kola, coffee, cashew and tea: breeding improved varieties and developing pest, disease and processing methods.

whyNot.D: NIFOR, near Benin City, researches oil palm and other palms.
whyNot.C: NRCRI is at Umudike and works on root and tuber crops.
whyNot.A: IAR is at Samaru, Zaria, attached to Ahmadu Bello University.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The National Root Crops Research Institute, which develops improved varieties of yam, cassava and cocoyam, is located at
questions.explanation: NRCRI is at Umudike, near Umuahia in Abia State. It works on root and tuber crops such as cassava, yam, cocoyam, sweet potato and ginger.

whyNot.A: Badeggi in Niger State is the home of the National Cereals Research Institute (rice and other cereals).
whyNot.B: Samaru, Zaria, is the home of the Institute for Agricultural Research.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In an area where farmers practise bush fallowing, the population grows rapidly over thirty years. The most likely result on the farmland is
options: longer fallow periods and richer soils
shorter fallow periods and falling soil fertility
a fall in the demand for farmland
more forest cover around each village
questions.explanation: More people need more land for food. Farmers return to fallow plots before the soil has recovered, so fallow periods shorten, fertility falls and yields decline unless fertiliser or manure is used.

whyNot.A: Pressure on land shortens fallows; it does not lengthen them.
whyNot.D: Forest cover usually falls as more land is cleared for farming.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Cassava is normally propagated by
questions.explanation: Cassava is propagated vegetatively by stem cuttings about 20–25 cm long, each with several nodes, taken from mature, healthy stems.

whyNot.C: Setts are used to propagate yam.
whyNot.D: Suckers are used for plantain, banana and pineapple.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: On a sloping farm in Enugu State, which practice best reduces soil erosion?
options: Making ridges across the slope along the contours
Making ridges up and down the slope
Clearing all the vegetation from the slope
Burning the crop residues after harvest
questions.explanation: Ridges made across the slope (contour ridging) slow down running water and trap soil, reducing sheet, rill and gully erosion.

whyNot.B: Ridges up and down the slope act as channels and speed up run-off.
whyNot.D: Burning removes the cover that protects soil from raindrops and run-off.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Maize streak disease, which produces narrow broken yellow streaks along maize leaves, is caused by
options: a bacterium spread in the seed
a fungus spread by rain splash
questions.explanation: Maize streak is caused by maize streak virus, carried from plant to plant by leafhoppers (Cicadulina species). Resistant varieties and early planting are the main controls.

whyNot.D: Fungal leaf diseases of maize include rust and leaf blight, not streak.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Groundnut rosette disease, which stunts the plants and makes the leaves small and bunched, is spread by
questions.explanation: Groundnut rosette is a virus disease spread by the groundnut aphid (Aphis craccivora). Early, dense planting and resistant varieties reduce it.

whyNot.A: Whiteflies spread cassava mosaic disease.
whyNot.C: Mealybugs spread cocoa swollen shoot virus.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Yam is planted at 1 m × 1 m, one sett per stand, on a plot of 0.5 ha. How many setts are needed? (1 ha = 10,000 m²)
questions.explanation: Each stand occupies 1 m × 1 m = 1 m². Area = 0.5 × 10,000 = 5,000 m². Number of setts = 5,000 ÷ 1 = 5,000.

whyNot.B: 10,000 is the number needed for a full hectare.
whyNot.D: 50,000 comes from a slip in converting 0.5 ha to square metres.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A farmer wants to apply 60 kg of nitrogen per hectare to 1.5 ha using NPK 15-15-15. How many 50 kg bags of the fertiliser does he need?
questions.explanation: NPK 15-15-15 contains 15% N. Fertiliser per hectare = 60 ÷ 0.15 = 400 kg. For 1.5 ha: 400 × 1.5 = 600 kg. Bags = 600 ÷ 50 = 12 bags.

whyNot.A: 8 bags is the fertiliser for only 1 ha (400 ÷ 50).
whyNot.C: 6 bags divides 600 kg by 100 instead of by the 50 kg bag size.
whyNot.B: 2 bags treats the 90 kg of nitrogen as if it were the fertiliser itself.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A soil test shows that a farm in Cross River State has a pH of 4.5. Which of these should the farmer apply to correct the problem?
questions.explanation: pH 4.5 is strongly acidic. Agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) neutralises soil acidity and raises the pH towards the range most crops prefer (about 6–7).

whyNot.D: Ammonium sulphate is an acid-forming fertiliser and would lower the pH further.
whyNot.B: Sulphur is used to make soils more acidic, the opposite of what is needed.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Striga (witchweed) is a serious problem in sorghum and maize fields in northern Nigeria because it
options: attaches to the crop's roots and draws water and nutrients from them
feeds on the grains while they are in storage
climbs over the crop and shades it out completely
releases a gas that kills the crop's leaves
questions.explanation: Striga is a parasitic weed. Its seeds germinate near cereal roots, attach to them and take water and nutrients, stunting the crop and greatly reducing yield. Rotation with legumes and resistant varieties help control it.

whyNot.C: Striga is a short plant that damages the crop underground, not a climbing weed.
whyNot.B: Grain in storage is attacked by insects such as weevils, not by weeds.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The insects Sahlbergella singularis and Distantiella theobroma, which suck sap from young shoots and pods, are pests of
questions.explanation: These are cocoa capsids (mirids). Their feeding leaves black lesions on shoots and pods, and heavy attack kills branches and opens the canopy. They are controlled with recommended insecticides and good farm sanitation.

whyNot.B: Major insect pests of maize include stem borers such as Busseola fusca.
whyNot.A: A major insect pest of yam is the yam beetle (Heteroligus meles).

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which type of soil is generally best for growing most arable crops?
questions.explanation: Loam is a balanced mixture of sand, silt and clay with good organic matter. It drains well yet holds enough water and nutrients, and is easy to work.

whyNot.B: Clay holds water but drains poorly, becomes waterlogged and is hard to till.
whyNot.A: Sandy soil drains too fast and holds few nutrients.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A young goat is called a
questions.explanation: The young of a goat is a kid; the act of giving birth in goats is called kidding.

whyNot.A: A lamb is a young sheep.
whyNot.D: A calf is a young cow.
whyNot.B: A piglet is a young pig.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In which system of poultry management are the birds kept on the floor of a house covered with wood shavings or rice husks?
questions.explanation: In the deep litter system birds live on the floor of a house covered with absorbent material such as wood shavings, which soaks up droppings and is turned to keep it dry.

whyNot.D: In the battery cage system birds are kept in wire cages, not on litter.
whyNot.C: In the free-range system birds roam outside during the day.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Trimming part of the upper beak of laying hens is done mainly to
options: protect the birds from Newcastle disease
increase the size of the eggs
questions.explanation: Debeaking (beak trimming) reduces the damage birds can do when they peck one another, so it prevents feather pulling, egg eating and cannibalism, especially in crowded houses.

whyNot.D: Egg size depends on breed, age and feed, not on the beak.
whyNot.A: Newcastle disease is prevented by vaccination.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The gestation period of a sow is approximately
questions.explanation: A sow is pregnant for about 114 days, often remembered as 3 months, 3 weeks and 3 days. Giving birth in pigs is called farrowing.

whyNot.B: About 150 days is the gestation period of goats and sheep.
whyNot.A: About 283 days is the gestation period of cattle.
whyNot.C: 21 days is the length of the sow's oestrous (heat) cycle, not her pregnancy.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Anthrax, which can kill cattle suddenly with dark, unclotted blood oozing from the body openings, is caused by
questions.explanation: Anthrax is caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis. Its spores survive in soil for many years. Carcasses must not be opened but burned or buried deep, and animals are vaccinated in risky areas.

whyNot.B: Viral cattle diseases include foot-and-mouth disease.
whyNot.D: Protozoan cattle diseases include trypanosomiasis and red water.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Peste des petits ruminants (PPR), which causes fever, discharge from the eyes and nose, mouth sores and diarrhoea in goats, is caused by
questions.explanation: PPR is a highly contagious viral disease of goats and sheep. There is no cure; it is prevented by vaccination and by isolating sick animals.

whyNot.D: PPR is not bacterial, so antibiotics only help control secondary infections.
whyNot.A: Tick-borne protozoa cause diseases such as babesiosis (red water), not PPR.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A newborn calf should receive its mother's first milk (colostrum) within hours of birth mainly because colostrum
options: makes the calf's rumen begin to digest grass
is the only milk that has no water in it
contains antibodies that protect the calf against disease
contains no fat, so it is easy to digest
questions.explanation: Colostrum is rich in antibodies (immunoglobulins), vitamins and protein. The newborn's gut can absorb these antibodies only in the first hours of life, giving it immunity until its own system develops.

whyNot.D: Colostrum is actually richer in fat and protein than ordinary milk.
whyNot.A: The rumen develops later, as the calf starts eating solid feed.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The Red Sokoto (Maradi) goat of northern Nigeria is especially valued for its
questions.explanation: The Red Sokoto goat produces a fine, high-quality skin that is prized for leather (traditionally sold as 'Morocco leather'), in addition to its meat.

whyNot.A: Trypanotolerance is associated with the West African Dwarf goat and N'Dama cattle of the humid South.
whyNot.D: Goats in Nigeria are not kept for wool; wool comes from certain breeds of sheep.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.context: A farmer wants to make 100 kg of goat concentrate containing 17% crude protein (CP) from maize (10% CP) and groundnut cake (45% CP), using the Pearson square.
questions.stem: How much of each ingredient should she use?
options: 20 kg maize and 80 kg groundnut cake
50 kg maize and 50 kg groundnut cake
80 kg maize and 20 kg groundnut cake
62 kg maize and 38 kg groundnut cake
questions.explanation: Pearson square: parts of maize = 45 − 17 = 28; parts of groundnut cake = 17 − 10 = 7; total = 35. Maize = 28 ÷ 35 × 100 = 80 kg; groundnut cake = 7 ÷ 35 × 100 = 20 kg. Check: 0.8 × 10 + 0.2 × 45 = 8 + 9 = 17% CP.

whyNot.A: This swaps the two ingredients; it would give 0.2 × 10 + 0.8 × 45 = 38% CP.
whyNot.B: Equal amounts give (10 + 45) ÷ 2 = 27.5% CP, far above 17%.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A high-yielding dairy cow collapses and cannot stand a day after calving; her body is cold and she is drowsy. This milk fever is caused by a sudden shortage in her blood of
questions.explanation: Milk fever (parturient paresis) is hypocalcaemia: the start of heavy milk production drains calcium from the blood faster than the cow can replace it, so the muscles cannot work. It is treated with calcium borogluconate injection.

whyNot.A: Iron shortage causes anaemia, as in young piglets, not collapse at calving.
whyNot.D: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and poor growth, not milk fever.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The reward for the entrepreneur who organises the other factors of production and bears the risk of a farm business is
questions.explanation: The entrepreneur (manager) combines land, labour and capital and takes the risk of loss. His reward is profit; land earns rent, labour earns wages and capital earns interest.

whyNot.D: Rent is the reward for land.
whyNot.C: Wages are the reward for labour.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: An extension agent in Kwara State wants to tell thousands of farmers quickly about an armyworm outbreak. The most suitable method is
options: a visit to each farmer's farm
a meeting with one village group
a radio announcement in the local language
questions.explanation: Mass media methods such as radio reach very many people quickly and cheaply. Radio in local languages is widely heard by rural farmers, so it suits urgent warnings.

whyNot.A: Individual farm visits are effective but reach very few farmers at a time.
whyNot.C: A result demonstration takes a whole season to show its result.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A farmer grew cassava on 2 ha and harvested 20 tonnes per hectare, which he sold at ₦80,000 per tonne. Variable costs were ₦1,450,000 and fixed costs were ₦300,000. What was the gross margin for the whole farm?
questions.explanation: Total revenue = 2 × 20 × ₦80,000 = ₦3,200,000. Gross margin = total revenue − variable costs = ₦3,200,000 − ₦1,450,000 = ₦1,750,000. Fixed costs are left out of a gross margin.

whyNot.C: ₦1,450,000 also deducts the fixed costs; that is net profit.
whyNot.B: ₦3,200,000 is the total revenue.
whyNot.D: ₦875,000 is the gross margin per hectare, not for the whole 2 ha.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A fish farm earned total revenue of ₦1,200,000 in a season. Its total variable cost was ₦500,000 and its total fixed cost was ₦250,000. What was the profit?
questions.explanation: Total cost = variable cost + fixed cost = ₦500,000 + ₦250,000 = ₦750,000. Profit = total revenue − total cost = ₦1,200,000 − ₦750,000 = ₦450,000.

whyNot.D: ₦700,000 subtracts only the variable cost; that is the gross margin.
whyNot.A: ₦950,000 subtracts only the fixed cost.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Rice farmers in Kebbi State form a society to collect their paddy together, process it and sell it in bulk to get better prices. This is an example of a
questions.explanation: A marketing cooperative is formed by producers to sell their produce jointly. Bulking gives them more bargaining power and cuts out some middlemen.

whyNot.C: A consumer cooperative buys goods in bulk for members to use, not to sell their produce.
whyNot.B: A thrift and credit cooperative pools savings and lends to members.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which of the following is a useful function of middlemen in the marketing of farm produce?
options: They always reduce the price that consumers pay
They set the official price of each crop
They grow the crops on behalf of farmers
They buy small lots from many farmers and assemble them in bulk
questions.explanation: Middlemen collect (assemble) small quantities from many scattered farmers, transport and store them, and break bulk for retailers. This links farmers to distant markets, although their margins raise final prices.

whyNot.A: The extra margins of middlemen usually raise, not lower, the price consumers pay.
whyNot.B: Middlemen trade at market prices; they do not fix official prices.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: When the price of a paint bucket of garri rises from ₦1,000 to ₦1,200, the quantity demanded in a market falls from 500 to 450 buckets a week. What is the price elasticity of demand, and is demand elastic or inelastic?
questions.explanation: % change in quantity = (450 − 500) ÷ 500 × 100 = −10%. % change in price = (1,200 − 1,000) ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 20%. Elasticity = 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5 (ignoring the sign). Since it is less than 1, demand is inelastic, as expected for a staple food.

whyNot.C: 2.0 divides the percentage change in price by the change in quantity, the wrong way round.
whyNot.A: An elasticity below 1 means demand is inelastic, not elastic.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The farm record in which a farmer writes down the activities carried out on the farm each day, such as weeding, spraying and visitors received, is the
questions.explanation: The farm diary is a day-by-day record of what happens on the farm. It helps the farmer plan, remember dates (for example of vaccination) and explain results.

whyNot.D: An inventory lists the farm's assets and their values at a given date.
whyNot.A: A cash analysis book records money received and paid out.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: When a bank asks a farmer to pledge his land title before it grants him a loan, the land title serves as
options: a grant that need not be repaid
the repayment period of the loan
questions.explanation: Collateral is an asset pledged to the lender. If the borrower fails to repay, the lender can take the asset. Lack of acceptable collateral is a major reason small farmers find it hard to get bank loans.

whyNot.D: Interest is the charge paid for borrowing money.
whyNot.A: A grant is free money; a pledged asset backs a loan that must be repaid.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: The main purpose of agricultural insurance, such as that offered by the Nigerian Agricultural Insurance Corporation, is to
options: provide farmers with free fertiliser and seeds each year
lend farmers money to buy land at low interest
compensate farmers for losses from risks such as flood, fire or disease
guarantee farmers a fixed price for every crop they sell
questions.explanation: Insurance spreads risk: the farmer pays a premium, and if an insured risk such as flood, fire, drought or disease destroys crops or livestock, he is compensated and can continue farming.

whyNot.D: Guaranteed prices are a price-support policy, not insurance.
whyNot.B: Lending for land purchase is the work of credit institutions, not insurers.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which small hand tool is most suitable for lifting seedlings from a nursery and transplanting them?
questions.explanation: A hand trowel is a small scoop-shaped tool that lifts a seedling with a ball of soil around its roots and digs the small hole for transplanting.

whyNot.B: A pick-axe breaks hard ground; it would destroy seedlings.
whyNot.D: A sickle is for cutting grass and harvesting cereals.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which implement is used for primary tillage, cutting and turning over the soil to bury weeds and trash?
questions.explanation: Ploughing is primary tillage: the disc plough cuts into the soil, turns it over and buries weeds and crop residues.

whyNot.B: The disc harrow does secondary tillage, breaking clods after ploughing.
whyNot.A: A planter sows seeds.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which of these should a tractor operator check every day before starting the engine?
options: Tightness of the cylinder head bolts
questions.explanation: Daily checks include engine oil level, coolant (radiator water), fuel, tyre pressure and the air cleaner. Running the engine low on oil can ruin it quickly.

whyNot.A: Clutch plates are inspected during periodic servicing, not daily.
whyNot.C: Cylinder head bolts are checked only during major servicing or repairs.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which of these is a major obstacle to the use of tractors on many Nigerian farms?
options: Very low cost of spare parts
Too much flat and well-drained land
questions.explanation: Most Nigerian farmers have small, fragmented plots on which large machines cannot work economically. High machine cost, scarce spare parts and few trained operators add to the problem.

whyNot.A: Spare parts are usually scarce and expensive, which hinders mechanisation.
whyNot.B: There is a shortage, not an oversupply, of trained operators and mechanics.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which tractor-drawn implement is used to form heaps of soil into long raised rows for planting yam or cassava?
questions.explanation: A ridger has mouldboards that throw soil to both sides, forming ridges and furrows. Ridges give root and tuber crops loose soil to grow in and help drainage.

whyNot.B: A mower cuts grass or forage.
whyNot.D: A sheller removes grains such as maize from the cob.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A tractor pulls a harrow of working width 2 m at 6 km/h with a field efficiency of 75%. How long will it take to harrow a 9 ha field?
questions.explanation: Theoretical capacity = 2 m × 6,000 m per hour = 12,000 m² = 1.2 ha per hour. Effective capacity = 1.2 × 0.75 = 0.9 ha per hour. Time = 9 ÷ 0.9 = 10 hours.

whyNot.B: 7.5 hours uses 1.2 ha per hour and ignores the 75% efficiency.
whyNot.C: 13.5 hours multiplies by 1.5 instead of dividing by the capacity.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In land surveying on a farm, the prismatic compass is used to
options: find the height of a building
measure the length of a boundary
mark out straight lines with poles
measure the bearing of a line
questions.explanation: The prismatic compass measures the direction (bearing) of a survey line from magnetic north. Lengths are measured with chains or tapes, and straight lines are marked with ranging poles.

whyNot.B: Lengths are measured with a chain or measuring tape.
whyNot.C: Ranging poles mark out straight lines.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: A rectangular cassava farm measures 400 m by 250 m. What is its area in hectares?

whyNot.C: 100 ha comes from dividing by 1,000 instead of 10,000.
whyNot.A: 65 comes from adding the two sides (650) and then dividing by 10.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: In the petrol engine of a small farm water pump, the part that mixes fuel with air in the right proportion before it enters the cylinder is the
questions.explanation: In a petrol engine the carburettor atomises petrol and mixes it with air in the correct ratio; the mixture is drawn into the cylinder and ignited by the spark plug.

whyNot.D: A fuel injector pump forces diesel into the cylinders of a diesel engine; it does not pre-mix fuel with air.
whyNot.C: The spark plug ignites the mixture; it does not mix it.

questions.subject: agricultural-science
questions.stem: Which piece of equipment is carried on the back to spray pesticides on vegetables?
questions.explanation: A knapsack sprayer is a tank carried on the back with a hand pump and nozzle, used to apply pesticides and herbicides as a fine spray.

whyNot.A: A watering can supplies water, not a fine pesticide spray.
whyNot.C: A seed drill sows seeds in rows.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: On the Nigerian national flag, what does the green colour stand for?
options: The blood of those who died for independence
Unity and peace among the people
Agriculture and the natural wealth of the land
The oil and gas wealth of the Niger Delta
questions.explanation: Nigeria's flag has three vertical bands: green, white, green. The green stands for agriculture and the country's natural wealth, while the white band in the middle stands for unity and peace.

whyNot.B: Unity and peace is the meaning of the white band, not the green.
whyNot.A: There is no red on Nigeria's flag, and no colour on it stands for blood.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: On Nigeria's coat of arms, what do the two white horses that support the shield represent?
questions.explanation: The two white horses (chargers) on either side of the shield represent dignity. The red eagle on top stands for strength, the black shield for Nigeria's fertile soil, and the white wavy Y for the Rivers Niger and Benue.

whyNot.B: Strength is shown by the red eagle at the top.
whyNot.C: The fertile soil is shown by the black colour of the shield.
whyNot.D: The two rivers are shown by the white wavy Y on the shield.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which section of the 1999 Constitution sets out the duties of every Nigerian citizen, such as respecting the national flag and paying taxes promptly?
questions.explanation: Section 24 lists the duties of citizens: to abide by the Constitution and respect the national flag, anthem and pledge, help maintain law and order, contribute to the community, and declare income honestly and pay taxes promptly.

whyNot.D: Section 33 guarantees the right to life.
whyNot.B: Section 14 deals with the government and the people (for example, that sovereignty belongs to the people).
whyNot.C: Section 1 declares the supremacy of the Constitution.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Ada was born in Kano in 2008. Her father is a Nigerian citizen and her mother is a Ghanaian. By which means is Ada a citizen of Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Under section 25, a person born in Nigeria after 1 October 1960, either of whose parents (or any of whose grandparents) is a Nigerian citizen, is a citizen by birth. Ada was born in Nigeria and her father is Nigerian, so she is a citizen by birth.

whyNot.A: Registration (section 26) is for people such as a foreign woman married to a Nigerian man; Ada qualifies by birth already.
whyNot.D: Naturalisation (section 27) is for foreigners who apply after many years of living in Nigeria.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Tunde finds a wallet containing ₦50,000 and the owner's ID card at a bus stop in Ibadan. He takes it to the owner's address and returns everything. Which value has he shown?
questions.explanation: Honesty means being truthful and not taking what belongs to others. Tunde could have kept the money, but he returned it in full to its rightful owner, which is honesty (integrity).

whyNot.B: Self-reliance is depending on your own effort and skills to meet your needs.
whyNot.A: Tolerance is accepting people whose beliefs, culture or opinions differ from yours.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which federal agency has the main duty of promoting national values and educating citizens about government policies and programmes?
questions.explanation: The National Orientation Agency (NOA) is responsible for public enlightenment: it mobilises citizens, promotes national values such as patriotism and discipline, and explains government policies to the people.

whyNot.D: The NYSC organises the one-year service of young graduates to promote national unity.
whyNot.B: The NBC regulates radio and television broadcasting.
whyNot.C: INEC organises federal and state elections.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Under the 1999 Constitution, which group of Nigerian citizens cannot be deprived of their citizenship by the President?
options: Naturalised citizens who have lived in Nigeria for over ten years
questions.explanation: Section 30 allows the President to deprive a person of citizenship in certain cases (for example, disloyalty or a prison sentence of three years or more soon after naturalisation), but it applies only to persons who are not citizens by birth. Citizenship by birth cannot be taken away by deprivation.

whyNot.D: Section 30(2) allows a citizen by registration to be deprived of citizenship for acts or speech showing disloyalty to Nigeria.
whyNot.B: Naturalised citizens can be deprived of citizenship under section 30.
whyNot.C: Length of residence does not protect a naturalised citizen; they are still not citizens by birth.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Chika, a Nigerian by birth, becomes a British citizen while working in London. According to the 1999 Constitution, what happens to her Nigerian citizenship?
options: She remains a Nigerian citizen, because a citizen by birth may also hold another country's citizenship
She becomes a Nigerian citizen by registration instead of by birth
She loses Nigerian citizenship as soon as she becomes British
She must give up British citizenship within one year to remain Nigerian
questions.explanation: Section 28 says a person forfeits Nigerian citizenship by acquiring another country's citizenship only if he or she is NOT a citizen by birth. A citizen by birth like Chika may hold dual citizenship and keeps her Nigerian citizenship.

whyNot.C: Automatic loss on taking another citizenship applies only to citizens by registration or naturalisation.
whyNot.D: The Constitution sets no such one-year deadline for a citizen by birth.
whyNot.B: Citizenship by birth does not change into citizenship by registration.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: The Nigerian national pledge begins, "I pledge to Nigeria my country, to be …". Which words come next?
questions.explanation: The pledge reads: "I pledge to Nigeria my country, to be faithful, loyal and honest, to serve Nigeria with all my strength, to defend her unity and uphold her honour and glory, so help me God."

whyNot.B: These words are not part of the pledge.
whyNot.C: The pledge speaks of defending Nigeria's unity, but these three words are not its wording.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which of the following best shows patriotism?
options: Leaving community work to government because it is government's duty
Reporting people seen vandalising a public power transformer to the police
Supporting only candidates from one's own ethnic group
Refusing to pay tax because some leaders are corrupt
questions.explanation: Patriotism is love for one's country shown by actions that protect and develop it. Reporting vandals protects public property that serves everyone, and section 24 asks citizens to help the authorities maintain law and order.

whyNot.D: Paying taxes promptly is a constitutional duty (section 24); refusing to pay harms the nation.
whyNot.C: Voting only along ethnic lines is tribalism, which weakens national unity.
whyNot.A: Citizens are expected to contribute to the advancement of their communities, not leave everything to government.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which chapter of the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria contains the fundamental human rights?
questions.explanation: Chapter IV (sections 33 to 46) contains the fundamental rights, such as the right to life, dignity, personal liberty, fair hearing and freedom of expression.

whyNot.D: Chapter II contains the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy.
whyNot.A: Chapter III deals with citizenship.
whyNot.B: Chapter VI deals with the executive.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: In which year did the United Nations General Assembly adopt the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
questions.explanation: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948. That date is celebrated every year as Human Rights Day.

whyNot.C: 1945 is the year the United Nations itself was founded.
whyNot.B: 1960 is the year Nigeria became independent.
whyNot.D: 1981 is the year the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights was adopted.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: A court convicts Musa of theft without allowing him to call witnesses or speak in his own defence. Which of his fundamental rights has been violated?
options: Right to dignity of the human person
Right to private and family life
questions.explanation: Section 36 guarantees the right to fair hearing: an accused person must be given adequate time and facilities to prepare a defence, to defend himself and to call witnesses before an independent court. Musa was denied all of these.

whyNot.B: Dignity of the human person (section 34) protects against torture, slavery and inhuman treatment.
whyNot.D: Freedom of movement (section 41) is about moving freely within Nigeria and leaving or entering it.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Officers beat a suspect in a police cell to force a confession. Which right guaranteed in section 34 of the Constitution has been violated?
options: Right to acquire and own property
Right to dignity of the human person
Right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion
questions.explanation: Section 34 protects the dignity of every person: no one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment. Beating a suspect to force a confession is torture.

whyNot.D: Fair hearing (section 36) concerns how a trial is conducted, not treatment in custody.
whyNot.C: Section 38 protects freedom of belief and worship.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Police ban a planned rally in a town where violent clashes between two communities are still going on. On which ground does section 45 of the Constitution allow such a restriction on freedom of assembly?
options: The fact that the organisers are students
The fact that the rally will criticise the government
Protecting the interests of the ruling party
questions.explanation: Section 45 allows laws that restrict some rights where reasonably justifiable in a democratic society in the interest of defence, public safety, public order, public morality or public health, or to protect the rights of others. A rally during ongoing violence threatens public safety and order.

whyNot.C: Protecting a party's interests is not a lawful ground for restricting rights.
whyNot.B: Criticising government is protected by freedom of expression (section 39); it is not a ground for a ban.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Under section 35 of the Constitution, a person arrested for an offence must be brought before a court within what period, where there is a court of competent jurisdiction within a radius of 40 kilometres?
questions.explanation: Section 35(5) defines a "reasonable time" for bringing an arrested person to court: one day where there is a competent court within 40 km, and two days or any longer period the court considers reasonable in other cases.

whyNot.C: Two days applies where there is no competent court within a 40 km radius.
whyNot.A: Seven days is not a period stated in section 35.
whyNot.D: Fourteen days is not a period stated in section 35.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: According to section 36 of the 1999 Constitution, a person charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed to be what until proved guilty?
questions.explanation: Section 36(5) says every person charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until he is proved guilty. The prosecution must prove the charge; the accused does not have to prove his innocence.

whyNot.A: Presuming guilt would reverse the burden of proof, which the Constitution forbids.
whyNot.D: An accused person keeps all fundamental rights, including fair hearing.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Chapter II of the Constitution says government shall provide free education when practicable. Why can a citizen not successfully sue the government in court for failing to do this?
options: Chapter II provisions are not justiciable, so courts cannot enforce them
Chapter II was removed from the Constitution by amendment
Only the National Human Rights Commission may sue the government
Education is a matter for state governments only
questions.explanation: The Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy in Chapter II are goals for government. Section 6(6)(c) says the courts' judicial powers do not extend to them, so they are non-justiciable. Chapter IV rights, by contrast, can be enforced in court.

whyNot.D: Education is on the concurrent list; federal, state and local governments all have roles.
whyNot.C: Any person whose enforceable right is violated may go to court; that is not the reason here.
whyNot.B: Chapter II is still part of the 1999 Constitution.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Under section 46 of the Constitution, a person who claims that any of his fundamental rights has been, or is likely to be, violated may apply for redress to which court?
options: A High Court in that state
questions.explanation: Section 46(1) gives special jurisdiction to the High Court: any person who alleges that any provision of Chapter IV has been, is being or is likely to be contravened in any state may apply to a High Court in that state for redress.

whyNot.D: Customary courts handle matters of customary law such as marriage and inheritance.
whyNot.A: The Code of Conduct Tribunal tries public officers who break the Code of Conduct.
whyNot.B: Magistrates' courts are not given this special jurisdiction under section 46.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which body established by the Federal Government in 1995 monitors, investigates and reports on human rights abuses in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) was set up in 1995 to promote and protect human rights. It receives complaints, investigates abuses and advises government on human rights.

whyNot.D: The Public Complaints Commission (the ombudsman) handles complaints about administrative injustice by officials.
whyNot.A: The ICPC fights corruption in public offices.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Democracy is popularly defined as "government of the people, by the people, for the people". Who gave this definition?
questions.explanation: This definition comes from Abraham Lincoln, President of the United States, in his Gettysburg Address of 1863. It stresses that power comes from the people and is used for their benefit.

whyNot.D: A. V. Dicey is known for popularising the concept of the rule of law.
whyNot.C: Montesquieu is known for the theory of separation of powers.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which British jurist popularised the concept of the rule of law in his book on the law of the constitution (1885)?
questions.explanation: Albert Venn Dicey, in Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885), explained the rule of law through three principles: supremacy of the law, equality before the law, and protection of individual rights.

whyNot.A: Montesquieu wrote about separation of powers.
whyNot.C: Lincoln is known for his definition of democracy.
whyNot.B: Max Weber is known for his theory of bureaucracy.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: The son of a wealthy businessman and a market trader are charged with the same offence. Both are tried in the same kind of court under the same law and receive the same punishment. Which principle of the rule of law does this show?
questions.explanation: Equality before the law means every person, rich or poor, powerful or ordinary, is subject to the same laws and the same courts. Treating both men in the same way is this principle at work.

whyNot.C: Separation of powers is about dividing government functions among the legislature, executive and judiciary.
whyNot.A: Federal character concerns fair spread of appointments among states and groups.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Section 308 of the 1999 Constitution protects the President, Vice-President, Governors and Deputy Governors from civil or criminal proceedings while in office. Why is this regarded as a limitation on the rule of law?
options: It weakens the independence of the legislature
It prevents citizens from voting in elections
It gives the courts too much power over the executive
It goes against the principle of equality before the law
questions.explanation: The rule of law says no one is above the law. The immunity in section 308 means these officials cannot be sued or prosecuted while in office, so they are not treated equally with other citizens during that time. This makes it a limitation on the rule of law.

whyNot.A: The immunity clause concerns the executive, not the powers of the legislature.
whyNot.C: Immunity reduces, rather than increases, the courts' power over these officials.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Direct democracy, in which all adult male citizens met in an assembly to make decisions themselves, is most associated with which ancient society?
questions.explanation: Direct democracy was practised in ancient Athens, a Greek city-state, where adult male citizens gathered in the Assembly to debate and vote on laws. It worked because the city was small; large modern states use representative democracy instead.

whyNot.D: The Oyo Empire was ruled by the Alaafin with checks from the Oyo Mesi; it was not a direct democracy.
whyNot.B: Ancient Egypt was ruled by pharaohs.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: The Supreme Court declares a law passed by the National Assembly null and void because it conflicts with the Constitution. What is this power of the courts called?
questions.explanation: Judicial review is the power of the courts to examine laws and government actions and declare them void if they go against the Constitution. It is one way the judiciary checks the legislature and executive.

whyNot.A: Judicial precedent means lower courts follow earlier decisions of higher courts.
whyNot.C: Delegated legislation is law made by bodies such as ministries under powers given by the legislature.
whyNot.B: A veto is the executive's refusal to sign a bill, not a court's power.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Voters in a senatorial district sign a petition, supported by more than half of the registered voters there, to remove their senator before the end of his term. This process is called
questions.explanation: Recall allows voters to remove their elected representative before the term ends. Section 69 of the Constitution provides for recalling a member of the National Assembly through a petition signed by more than one-half of the registered voters in the constituency, followed by a vote.

whyNot.C: A referendum is a direct vote by citizens on a proposal or issue, not on removing a particular representative.
whyNot.A: Impeachment is removal by the legislature itself, used for the President, Governors and their deputies.
whyNot.D: A by-election is held to fill a seat that has become vacant.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: What is the minimum age at which a Nigerian citizen may register and vote in elections?
questions.explanation: Nigeria practises universal adult suffrage. Every citizen who has attained 18 years of age and is registered may vote in elections.

whyNot.A: 16 is too young to vote in Nigeria.
whyNot.D: 21 is not Nigeria's voting age; any citizen aged 18 or above may register.
whyNot.B: 25 is not the voting age; it is closer to the minimum ages for contesting some offices.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which body conducts elections into local government councils in a Nigerian state?
options: The state Ministry of Local Government
questions.explanation: The Constitution gives each state's Independent Electoral Commission (SIEC) the power to organise elections into local government councils in that state. INEC conducts elections for the President, Governors, the National Assembly and State Houses of Assembly.

whyNot.D: INEC does not conduct local government council elections.
whyNot.B: A ministry is part of the executive and is not an electoral body.
whyNot.C: The House of Assembly makes laws; it does not run elections.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Many eligible voters in a ward refuse to register or vote because they believe their votes will not count. This attitude is called
questions.explanation: Political apathy is a lack of interest in, or withdrawal from, political activities such as voting. It weakens popular participation, which democracy needs to be truly representative.

whyNot.A: Political socialisation is the process by which people learn political values and attitudes.
whyNot.C: Political culture is the shared political beliefs and attitudes of a whole society.
whyNot.D: Franchise is the right to vote itself.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which agency is responsible for arresting and prosecuting people who traffic in hard drugs such as cocaine and heroin in Nigeria?
options: National Agency for the Control of AIDS (NACA)
National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC)
National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP)
questions.explanation: The NDLEA enforces Nigeria's laws against illegal drugs: it arrests and prosecutes drug traffickers, seizes drugs, and also works to reduce drug demand through education and rehabilitation.

whyNot.C: NAFDAC regulates the quality of food, drugs and cosmetics, not the prosecution of hard-drug traffickers.
whyNot.D: NAPTIP fights trafficking in persons, not in drugs.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which agency was set up in 2003 to fight trafficking in persons in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: The National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP) was established in 2003 under the Trafficking in Persons law. It investigates and prosecutes traffickers and rescues and rehabilitates victims.

whyNot.D: The NDLEA deals with illegal drugs.
whyNot.A: The EFCC deals with economic and financial crimes such as fraud and money laundering.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which of the following can transmit HIV from one person to another?
questions.explanation: HIV spreads through infected body fluids such as blood, semen, vaginal fluids and breast milk. Sharing unsterilised razors, needles or other sharp objects can pass infected blood into a cut. Casual contact does not spread it.

whyNot.B: HIV is not spread by casual contact like handshakes.
whyNot.D: Mosquitoes do not transmit HIV.
whyNot.C: HIV does not survive in a way that lets it spread through toilet seats.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Bola buys codeine cough syrup without a prescription and drinks it every day to "feel high". What is Bola doing?
questions.explanation: Drug abuse is the use of a drug for a non-medical purpose, in excessive amounts or without a doctor's prescription. Bola uses codeine to get high, not to treat a cough, so he is abusing it.

whyNot.B: Drug trafficking is dealing in or transporting illegal drugs on a large scale.
whyNot.A: Drug peddling is selling drugs illegally, usually in small quantities.
whyNot.C: Drug smuggling is moving drugs across borders illegally.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which of the following is a direct effect of clashes between secret cults in tertiary institutions?
options: Loss of lives and disruption of the academic calendar
More foreign students applying for admission
Better relations between students and staff
questions.explanation: Cult clashes often lead to killings, injuries and destruction of property. Institutions may be closed for safety, which disrupts lectures and examinations and delays graduation.

whyNot.C: Violence and closures delay students, so they do not raise graduation rates.
whyNot.D: Cultism creates fear and threats against staff and students, harming relations.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Parents in some rural communities hand their children over to people who promise them good jobs in the city, but the children end up in forced labour. Which factor most often pushes parents into this?
options: Too many schools in rural areas
Poverty and lack of opportunities at home
Good roads between villages and cities
questions.explanation: Traffickers take advantage of poverty and unemployment. Parents who cannot feed or educate their children are easily deceived by promises of good jobs and money, so poverty is a major push factor in human trafficking.

whyNot.D: Religious belief is not the usual cause of giving children to traffickers.
whyNot.A: Plenty of schools would keep children learning at home, not push them away.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: How does HIV cause AIDS in an infected person?
options: It destroys red blood cells, causing anaemia
It attacks only the liver, causing jaundice
It blocks blood vessels in the heart
It destroys white blood cells (CD4 cells) that help the body fight infections
questions.explanation: HIV attacks CD4 cells, a type of white blood cell in the immune system. As their number falls, the body can no longer fight infections. The late stage, when many serious infections appear, is called AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome).

whyNot.A: HIV targets the immune system's white blood cells, not red blood cells.
whyNot.B: HIV is not a liver disease; hepatitis viruses attack the liver.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which statement about antiretroviral therapy (ART) for people living with HIV is correct?
options: It removes the virus completely from the body after one course of treatment
It is a vaccine given to prevent HIV infection
It suppresses the virus so the person can live a long, healthy life, but it does not cure HIV
It is only useful after a person has developed full-blown AIDS
questions.explanation: Antiretroviral drugs reduce the amount of HIV in the body and protect the immune system. Taken every day, they allow people living with HIV to live long and healthy lives and greatly reduce the chance of passing on the virus. They do not cure HIV, so treatment must continue for life.

whyNot.A: There is no cure for HIV yet; stopping ART lets the virus multiply again.
whyNot.B: There is currently no approved vaccine against HIV.
whyNot.D: ART works best when started early, soon after diagnosis.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes human trafficking from migrant smuggling?
options: Trafficking ends once the person arrives at the destination
Trafficking can only take place across international borders
Trafficking involves exploiting the victim through force, fraud or coercion
Trafficking requires the victim to pay a fee for the journey
questions.explanation: Migrant smuggling is helping someone cross a border illegally, usually with their consent and for a fee, and the relationship ends on arrival. Human trafficking is about exploitation: victims are recruited or moved by force, deception or coercion and then exploited for labour, sex or other purposes, and it can happen within one country.

whyNot.B: Trafficking can happen within a country, for example from a village to a city.
whyNot.D: Paying a fee for the journey is typical of smuggling; trafficking is defined by exploitation.
whyNot.A: Exploitation usually continues after arrival in trafficking, unlike smuggling.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which of these drugs is classified as a stimulant?
questions.explanation: Stimulants speed up the activity of the brain and nervous system, raising alertness and heart rate. Cocaine is a strong stimulant. Abuse can cause heart problems, anxiety and addiction.

whyNot.A: Heroin is an opioid (narcotic) that slows down the nervous system.
whyNot.C: Diazepam is a sedative (depressant).
whyNot.B: Alcohol is a depressant, even though it may first make people feel lively.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: What is the main function of the civil service?
options: To interpret laws and settle disputes
To make laws for the country
To implement government policies and programmes
questions.explanation: The civil service is the body of permanent, non-political officials who work in government ministries and departments. Its main job is to carry out (implement) the policies and decisions of government; it also advises ministers.

whyNot.B: Making laws is the work of the legislature.
whyNot.A: Interpreting laws is the work of the judiciary.
whyNot.D: Elections are conducted by electoral commissions such as INEC.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Who is the administrative head and accounting officer of a federal ministry?
options: The Head of the Civil Service of the Federation
questions.explanation: The Permanent Secretary is the most senior career civil servant in a ministry. He or she manages the ministry's staff and is its accounting officer, responsible for how its money is spent. The Minister is the political head.

whyNot.D: The Minister is the political head who sets policy direction, not the administrative head.
whyNot.A: The Head of the Civil Service oversees the whole federal civil service, not a single ministry.
whyNot.C: The Auditor-General audits government accounts.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which statement best describes a pressure group?
options: A committee of the legislature that examines bills
A government agency that regulates trade unions
An organised group that contests elections in order to form a government
An organised group that tries to influence government policy without seeking to control government
questions.explanation: A pressure (interest) group is an association of people with common interests that tries to influence government decisions in their favour. Unlike a political party, it does not field candidates to win power.

whyNot.C: Contesting elections to form government is what a political party does.
whyNot.B: A pressure group is a private association, not a government agency.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Civil servants do not receive public praise or blame for the policies they help to make; the minister takes responsibility instead. Which principle of the civil service is this?
questions.explanation: Anonymity means civil servants remain unnamed and in the background. The minister answers publicly for the ministry's policies, so civil servants are protected and can give honest advice.

whyNot.A: Neutrality means civil servants do not take sides in party politics.
whyNot.C: Permanence means civil servants keep their jobs when governments change.
whyNot.B: Meritocracy means recruitment and promotion are based on ability.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a pressure group in Nigeria?
options: The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency
questions.explanation: The Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) is a federation of trade unions that presses government on workers' welfare, wages and policies. It is a classic interest (pressure) group outside government.

whyNot.C: INEC is a government body that conducts elections.
whyNot.B: The Senate is part of the legislature.
whyNot.D: The NDLEA is a government law-enforcement agency.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Leaders of the Nigerian Bar Association meet privately with members of the National Assembly to persuade them to amend a bill. Which method of pressure groups is this?
questions.explanation: Lobbying is direct, often private, contact with lawmakers or officials to persuade them to support a group's position. Meeting legislators to argue for changes to a bill is lobbying.

whyNot.D: A strike is when workers stop work to press their demands.
whyNot.A: A boycott is refusing to buy, use or take part in something as a protest.
whyNot.C: Litigation is taking a case to court.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: A retired teacher's pension has been delayed for two years because officials keep losing her file. Which body can she complain to, free of charge, about this administrative injustice?
questions.explanation: The Public Complaints Commission is Nigeria's ombudsman. It investigates complaints from citizens about injustice, delay or abuse by government officials and agencies, and its services are free.

whyNot.C: The Code of Conduct Tribunal tries public officers for breaches of the Code of Conduct, such as false asset declaration.
whyNot.B: The Federal Character Commission monitors the fair spread of public appointments.
whyNot.A: The NOA does public enlightenment, not complaints about officials.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: What is the main difference between a political party and a pressure group?
options: A political party is registered by the courts; a pressure group is registered by INEC
A political party works only at state level; a pressure group works only at federal level
A political party has members; a pressure group has no members
A political party seeks to win elections and control government; a pressure group only seeks to influence government
questions.explanation: Both are organised groups, but their aims differ. A political party presents candidates to win elections and form a government. A pressure group stays outside government and tries to influence its decisions on behalf of its members or a cause.

whyNot.A: INEC registers political parties, not pressure groups.
whyNot.C: Pressure groups such as trade unions have many members.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: A file needing one approval passes through fourteen desks in a ministry and takes six months to be treated. Which problem of the civil service does this show?
questions.explanation: Red tape is excessive following of rules and procedures, which causes unnecessary delay. Passing a simple file through many desks for months is a clear case.

whyNot.B: Nepotism is favouring relatives in appointments or contracts.
whyNot.A: Anonymity is a principle of the civil service, not a problem of delay.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Section 14(3) of the 1999 Constitution requires that appointments into federal government agencies reflect the "federal character" of Nigeria. What is the purpose of this principle?
options: To keep civil servants out of party politics
To give every state the same population
To ensure only the best-qualified candidates are ever appointed
To prevent a few states or ethnic groups from dominating government agencies
questions.explanation: The federal character principle aims to promote national unity and loyalty by making sure that appointments in government and its agencies are spread among the states and groups, so that no few states, ethnic or other groups dominate.

whyNot.C: Federal character balances merit with fair spread; its aim is not merit alone.
whyNot.A: Keeping civil servants out of party politics is the principle of neutrality.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: What does the red eagle at the top of Nigeria's coat of arms represent?
questions.explanation: On the coat of arms, the red eagle stands for strength. The white horses stand for dignity and the black shield for Nigeria's fertile soil.

whyNot.A: Dignity is represented by the two white horses.
whyNot.D: Fertile soil is represented by the black shield.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: What is the national motto of Nigeria, as stated in the 1999 Constitution?
options: Peace and Unity, Justice and Progress
Unity and Strength, Faith and Progress
Unity and Faith, Peace and Progress
Faith and Labour, Peace and Unity
questions.explanation: Section 15(1) of the Constitution states that the motto of Nigeria shall be "Unity and Faith, Peace and Progress". It also appears on the coat of arms.

whyNot.B: This mixes up the words; "strength" is not in the motto.
whyNot.A: "Justice" is not in the motto.
whyNot.D: This is not Nigeria's motto.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: On Nigeria's coat of arms, what does the white wavy Y-shaped band on the black shield represent?
options: The Rivers Niger and Benue meeting at Lokoja
The roads linking the north and the south
questions.explanation: The wavy white Y shows the two main rivers, the Niger and the Benue, which meet (their confluence) at Lokoja in Kogi State before flowing south to the sea.

whyNot.B: The coat of arms has no symbol for ethnic groups.
whyNot.C: The arms of government are not shown on the coat of arms.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which national anthem was first used when Nigeria became independent in 1960, was replaced in 1978, and was restored as the national anthem by law in 2024?
questions.explanation: "Nigeria, We Hail Thee" was the anthem at independence in 1960. In 1978 it was replaced by "Arise, O Compatriots". The National Anthem Act of 2024 restored "Nigeria, We Hail Thee" as the national anthem.

whyNot.D: "Arise, O Compatriots" was the anthem from 1978 until 2024; it replaced the 1960 anthem.
whyNot.A: This is not the title of a Nigerian national anthem.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Who designed Nigeria's green-white-green national flag?
questions.explanation: Michael Taiwo Akinkunmi, then a Nigerian student in London, designed the flag in 1959 for a competition. It was first raised at independence on 1 October 1960.

whyNot.B: Herbert Macaulay was a nationalist often called the father of Nigerian nationalism.
whyNot.D: Nnamdi Azikiwe was a nationalist leader and Nigeria's first President.
whyNot.C: Obafemi Awolowo was a nationalist leader and Premier of the Western Region.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: In a Jos neighbourhood, Christian and Muslim families attend each other's weddings and naming ceremonies and help one another during festivals. Which value are they showing?
questions.explanation: Tolerance means accepting and respecting people whose beliefs or ways of life differ from yours. The families respect each other's faiths and live peacefully together, which is religious tolerance.

whyNot.B: Self-reliance is depending on one's own effort to meet one's needs.
whyNot.A: Contentment is being satisfied with what one has lawfully obtained.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Grace, a Kenyan woman, marries Emeka, a Nigerian citizen. By which means does the 1999 Constitution most directly allow her to become a Nigerian citizen?
questions.explanation: Section 26 allows registration as a citizen for a woman who is or has been married to a Nigerian citizen (and for some persons with a Nigerian grandparent), subject to conditions such as good character. This is the direct route for Grace.

whyNot.A: Citizenship by birth depends on one's own birth and parentage, which Grace does not have.
whyNot.D: Naturalisation is for other foreigners and requires many years of residence; marriage gives a more direct route.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Under section 27 of the 1999 Constitution, a foreigner applying for citizenship by naturalisation must normally have lived in Nigeria for a continuous period of how many years immediately before applying?
questions.explanation: Section 27(2)(g) requires residence in Nigeria for a continuous period of fifteen years immediately before the application (or, alternatively, twelve continuous months plus at least fifteen years in total during the previous twenty years). Other conditions include good character and the ability to contribute to Nigeria.

whyNot.D: Five years is far shorter than the period required.
whyNot.B: Ten years is shorter than the fifteen years stated in section 27.
whyNot.C: Twenty-five years is longer than required.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which of the following is listed in section 24 of the 1999 Constitution as a duty of every citizen?
options: Declaring income honestly to the appropriate agencies and paying tax promptly
Belonging to a cultural association in one's state of origin
Voting in every election held in Nigeria
questions.explanation: Section 24 lists duties including respecting the Constitution, flag, anthem and pledge; enhancing Nigeria's prestige; respecting others' dignity; contributing to the community; helping maintain law and order; and declaring income honestly and paying taxes promptly.

whyNot.A: Joining a party is a right (freedom of association), not a constitutional duty.
whyNot.D: Voting is a civic responsibility, but section 24 does not make it a constitutional duty.
whyNot.C: Membership of a cultural association is a personal choice.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: On what date did Nigeria become an independent country?
questions.explanation: Nigeria gained independence from Britain on 1 October 1960, which is celebrated every year as Independence Day.

whyNot.B: 1 October 1963 is when Nigeria became a republic.
whyNot.D: 12 June 1993 is the date of the annulled presidential election, now marked as Democracy Day.
whyNot.C: 29 May 1999 is when civilian rule returned under the 1999 Constitution.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which fundamental right is guaranteed by section 33 of the 1999 Constitution?
questions.explanation: Section 33 states that every person has a right to life and no one shall be intentionally deprived of life, except in execution of a court sentence for a criminal offence of which he has been found guilty.

whyNot.C: Freedom of expression and the press is in section 39.
whyNot.B: Personal liberty is in section 35.
whyNot.D: Freedom of movement is in section 41.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Which statement best defines human rights?
options: Rights enjoyed only by adults who are registered voters
Favours that government may grant or withdraw at will
Basic rights and freedoms that every person is entitled to simply because he or she is a human being
Privileges given only to citizens who pay tax
questions.explanation: Human rights are the basic entitlements every person has by virtue of being human, such as the right to life, dignity and fair hearing. They are universal and are protected by law, for example in Chapter IV of the Constitution.

whyNot.D: Human rights do not depend on paying tax.
whyNot.A: Children and non-voters also have human rights.
whyNot.B: Rights are protected by law; government cannot simply withdraw them at will.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: The African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights was adopted in 1981 by which organisation?
options: Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS)
questions.explanation: The African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (also called the Banjul Charter) was adopted by the OAU, now the African Union, in 1981. Nigeria has made it part of its domestic law.

whyNot.C: ECOWAS is a regional body for West Africa only.
whyNot.B: The UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: A newspaper is shut down by government agents for publishing articles that criticise government policies. Which right is most directly violated?
options: Right to private and family life
Right to dignity of the human person
Freedom of expression and the press
questions.explanation: Section 39 guarantees freedom of expression, including the freedom to hold opinions and to receive and pass on ideas and information, and the right to own and operate a medium such as a newspaper. Closing a paper for criticism violates this right.

whyNot.A: Private and family life (section 37) protects homes, correspondence and phone conversations.
whyNot.D: Freedom of movement (section 41) is about travelling within and out of Nigeria.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Amina is refused a job in a federal agency only because of her state of origin, although she is fully qualified. Which right in section 42 has been violated?
options: Right to peaceful assembly and association
Right to acquire and own property
questions.explanation: Section 42 protects citizens from being disadvantaged simply because of their community, ethnic group, place of origin, sex, religion or political opinion. Refusing Amina a job only because of her state of origin is discrimination.

whyNot.B: Fair hearing (section 36) concerns trials and decisions affecting one's rights.
whyNot.A: Assembly and association (section 40) is about gathering and forming or joining groups.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Security agents secretly tap a journalist's phone calls without any court order or lawful authority. Which right is violated?
options: Right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Right to private and family life
questions.explanation: Section 37 guarantees and protects the privacy of citizens, their homes, correspondence, telephone conversations and telegraphic communications. Unlawful phone tapping violates this right.

whyNot.C: The right to life protects against being unlawfully killed.
whyNot.A: Section 38 protects freedom of belief and worship.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Government takes over Mr Bello's land compulsorily to build a public road. Under section 44 of the Constitution, what must government do?
options: Ask the National Assembly to approve each acquisition
Give him another plot in the same street within ten years
Nothing, since all land belongs to government
Pay prompt compensation and allow him access to court over the amount
questions.explanation: Section 44 says no property shall be taken compulsorily except under a law that requires prompt payment of compensation and gives the owner a right of access to a court to decide his interest and the amount of compensation.

whyNot.C: Even when land is acquired for public use, the Constitution requires compensation.
whyNot.B: Section 44 requires compensation, not a replacement plot after ten years.
whyNot.A: Section 44 does not require National Assembly approval for each acquisition.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: A court order directing that a detained person be brought before the court so that the legality of the detention can be examined is called
questions.explanation: Habeas corpus (Latin for "you shall have the body") requires those holding a person to produce him in court and justify the detention. If there is no lawful reason, the person is released. It protects personal liberty.

whyNot.A: Mandamus is an order compelling a public body to perform a duty.
whyNot.D: Certiorari is an order bringing a lower court's decision up for review.
whyNot.C: An injunction is an order stopping someone from doing something (or requiring it).

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: Human Rights Day, which marks the adoption of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, is celebrated every year on
questions.explanation: The UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948, so 10 December is Human Rights Day.

whyNot.C: 1 December is World AIDS Day.
whyNot.A: 26 June is the International Day Against Drug Abuse and Illicit Trafficking.
whyNot.D: 12 June is Democracy Day in Nigeria.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is forced to break stones in a quarry every day without pay. Which right in the 1999 Constitution protects people from being required to perform forced or compulsory labour?
options: Right to dignity of the human person
questions.explanation: Section 34(1) on the dignity of the human person says no person shall be subjected to torture or degrading treatment, held in slavery or servitude, or required to perform forced or compulsory labour.

whyNot.B: Personal liberty (section 35) protects against unlawful arrest and detention; forced labour is covered under dignity in section 34.
whyNot.A: Freedom of movement (section 41) is about travel within and out of Nigeria.

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: The word "democracy" comes from two Greek words, demos and kratos. What do they mean?
questions.explanation: Demos means "people" and kratos means "rule" or "power". Democracy therefore means rule by the people.

whyNot.A: "City" in Greek is polis, the root of "politics".
whyNot.D: These words describe the number of rulers in other systems, not the roots of "democracy".

questions.subject: civic-education
questions.stem: The theory of separation of powers is most closely associated with which writer?
