questions.explanation: Acts 3:1-8 tells how Peter and John went up to the temple at the hour of prayer. Peter said, in effect, 'I have no silver and gold, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk.' The man leapt up and entered the temple praising God.

whyNot.A: Peter gave healing instead of money.
whyNot.D: Laying on of hands for the Spirit is linked to the Samaritan believers (Acts 8:17), not this healing.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: What was the sin of Ananias and his wife Sapphira in Acts 5?
options: They offered money to buy the power of the Holy Spirit
They kept back part of the price of their land and lied about it
They refused to sell their land to help the poor
They denied Jesus before the high priest
questions.explanation: Acts 5:1-11 says they sold a property, kept back some of the money, and brought the rest as if it were the full price. Peter said the land and money were theirs to keep; their sin was lying to the Holy Spirit and to God. Both died, and great fear came on the church.

whyNot.C: They did sell the land; Peter said they were free not to sell it.
whyNot.A: Offering money for the Spirit's power was the sin of Simon the magician (Acts 8:18-20).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: At the stoning of Stephen, the witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man. Who was he?
questions.explanation: Acts 7:58 says the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul, and Acts 8:1 adds that Saul approved of his execution. This Saul later became the apostle Paul after his conversion (Acts 9).

whyNot.D: Gamaliel was a Pharisee teacher who advised the council earlier (Acts 5:34).
whyNot.B: Philip was one of the Seven, like Stephen, and was not among his killers.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: When Philip met the Ethiopian eunuch on the road to Gaza, which book was the eunuch reading?
questions.explanation: Acts 8:26-35 says the eunuch, an official of Candace queen of the Ethiopians, was reading the prophet Isaiah in his chariot, the passage about one led like a sheep to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7-8). Starting from this scripture, Philip told him the good news about Jesus, and the eunuch was baptised.

whyNot.C: The passage quoted in Acts 8:32-33 comes from Isaiah 53, not Jeremiah.
whyNot.B: Peter quoted Psalms at Pentecost, but the eunuch was reading Isaiah.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In which city were the disciples first called Christians?
questions.explanation: Acts 11:25-26 says Barnabas brought Saul to Antioch, where they taught a great many people for a whole year, and in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.

whyNot.A: The church began in Jerusalem, but the name 'Christians' was first used at Antioch.
whyNot.D: Damascus is where Saul was going when he was converted (Acts 9).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: What was the main question settled by the Council of Jerusalem in Acts 15?
options: Whether the apostles should obey the Jewish council
Whether Gentile believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses
Who should replace Judas Iscariot as an apostle
How widows should be served in the daily distribution
questions.explanation: Some men from Judea taught that Gentiles could not be saved unless they were circumcised according to the custom of Moses (Acts 15:1, 5). After Peter, Barnabas, Paul and James spoke, the council decided not to trouble the Gentiles with circumcision, asking them only to abstain from things polluted by idols, sexual immorality, what has been strangled and blood (Acts 15:19-20, 28-29).

whyNot.C: Matthias replaced Judas in Acts 1.
whyNot.D: The neglect of widows led to the choice of the Seven in Acts 6.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: After an earthquake opened the prison at Philippi, the jailer asked Paul and Silas what he must do to be saved. What was their answer?
options: Be circumcised and keep the law of Moses
Go to the temple in Jerusalem and offer a sacrifice
Release all the prisoners and leave the city
Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household
questions.explanation: Acts 16:25-34 says Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns at midnight when an earthquake opened the doors. The jailer, about to kill himself, was stopped by Paul. He asked what he must do to be saved, and they said, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.' He and his family were baptised.

whyNot.A: Paul taught that salvation is by faith in Christ, not by circumcision (compare Acts 15).
whyNot.C: No prisoner escaped, and Paul did not ask the jailer to free them.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: At Lystra, after Paul healed a man crippled from birth, the crowd thought the apostles were gods. What names did they give them?
options: Paul was called Zeus and Barnabas was called Hermes
Paul was called Apollo and Barnabas was called Hermes
Barnabas was called Apollo and Paul was called Mars
Barnabas was called Zeus and Paul was called Hermes
questions.explanation: Acts 14:8-12 says the crowd shouted that the gods had come down in human form. They called Barnabas Zeus, and Paul Hermes, because Paul was the chief speaker (Hermes was seen as the messenger of the gods). The apostles tore their garments and urged them to turn to the living God.

whyNot.A: This reverses the names; Paul, the main speaker, was called Hermes.
whyNot.C: Apollo and Mars are not mentioned in the Lystra account.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Complete Paul's teaching in Romans 6:23: 'The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is …'
options: eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord
riches and honour in this present age
peace with all men on earth
questions.explanation: Romans 6:23 contrasts what sin earns (death) with what God gives freely as a gift: eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. Salvation is a gift of grace, not something earned.

whyNot.B: Paul contrasts the gift of life in Christ with what the law could do; the gift is not the law.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In Romans 5:1, Paul writes that since we have been justified by faith, we have something with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. What is it?
questions.explanation: Romans 5:1 says that, being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Justification means being declared right with God, and the result is reconciliation instead of hostility.

whyNot.A: Paul says the result of justification is peace, not fear.
whyNot.B: Paul teaches that justification comes by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In 1 Corinthians 13, Paul names three things that remain: faith, hope and love. Which does he call the greatest?
questions.explanation: 1 Corinthians 13:13 says that faith, hope and love abide, but the greatest of these is love (the King James Version says 'charity'). Paul explains in the chapter that without love even great gifts are worth nothing, and that love is patient and kind.

whyNot.D: Faith is one of the three that remain, but love is called the greatest.
whyNot.B: Paul says prophecies will pass away (1 Corinthians 13:8).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed by Paul as part of the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22-23?
questions.explanation: Galatians 5:22-23 lists the fruit of the Spirit as love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. (The King James Version words some of these differently, e.g. longsuffering, gentleness, temperance.) Wisdom is not in this list in any version; the 'utterance of wisdom' is among the gifts of the Spirit in 1 Corinthians 12:8.

whyNot.A: Patience (long-suffering) is in the list in Galatians 5:22.
whyNot.B: Self-control is the last item in Galatians 5:23.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In the 'whole armour of God' in Ephesians 6, what is the sword of the Spirit?
questions.explanation: Ephesians 6:17 says to take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. Other parts are the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, shoes of the gospel of peace and the shield of faith (Ephesians 6:14-16).

whyNot.C: The gospel of peace is linked with the shoes (Ephesians 6:15).
whyNot.A: Faith is the shield (Ephesians 6:16).
whyNot.D: Righteousness is the breastplate (Ephesians 6:14).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Paul's letter to Philemon was written on behalf of which person?
options: Timothy, Paul's son in the faith
questions.explanation: In Philemon 10-16 Paul appeals for Onesimus, who had become a believer through Paul while Paul was in prison. Paul sends him back and asks Philemon to receive him no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother. The letter teaches forgiveness and Christian brotherhood.

whyNot.A: Timothy is named with Paul as a co-sender (Philemon 1), but the appeal is for Onesimus.
whyNot.C: Epaphroditus is mentioned in Philippians (Philippians 2:25), not as the subject of Philemon.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: James teaches that faith by itself, if it does not have works, is …
questions.explanation: James 2:14-17 asks what good it is to say you have faith while ignoring a brother or sister who lacks food and clothing. James 2:17 concludes that faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead. True faith shows itself in action.

whyNot.B: James says the opposite: faith without works is not enough to profit anyone.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In 1 Corinthians 1:10-13, Paul rebukes the church for quarrelling as members said 'I follow Paul', 'I follow Apollos', 'I follow Cephas'. Which problem was he addressing?
options: Doubts about the resurrection of the dead
Divisions in the church based on loyalty to leaders
questions.explanation: Paul appeals for unity because there were divisions among the Corinthians, with groups claiming different leaders. He asks, 'Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you?' (1 Corinthians 1:13). He later says, 'I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth' (1 Corinthians 3:6), so leaders are only servants.

whyNot.A: Lawsuits are dealt with in 1 Corinthians 6.
whyNot.C: Disorder at the Lord's Supper is dealt with in 1 Corinthians 11.
whyNot.B: Doubts about the resurrection are answered in 1 Corinthians 15.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: The Thessalonians were grieving over believers who had died. According to 1 Thessalonians 4:13-17, what will happen to them when the Lord comes?
options: The dead in Christ will rise first, then the living will be caught up with them
Only those who died as martyrs will be raised
They will remain in the grave until the end of the world
They will be raised after the living have gone to meet the Lord
questions.explanation: Paul tells them not to grieve as others do who have no hope. When the Lord descends from heaven, the dead in Christ will rise first; then those who are alive will be caught up together with them to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17). This is meant to encourage them.

whyNot.C: Paul teaches that the dead in Christ will rise at the Lord's coming.
whyNot.D: This reverses the order Paul gives: the dead rise first.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: A Christian trader in Onitsha asks whether he should pay the taxes required by the government. Which teaching of Paul in Romans 13 applies most directly?
options: Pay taxes only when the rulers are believers
Give to the church instead of paying taxes
Christians belong to heaven and need not obey earthly rulers
Be subject to the governing authorities and pay taxes to whom they are due
questions.explanation: Romans 13:1 says everyone should be subject to the governing authorities, since authority comes from God. Romans 13:6-7 adds that for this reason people pay taxes, and they should pay to all what is owed: taxes, revenue, respect and honour.

whyNot.C: Paul teaches the opposite: believers should obey governing authorities.
whyNot.A: Paul gives no such condition; the Roman rulers of his day were not believers.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Moses told God he was slow of speech and of tongue. Whom did God appoint to speak for him?
questions.explanation: In Exodus 4:10-16 Moses made excuses about his speech. God was angry but said that Aaron the Levite, Moses' brother, could speak well; Aaron would be a mouth for Moses, and Moses would tell him what to say.

whyNot.A: Joshua served as Moses' assistant and later his successor, not his spokesman before Pharaoh.
whyNot.C: Jethro advised Moses on judging the people (Exodus 18), but did not speak for him.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Why did God tell Moses and Aaron that they would not lead Israel into the Promised Land?
options: They sent spies who brought back a bad report
At Meribah they did not honour God as holy when Moses struck the rock
They allowed the people to make a golden calf at Sinai
They married women from Moab and Midian
questions.explanation: In Numbers 20:7-12 God told Moses to speak to the rock so that it would give water. Instead Moses spoke angrily to the people and struck the rock twice. God said that because they did not believe Him, to uphold Him as holy, they would not bring the assembly into the land. Moses later saw the land from Mount Nebo (Deuteronomy 34:1-4).

whyNot.C: Aaron made the golden calf (Exodus 32), but this is not the reason given for being kept out of Canaan.
whyNot.A: Ten of the spies brought a bad report (Numbers 13-14); Joshua and Caleb did not, and Moses was not punished for it.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Who hid the two spies sent by Joshua to Jericho?
questions.explanation: Joshua 2:1-6 says Joshua sent two spies from Shittim to Jericho. They came to the house of Rahab, who hid them on her roof under stalks of flax and sent the king's men away. In return they promised to spare her family, and she tied a scarlet cord in her window (Joshua 2:18).

whyNot.C: Deborah was a later judge of Israel (Judges 4).
whyNot.D: Miriam was the sister of Moses and Aaron.
whyNot.A: Jael killed Sisera in the time of Deborah (Judges 4:21).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In his farewell speech at Shechem, Joshua challenged Israel to choose whom they would serve. What did he declare for himself?
options: I will serve the LORD if the people agree to do so
As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD
Let the priests choose for all Israel
I will serve the gods my fathers served beyond the River
questions.explanation: In Joshua 24:14-15 Joshua told the people to put away foreign gods and choose that day whom they would serve, whether the gods of their ancestors or the gods of the Amorites. He declared that he and his household would serve the LORD. The people then promised to serve the LORD too.

whyNot.D: Joshua told Israel to put away those gods, not to serve them.
whyNot.A: Joshua made his choice before the people answered; it did not depend on them.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: At Gilgal, Saul grew impatient when Samuel delayed and the people began to scatter. What did Saul do that led Samuel to rebuke him?
options: He made a treaty with the Philistines
He spared Agag, king of the Amalekites
He went to consult a medium at Endor
He offered the burnt offering himself
questions.explanation: 1 Samuel 13:8-14 says Saul waited seven days for Samuel, then offered the burnt offering himself. Samuel arrived as he finished and told him he had acted foolishly and not kept God's command, so his kingdom would not continue; God had sought a man after His own heart.

whyNot.C: Saul consulted the medium at Endor much later, before his last battle (1 Samuel 28).
whyNot.B: Sparing Agag was a separate act of disobedience (1 Samuel 15).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: When Samuel went to Jesse's house to anoint a new king, he thought Eliab must be God's choice. What did God tell Samuel?
options: The king must be the tallest man in Israel
The eldest son must always be chosen as king
The new king must come from the tribe of Benjamin
Man looks on outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart
questions.explanation: In 1 Samuel 16:6-7 God told Samuel not to look at Eliab's appearance or height, because the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart. God chose David, the youngest son, who was keeping the sheep (1 Samuel 16:11-13).

whyNot.B: God chose David, Jesse's youngest son, not the eldest.
whyNot.C: Saul was from Benjamin, but David was from Judah.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: When David had the chance to kill Saul in a cave at En-gedi, what did he do?
options: He killed Saul and took his crown and spear
He cut off a corner of Saul's robe but refused to harm him
He called his men to arrest Saul and take him to Hebron
He handed Saul over to the Philistines
questions.explanation: 1 Samuel 24:1-7 says Saul entered a cave where David and his men were hiding. David secretly cut off a corner of Saul's robe, but even this troubled his conscience. He would not harm the LORD's anointed and restrained his men. This shows David's respect for God's appointed leader.

whyNot.A: Saul died later on Mount Gilboa in battle with the Philistines (1 Samuel 31).
whyNot.C: David let Saul go and spoke to him from a distance; he did not arrest him.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: What does 1 Kings 11 give as the reason Solomon's heart turned away from the LORD in his old age?
options: The priests refused to serve in his temple
His many foreign wives turned his heart after other gods
The prophet Nathan anointed another king
He was defeated in battle by the Egyptians
questions.explanation: 1 Kings 11:1-6 says Solomon loved many foreign women, including Pharaoh's daughter and women of Moab, Ammon, Edom, Sidon and the Hittites. He had 700 wives and 300 concubines, and when he was old they turned his heart after other gods such as Ashtoreth and Milcom. God then said the kingdom would be torn from his son.

whyNot.D: Solomon was allied with Egypt by marriage; no such defeat is the reason given.
whyNot.C: Nathan had helped make Solomon king (1 Kings 1); he did not anoint a rival.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: The prophet Ahijah of Shiloh tore his new garment into twelve pieces in front of Jeroboam. How many pieces did he tell Jeroboam to take, and what did they mean?
options: Ten pieces, for ten tribes that God would give him
Twelve pieces, for all the tribes of Israel
One piece, for the tribe of Ephraim
Two pieces, for Judah and Benjamin
questions.explanation: In 1 Kings 11:29-31 Ahijah told Jeroboam to take ten pieces, because God was about to tear the kingdom from Solomon's hand and give him ten tribes. One tribe would remain with Solomon's son for the sake of David and Jerusalem. This was fulfilled when the kingdom divided (1 Kings 12).

whyNot.B: Jeroboam was not given all twelve pieces; part remained with David's house.
whyNot.D: Judah (with Benjamin) stayed with Rehoboam, not Jeroboam.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Jeroboam feared his people would return to Rehoboam if they kept going to Jerusalem to worship. What did he do?
options: He banned all sacrifices in the northern kingdom
He made two golden calves and set them at Bethel and Dan
He built a new temple at Shiloh for the ark
He moved his capital to Jerusalem
questions.explanation: 1 Kings 12:26-30 says Jeroboam made two calves of gold and told the people it was too much to go up to Jerusalem. He set one in Bethel and the other in Dan, and this became a sin. He also appointed priests who were not Levites (1 Kings 12:31).

whyNot.C: The ark remained in Jerusalem; Jeroboam did not build a temple at Shiloh.
whyNot.A: Jeroboam did not ban sacrifices; he set up his own shrines and feasts (1 Kings 12:32).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: During the drought that Elijah announced to Ahab, how was Elijah fed at the brook Cherith?
options: A widow shared her flour and oil
An angel baked a cake for him
Obadiah brought him food from the palace
Ravens brought him bread and meat
questions.explanation: 1 Kings 17:2-6 says God told Elijah to hide by the brook Cherith, east of the Jordan. The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning and evening, and he drank from the brook until it dried up.

whyNot.A: The widow of Zarephath fed him later, after the brook dried up (1 Kings 17:8-16).
whyNot.B: An angel provided a cake when Elijah fled from Jezebel (1 Kings 19:5-6).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: After Naboth the Jezreelite was killed so that Ahab could take his vineyard, what did Elijah tell Ahab?
options: God would forgive him because he was king
Dogs would lick his blood where they had licked Naboth's
He must pay Naboth's family double the price
His son would build a temple on the vineyard
questions.explanation: Naboth refused to sell his ancestral vineyard. Jezebel arranged false witnesses and he was stoned (1 Kings 21:1-16). God sent Elijah to tell Ahab that in the place where dogs licked Naboth's blood, they would lick Ahab's own blood (1 Kings 21:19), and that dogs would eat Jezebel (1 Kings 21:23).

whyNot.A: Elijah announced judgement, showing that even a king is under God's law.
whyNot.C: No payment is mentioned; Elijah pronounced doom on Ahab's house.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Who told Amos to go back to Judah and stop prophesying at Bethel, because it was the king's sanctuary?
questions.explanation: Amos 7:10-13 says Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent a message to King Jeroboam accusing Amos of conspiracy. He told Amos to flee to Judah, earn his bread there and prophesy there, but never again at Bethel, the king's sanctuary.

whyNot.D: Amaziah sent a report to Jeroboam, but it was Amaziah who spoke to Amos.
whyNot.B: Hananiah opposed Jeremiah (Jeremiah 28), not Amos.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Amos saw the Lord standing beside a wall with a plumb line in His hand (Amos 7:7-8). What did the plumb line represent?
options: God measuring Israel by His standard before judgement
God promising rain after the drought
God rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem
God choosing builders for the temple
questions.explanation: A plumb line is used to test whether a wall is straight. God said He was setting a plumb line in the midst of His people Israel and would never again pass by them (Amos 7:8). Israel was being measured and found crooked, so judgement would come.

whyNot.C: The vision is about judgement on Israel, not rebuilding.
whyNot.B: Rain after drought is part of Elijah's story (1 Kings 18), not Amos's vision.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In Hosea 6:6, God says, 'I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice.' What was God asking of Israel?
options: A complete end to all worship at the temple
Faithful love and knowledge of God rather than empty rituals
Sacrifices offered only by the high priest
questions.explanation: Israel's love for God was like a morning cloud that quickly disappears (Hosea 6:4). God wanted steadfast love and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings (Hosea 6:6). Rituals without loyalty and right living do not please God. Jesus quoted this verse in Matthew 9:13.

whyNot.A: Hosea is not abolishing worship but condemning worship without love.
whyNot.C: God was saying sacrifices alone were not what He wanted.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In which year did Isaiah see the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up?
options: In the year that King Uzziah died
In the year that Jerusalem was destroyed
In the first year of King Cyrus
In the year that King Josiah was born
questions.explanation: Isaiah 6:1 says, 'In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up.' In this vision Isaiah saw the seraphim, confessed his sin, was cleansed and received his call.

whyNot.B: Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 586 BC, long after Isaiah's call.
whyNot.C: Cyrus of Persia ruled long after Isaiah's call; Isaiah's vision is dated by King Uzziah's death.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: When God called Jeremiah to be a prophet to the nations, what excuse did Jeremiah first give?
options: He was a herdsman, not a prophet
He was already serving as a priest
He did not know how to speak because he was only a youth
He was a man of unclean lips
questions.explanation: In Jeremiah 1:6 Jeremiah said, 'Ah, Lord GOD! I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth.' God told him not to say this, for he must go wherever God sent him, and God touched his mouth and put His words in it (Jeremiah 1:7-9).

whyNot.D: The 'unclean lips' confession belongs to Isaiah (Isaiah 6:5).
whyNot.A: Amos described himself as a herdsman (Amos 7:14).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Jeremiah was let down into a muddy cistern by officials of King Zedekiah. Who obtained the king's permission and rescued him?
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 38:6-13 says the officials put Jeremiah in the cistern of Malchiah, where he sank in the mud. Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch in the king's house, pleaded with King Zedekiah, then used ropes and old rags to draw Jeremiah out.

whyNot.B: Baruch was Jeremiah's scribe who wrote down his words (Jeremiah 36:4).
whyNot.C: Hananiah was the false prophet who opposed Jeremiah (Jeremiah 28).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Jeremiah wore a wooden yoke to show that the nations should serve the king of Babylon. What did the prophet Hananiah do?
options: He broke the yoke and said Babylon's yoke would be broken within two years
He put on an iron yoke to support Jeremiah's message
He told the king to have Jeremiah killed at once
He carried the yoke to Babylon as a gift
questions.explanation: In Jeremiah 28:10-11 Hananiah took the yoke from Jeremiah's neck and broke it, claiming that within two years God would break Nebuchadnezzar's yoke. God told Jeremiah that Hananiah had made the people trust in a lie and that a yoke of iron would replace the wooden one. Hananiah died that same year (Jeremiah 28:17).

whyNot.B: The iron yoke was God's word through Jeremiah in reply to Hananiah (Jeremiah 28:13-14), not something Hananiah wore.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Where was Ezekiel when the heavens were opened and he saw visions of God?
options: On Mount Carmel after the fire fell
In the temple at Jerusalem during a feast
Among the exiles by the river Chebar in Babylonia
At Anathoth in the land of Benjamin
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 1:1-3 says Ezekiel, a priest and the son of Buzi, was among the exiles by the Chebar canal (river) in the land of the Chaldeans when the heavens were opened and he saw visions of God. He prophesied to the exiles in Babylon.

whyNot.A: Mount Carmel is linked with Elijah (1 Kings 18).
whyNot.D: Anathoth was the home town of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:1).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: How old was Jesus when his parents found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers?
questions.explanation: Luke 2:41-49 says that when Jesus was twelve years old the family went up to Jerusalem for the Passover. Jesus stayed behind, and after three days his parents found him in the temple listening to the teachers and asking them questions. He said he must be in his Father's house.

whyNot.A: Jesus was circumcised and named at eight days old (Luke 2:21).
whyNot.C: Jesus was about thirty when he began his ministry (Luke 3:23).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: When Jesus called Simon (Peter) and Andrew by the Sea of Galilee, what work were they doing?
options: They were fishermen casting a net into the sea
They were tentmakers working in the market
They were shepherds keeping their flocks
They were tax collectors sitting at the tax booth
questions.explanation: Matthew 4:18-20 says Jesus saw Simon called Peter and Andrew his brother casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. He said, 'Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men,' and immediately they left their nets and followed him.

whyNot.D: Matthew (Levi) was called from the tax booth (Matthew 9:9).
whyNot.B: Paul, Aquila and Priscilla were tentmakers (Acts 18:3).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: For how much money did Judas Iscariot agree with the chief priests to betray Jesus?
questions.explanation: Matthew 26:14-16 says Judas asked the chief priests what they would give him to deliver Jesus, and they paid him thirty pieces of silver. Later, filled with remorse, he threw the money down in the temple (Matthew 27:3-5).

whyNot.B: Twenty pieces of silver was the price for which Joseph was sold by his brothers (Genesis 37:28).
whyNot.D: Over three hundred denarii was the value of the ointment poured on Jesus at Bethany (Mark 14:5), not the price of betrayal.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: When Mary and Joseph presented the baby Jesus in the temple, the righteous man Simeon took him in his arms. What did Simeon declare?
options: The child should be named John
The child would be killed by Herod in Bethlehem
The family must flee to Egypt at once
He could now depart in peace, for he had seen God's salvation
questions.explanation: Luke 2:25-32 says the Holy Spirit had revealed to Simeon that he would not die before seeing the Lord's Christ. Holding Jesus, he blessed God and said he could now depart in peace, for his eyes had seen God's salvation, a light for the Gentiles and glory for Israel.

whyNot.A: The name John was given to the son of Zechariah and Elizabeth (Luke 1:60-63).
whyNot.C: The warning to flee to Egypt came to Joseph in a dream (Matthew 2:13).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Jesus asked a Samaritan woman for a drink at Jacob's well. Why was she surprised?
options: Jews did not normally have dealings with Samaritans
Jesus had no money to buy water
Women were not allowed to draw water
The well had dried up long before
questions.explanation: John 4:5-9 says Jesus, tired from his journey, sat by Jacob's well near Sychar in Samaria. When he asked the woman for a drink, she asked how he, a Jew, could ask her, a Samaritan woman, for water, because Jews had no dealings with Samaritans. Jesus then spoke to her about living water.

whyNot.D: The woman had come to draw water, so the well had not dried up.
whyNot.C: She was drawing water herself; this was a normal task for women.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Which three disciples did Jesus take up the mountain where he was transfigured?
questions.explanation: Matthew 17:1-3 says Jesus took Peter, James and John his brother up a high mountain. He was transfigured before them, his face shining like the sun, and Moses and Elijah appeared, talking with him. A voice from the cloud said, 'This is my beloved Son; listen to him.'

whyNot.D: Andrew and Philip were apostles, but not part of this inner group at the Transfiguration.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Before raising Lazarus, Jesus told Martha, 'I am the resurrection and the life.' How long had Lazarus been in the tomb when Jesus arrived?
questions.explanation: John 11:17 says that when Jesus came to Bethany he found Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days. Martha even warned that there would be an odour (John 11:39). Jesus called Lazarus out, showing his power over death.

whyNot.A: Three days is linked to Jesus' own resurrection, not to Lazarus.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: A centurion at Capernaum asked Jesus only to say the word and his servant would be healed. How did Jesus respond?
options: He refused because the centurion was a Gentile
He marvelled and said he had not found such faith in Israel
He went to the centurion's house and laid hands on the servant
He told the centurion to show himself to the priest
questions.explanation: Matthew 8:5-13 says the centurion felt unworthy to have Jesus under his roof and trusted Jesus' word, as a man under authority. Jesus marvelled, said he had not found such faith in Israel, and the servant was healed at that very hour.

whyNot.C: The servant was healed at a distance by Jesus' word.
whyNot.D: Jesus told the healed leper, not the centurion, to show himself to the priest (Matthew 8:4).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: During the trial of Jesus, what did Pilate do when he saw that he could not calm the crowd?
options: He released Jesus and had Barabbas crucified
He sent Jesus to Rome to appear before Caesar
He washed his hands before the crowd and declared himself innocent of Jesus' blood
He sent Jesus back to Caiaphas for a new trial
questions.explanation: Matthew 27:24 says Pilate took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying he was innocent of this man's blood. He then released Barabbas and handed Jesus over to be crucified (Matthew 27:26).

whyNot.A: This is reversed: Pilate released Barabbas and handed Jesus over.
whyNot.B: Paul, not Jesus, was sent to Rome after appealing to Caesar (Acts 25:11-12).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: After the resurrection, Jesus asked Simon Peter three times by the Sea of Tiberias whether he loved him. What is the main significance of this?
options: Peter was restored after his threefold denial and given a pastoral charge
Peter was rebuked for going back to fishing
Peter was made to promise never to leave Galilee
Peter was told he would replace Judas among the twelve
questions.explanation: Peter had denied Jesus three times (John 18). In John 21:15-17 Jesus asked him three times, 'Do you love me?' and after each answer gave him a charge: feed my lambs, tend my sheep, feed my sheep. This restored Peter and gave him responsibility for caring for the believers.

whyNot.D: Matthias, not Peter, replaced Judas (Acts 1:26).
whyNot.B: Jesus helped them catch fish and ate with them; the questions were not a rebuke for fishing.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Why did the apostles ask the believers to choose seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom (Acts 6)?
options: The temple authorities demanded new leaders
The apostles were going out on missionary journeys
Judas Iscariot had to be replaced among the apostles
The Hellenist widows were being neglected in the daily distribution of food
questions.explanation: Acts 6:1-4 says the Hellenists complained that their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. The apostles did not want to neglect preaching and prayer to serve tables, so seven men, including Stephen and Philip, were chosen and appointed to this duty.

whyNot.C: Judas was replaced by Matthias alone (Acts 1:26).
whyNot.B: The apostles wanted to keep praying and preaching; they were not leaving Jerusalem at this point.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: When the council wanted to kill the apostles, Gamaliel advised them. What was the heart of his advice?
options: The apostles should be stoned at once to stop the movement
If this work is from men it will fail, but if it is from God they cannot stop it
The council should join the apostles and believe in Jesus
The apostles should be sent to Rome to stand trial
questions.explanation: Acts 5:34-39 says Gamaliel, a Pharisee and respected teacher of the law, reminded the council of Theudas and Judas the Galilean, whose movements came to nothing. He advised them to leave the apostles alone: if the plan was of men it would fail, but if of God they could not overthrow it and might be found fighting against God.

whyNot.A: Gamaliel argued against killing the apostles.
whyNot.C: Gamaliel urged caution, not conversion.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Why did Peter rebuke Simon the magician in Samaria?
options: Simon lied about the price of his land
Simon refused to be baptised by Philip
Simon offered money to buy the power to give the Holy Spirit
Simon claimed to be the Messiah
questions.explanation: Acts 8:18-20 says Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, and he offered them money for this power. Peter told him his silver would perish with him, because he thought he could obtain the gift of God with money. The word 'simony' comes from this story.

whyNot.B: Simon himself believed and was baptised (Acts 8:13).
whyNot.A: Lying about the price of land was the sin of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Where was Saul going when a light from heaven flashed around him and he heard Jesus speak to him?
options: To Tarsus, to visit his family
To Rome, to appeal to Caesar
To Damascus, to arrest followers of the Way
To Antioch, to preach to the Gentiles
questions.explanation: Acts 9:1-6 says Saul, still breathing threats against the disciples, got letters from the high priest to the synagogues at Damascus so he could bring followers of the Way bound to Jerusalem. Near Damascus a light flashed around him and he heard, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?'

whyNot.D: Saul preached at Antioch only after his conversion (Acts 11:26).
whyNot.B: Paul appealed to Caesar many years later (Acts 25:11).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: What was the lesson of Peter's vision of a sheet full of animals at Joppa, before he went to Cornelius?
options: Peter should leave Joppa and become a fisherman again
The Jewish food laws must be kept by every Gentile
God shows no partiality; Gentiles are not to be called unclean
Christians should no longer eat any meat
questions.explanation: In Acts 10:9-16 a voice told Peter to kill and eat, and when he refused, said, 'What God has made clean, do not call common.' At Cornelius' house Peter understood that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears Him and does what is right is acceptable (Acts 10:34-35).

whyNot.D: The vision told Peter to eat, not to stop eating meat.
whyNot.B: The vision showed that Gentiles were accepted, not that they must keep Jewish food laws.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Which apostle did King Herod kill with the sword, as recorded in Acts 12?
options: James, the brother of the Lord
questions.explanation: Acts 12:1-3 says Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church and killed James the brother of John with the sword. Seeing this pleased the Jews, he arrested Peter too, but an angel freed Peter from prison (Acts 12:6-11).

whyNot.A: Peter was arrested but miraculously released.
whyNot.D: Stephen was stoned by a crowd (Acts 7), not killed by Herod.
whyNot.C: James the Lord's brother was alive and led the Jerusalem Council later (Acts 15:13).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: At Paphos in Cyprus, a magician tried to turn the proconsul away from the faith. What happened to him?
options: The sons of Sceva were attacked by an evil spirit
Simon was rebuked and asked Peter to pray for him
Demetrius started a riot against Paul
Elymas was struck blind for a time, and the proconsul believed
questions.explanation: Acts 13:6-12 says Elymas (Bar-Jesus) opposed Paul and Barnabas and tried to turn the proconsul Sergius Paulus from the faith. Paul, filled with the Spirit, declared that he would be blind for a time; mist and darkness fell on him. The proconsul believed, astonished at the teaching of the Lord.

whyNot.B: Simon the magician was in Samaria (Acts 8).
whyNot.A: The sons of Sceva were at Ephesus (Acts 19:13-16).
whyNot.C: Demetrius the silversmith caused a riot in Ephesus (Acts 19:24-29).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Lydia, whose heart the Lord opened to Paul's message at Philippi, was known as …
options: a slave girl who had a spirit of divination
a seller of purple goods from the city of Thyatira
a disciple at Joppa full of good works
a tentmaker who worked with Aquila
questions.explanation: Acts 16:13-15 says Paul spoke to women gathered by the riverside at Philippi. Lydia, a seller of purple goods from Thyatira and a worshipper of God, listened, and the Lord opened her heart. She and her household were baptised, and she welcomed the missionaries into her home.

whyNot.D: Priscilla worked with her husband Aquila as a tentmaker (Acts 18:2-3).
whyNot.C: Tabitha (Dorcas) of Joppa was known for good works (Acts 9:36).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: At the Areopagus in Athens, Paul began his speech by referring to something he had seen in the city. What was it?
options: A temple of Artemis of the Ephesians
A synagogue built by a Roman officer
A statue of Caesar in the market
An altar inscribed 'To the unknown god'
questions.explanation: Acts 17:22-23 says Paul told the Athenians that he saw they were very religious, for he had found an altar with the inscription 'To the unknown god'. He said that what they worshipped as unknown, he would proclaim to them: the God who made the world.

whyNot.A: The temple of Artemis was in Ephesus (Acts 19:27), not Athens.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus who sold a field and gave the money to the apostles, was given another name by them. What was it, and what does it mean?
questions.explanation: Acts 4:36-37 says the apostles called Joseph Barnabas, which means 'son of encouragement'. He sold a field and laid the money at the apostles' feet. Later he encouraged the church at Antioch and introduced Saul to the apostles (Acts 9:27).

whyNot.D: Jesus gave Simon the name Peter (Cephas), meaning rock (John 1:42).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In Romans 12:1, Paul appeals to believers to present their bodies in a particular way. How?
options: As a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God
As burnt offerings at the temple in Jerusalem
As servants of the Roman emperor
As slaves to the law of Moses
questions.explanation: Romans 12:1-2 urges believers, by the mercies of God, to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is their spiritual worship. They are not to be conformed to this world but transformed by the renewal of their mind.

whyNot.B: Paul uses sacrifice as a picture; he does not ask for literal burnt offerings.
whyNot.D: Paul teaches freedom from the law as a way of salvation (Romans 7:6).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In 1 Corinthians 6:19, what does Paul say the believer's body is?
options: A tent that does not matter
A temple of the Holy Spirit
questions.explanation: Paul warns the Corinthians against sexual immorality and asks whether they do not know that their body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within them, which they have from God. They are not their own, for they were bought with a price, so they should glorify God in their body (1 Corinthians 6:19-20).

whyNot.C: Paul teaches that the body matters to God and must be used to glorify Him.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In 1 Corinthians 12, Paul compares the church to a human body with many parts. What is the main lesson?
options: Members with the same gift should form separate churches
Only those with the gift of tongues truly belong to the church
The leaders are the only important members of the church
Every member has a different gift, and all are needed for the good of the whole
questions.explanation: 1 Corinthians 12:12-27 teaches that just as the body is one but has many members, so is Christ's body. The eye cannot say to the hand, 'I have no need of you.' Each member has a part given by the Spirit, and the members should care for one another.

whyNot.B: Paul says not all speak in tongues (1 Corinthians 12:30), yet all belong.
whyNot.C: Paul says the weaker-seeming parts are indispensable.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Paul warns in Galatians 6:7, 'Do not be deceived: God is not mocked.' What principle follows?
options: Love covers a multitude of sins
The Lord gives and the Lord takes away
Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap
The first will be last and the last first
questions.explanation: Galatians 6:7-8 says whatever one sows, that will he also reap: the one who sows to his own flesh will reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will reap eternal life. Our actions have consequences.

whyNot.D: This is a saying of Jesus in the Gospels (Matthew 20:16).
whyNot.A: This saying is found in 1 Peter 4:8.
whyNot.B: These are the words of Job (Job 1:21).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: What does Paul teach about anger in Ephesians 4:26?
options: Anger is always a sin and must be confessed to the elders
Anger may be shown only towards unbelievers
Be angry but do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger
Keep your anger hidden until you can repay the offender
questions.explanation: Ephesians 4:26-27 says, in effect, 'Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil.' Anger must be controlled and dealt with quickly, so that it does not lead to sin or bitterness.

whyNot.A: Paul allows that one may be angry without sinning.
whyNot.D: Paul teaches against nursing anger and revenge (Romans 12:19).

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Writing from prison, Paul thanked the Philippians for their gift. What did he say he had learned in whatever situation he was?
questions.explanation: In Philippians 4:11-13 Paul says he has learned in whatever situation he is to be content. He knows how to be brought low and how to abound, facing plenty and hunger, and he can do all things through Christ who strengthens him.

whyNot.D: Paul says his strength comes from Christ, not from wealthy supporters.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Some believers in Thessalonica were living in idleness. What rule did Paul give in 2 Thessalonians 3:10?
options: Only the elders should work to support the church
If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat
Those who do not work should be fed by the church
Believers should stop work and wait for the Lord's return
questions.explanation: Paul reminds them of the command he gave when with them: if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10). He urges idle people to work quietly and earn their own living (3:12), and he himself worked so as not to be a burden.

whyNot.C: Paul says the opposite: those unwilling to work should not be fed.
whyNot.D: Paul corrects this idea; waiting for the Lord is no excuse for idleness.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: In 1 Timothy 4:12, Paul tells Timothy not to let anyone despise him for his youth. What does Paul ask Timothy to do instead?
options: Appoint older men to speak on his behalf
Leave the church and go back to Lystra
Set the believers an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity
Wait until he is older before he begins to teach
questions.explanation: 1 Timothy 4:12 says, 'Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.' A young leader earns respect by a godly life, not by age.

whyNot.D: Paul encourages Timothy to teach now (1 Timothy 4:11, 13).
whyNot.A: Paul wants Timothy himself to lead by example.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: Which epistle defines faith as the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen, and then lists heroes of faith such as Abel, Noah and Abraham?
questions.explanation: Hebrews 11:1 defines faith as the assurance of things hoped for and the conviction of things not seen. The chapter then recalls Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses and others who lived by faith, and Hebrews 11:6 adds that without faith it is impossible to please God.

whyNot.B: Romans speaks much of faith and mentions Abraham (Romans 4), but the definition and the list of heroes are in Hebrews 11.
whyNot.C: James stresses that faith must show in works (James 2), but this definition is in Hebrews.

questions.subject: christian-religious-studies
questions.stem: 1 John 4:20 says that anyone who claims to love God but hates his brother is a liar. What does this teach about Christian love?
options: Love for God must show itself in love for other people
Love for God is a private feeling that need not affect others
Love for others is more important than love for God
Believers should love only those who love them
questions.explanation: 1 John 4:20-21 argues that whoever does not love his brother, whom he has seen, cannot love God, whom he has not seen, and gives the command that whoever loves God must also love his brother. Love for God and love for neighbour cannot be separated.

whyNot.B: John says love for God that ignores others is false.
whyNot.C: John does not rank love for others above love for God; he says the two go together.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which verses of the Qur'an were the first to be revealed to Prophet Muhammad (SAW) in the Cave of Hira?
questions.explanation: The first revelation came through Angel Jibril in the Cave of Hira in 610 CE. It began with 'Read (Iqra') in the name of your Lord who created', which is Surah al-'Alaq (Surah 96), verses 1 to 5.

whyNot.D: Al-Fatihah opens the Qur'an as it is arranged in the mushaf, but it was not the first passage revealed.
whyNot.A: The opening verses of al-Muddaththir came after the first revelation, following a pause in revelation.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: How many surahs (chapters) are there in the Glorious Qur'an?
questions.explanation: The Qur'an has 114 surahs, beginning with Surah al-Fatihah (1) and ending with Surah an-Nas (114).

whyNot.A: 112 is the number of Surah al-Ikhlas, not the total number of surahs.
whyNot.C: 113 is the number of Surah al-Falaq, the second-to-last surah.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: During the caliphate of Abu Bakr, the collection of the Qur'an into one compiled copy was prompted mainly by the death of many memorisers (huffaz) at which battle?
questions.explanation: Many Companions who had memorised the Qur'an were killed at the Battle of Yamamah against the false prophet Musaylimah. Umar ibn al-Khattab feared that parts of the Qur'an could be lost, so he urged Abu Bakr to have it collected into one copy.

whyNot.B: Badr (2 AH) took place in the Prophet's lifetime, when he was still alive to recite and dictate the revelation.
whyNot.A: Uhud (3 AH) was also in the Prophet's lifetime, long before the compilation.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which Companion, a scribe of revelation, led the work of collecting the Qur'an into one copy under Caliph Abu Bakr?
questions.explanation: Zayd ibn Thabit had written down revelation for the Prophet (SAW) and had memorised the Qur'an. Abu Bakr chose him to gather the Qur'an from written materials and from those who had memorised it.

whyNot.A: Bilal ibn Rabah is remembered as the Prophet's mu'adhdhin (caller to prayer), not as the compiler of the Qur'an.
whyNot.B: Khalid ibn al-Walid was a military commander; he led the Muslim army at Yamamah.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: What is the main teaching of Surah al-'Asr (Surah 103)?
options: Believers should spend the whole night in prayer and recitation of the Qur'an
Humankind is in loss except those who believe, do good deeds, and urge one another to truth and patience
The People of the Book will be rewarded only if they follow their own scriptures
Wealth and children are the true measure of a person's success in this life
questions.explanation: Surah al-'Asr swears by time and declares that humankind is in loss, except those who have faith, do righteous deeds, and advise one another to truth and to patience. It teaches the value of time and the four qualities that save a person.

whyNot.D: The surah says the opposite: success comes from faith and good deeds, not from wealth or children.
whyNot.A: Night prayer is discussed in other surahs such as al-Muzzammil, not in al-'Asr.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which surah condemns people who repel the orphan, do not encourage feeding the poor, pray only to be seen, and refuse even small kindnesses?
questions.explanation: Surah al-Ma'un (Surah 107) describes the one who denies the Judgement: he pushes away the orphan, does not urge feeding the poor, is heedless of his prayer, prays to show off, and withholds small kindnesses (al-ma'un).

whyNot.A: Al-Kawthar is about the abundance Allah gave the Prophet and the command to pray and sacrifice.
whyNot.D: Al-Fil tells the story of Abrahah's army and the elephant.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Ayat al-Kursi (the Verse of the Throne) is found in which part of the Qur'an?
questions.explanation: Ayat al-Kursi is Qur'an 2:255, in Surah al-Baqarah. It begins 'Allah, there is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all' and describes Allah's knowledge and authority over the heavens and the earth.

whyNot.A: Surah Al 'Imran has only 200 verses, so it has no verse 255.
whyNot.C: Al-Ikhlas also teaches the oneness of Allah, but it is a separate four-verse surah, not Ayat al-Kursi.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which of the following is a main feature of the surahs revealed in Makkah?
options: They deal mainly with the hypocrites of the Muslim community
They set out the rules for running the Islamic state in Madinah
They give detailed laws on inheritance, marriage and divorce
They stress belief in one God, the Hereafter and the prophethood of Muhammad
questions.explanation: In Makkah the Muslims were a small, persecuted group among idol-worshippers, so the Makkan surahs mainly call people to tawhid, warn of the Day of Judgement and the Hereafter, and confirm the Prophet's mission. They are usually shorter, with short verses.

whyNot.C: Detailed family and inheritance laws came mostly in the Madinan surahs, such as an-Nisa'.
whyNot.A: The hypocrites (munafiqun) appeared in Madinah, so they are discussed in Madinan surahs.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.context: 'O mankind, We created you from a male and a female and made you into nations and tribes so that you may know one another. Surely the most honoured of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.' (Qur'an 49:13, meaning in English)
questions.stem: Which teaching does this verse most directly support?
options: A person's wealth decides his honour before Allah
The oldest nation should rule over all the others
A person's honour before Allah comes from piety, not from tribe or race
People should marry only within their own tribe or nation
questions.explanation: Qur'an 49:13 (Surah al-Hujurat) says all people come from one male and one female, and differences of nation and tribe exist so that people may know one another. The only basis of superiority is righteousness (taqwa), so tribalism and racism are rejected.

whyNot.D: The verse says tribes exist so that people may know one another; it does not limit marriage to one's tribe.
whyNot.A: The verse names righteousness, not wealth, as the measure of honour.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: After the deaths of Abu Bakr and Umar, the sheets (suhuf) of the Qur'an compiled under Abu Bakr were kept by which of the following?
questions.explanation: The compiled sheets stayed with Abu Bakr, then with Umar, and after Umar's death with his daughter Hafsah, a wife of the Prophet. Caliph Uthman later borrowed Hafsah's copy to make the standard copies he sent to the provinces.

whyNot.C: Aishah was also a wife of the Prophet, but the sheets passed to Umar's daughter, Hafsah.
whyNot.D: Khadijah died in Makkah before the Hijrah, many years before the Qur'an was compiled.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: In Islamic Studies, the term 'hadith' refers to
options: the verses of the Qur'an revealed in Madinah
the history of the rightly guided caliphs
the rulings agreed on by Muslim scholars
the sayings, actions and approvals of Prophet Muhammad (SAW)
questions.explanation: A hadith is a report of what the Prophet (SAW) said, did, or silently approved. Together these make up his Sunnah, the second source of Islamic law after the Qur'an.

whyNot.A: Madinan verses are part of the Qur'an itself, not hadith.
whyNot.C: Agreement of scholars on a ruling is ijma', a separate source of law.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: In the science of hadith, what is the isnad?
options: The grade given to a hadith by scholars
The book in which a hadith was finally recorded
The chain of narrators through whom a hadith was passed on
The actual text or wording of the hadith
questions.explanation: Every hadith has two parts: the isnad, the chain of people who narrated it from one to another back to the Prophet (SAW), and the matn, the text itself. Scholars study the isnad to judge whether a hadith is reliable.

whyNot.D: The text of the hadith is the matn.
whyNot.A: Grades such as sahih or da'if are given after examining the isnad and matn; they are not the isnad.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Who compiled al-Muwatta', one of the earliest surviving collections of hadith?
questions.explanation: Al-Muwatta' was compiled in Madinah by Imam Malik ibn Anas (died 179 AH), who also founded the Maliki school of law followed by most Muslims in Nigeria.

whyNot.D: Imam Muslim compiled the Sahih Muslim, about a century later.
whyNot.C: An-Nawawi compiled the famous Forty Hadith much later, in the 13th century CE.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: The hadith 'Actions are judged by intentions, and every person will have what he intended' was narrated by which Companion?
questions.explanation: This hadith is reported by Umar ibn al-Khattab and recorded by both al-Bukhari and Muslim. It is the first hadith in an-Nawawi's Forty Hadith and teaches that the reward of a deed depends on its intention (niyyah).

whyNot.C: Abu Hurayrah narrated the largest number of hadith, but not this one.
whyNot.B: Anas ibn Malik narrated the hadith about loving for your brother what you love for yourself.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which statement best describes a hadith qudsi?
options: Its meaning is from Allah, but its wording is the Prophet's
Its meaning and wording are both from Allah and it is part of the Qur'an
It is a report that scholars have judged to be fabricated
It is a saying of a Companion about the Prophet's character
questions.explanation: In a hadith qudsi the Prophet (SAW) reports what Allah said, but in his own words. Unlike the Qur'an, it is not recited in salat and is not counted as part of the Qur'an.

whyNot.B: Wording and meaning both from Allah describes the Qur'an itself.
whyNot.C: A fabricated report is called mawdu'.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Imam al-Bukhari, compiler of the Sahih al-Bukhari, was born in which town?
questions.explanation: Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari was born in Bukhara (in present-day Uzbekistan) in 194 AH, and his name 'al-Bukhari' means 'from Bukhara'. He travelled widely to gather hadith.

whyNot.D: Nishapur was the home town of Imam Muslim, compiler of Sahih Muslim.
whyNot.A: Madinah was the city of Imam Malik, compiler of al-Muwatta'.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Zainab saw a scholarship notice and hid it from her classmates so that she alone would apply. Which hadith teaching does her action go against?
options: Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should honour his guest
None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself
The strong man is the one who controls himself when angry
questions.explanation: The Prophet (SAW) said a person's faith is not complete until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself (narrated by Anas ibn Malik). Zainab wanted the benefit for herself and kept it from others, which is the opposite of this teaching.

whyNot.A: Honouring guests is a good teaching, but Zainab's action is about selfishness, not hospitality.
whyNot.D: Controlling anger is not the issue here; nothing in the story involves anger.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: A hadith whose chain of narrators is unbroken, whose narrators are all upright and precise, and which has no hidden defect is classified as
questions.explanation: Sahih (sound) is the highest grade. Its conditions are: a continuous chain, narrators of good character ('adl) with strong memory (dabt), no contradiction with stronger reports, and no hidden defect.

whyNot.B: A hasan hadith meets most conditions, but some narrators are less precise in memory than in a sahih one.
whyNot.A: A da'if (weak) hadith fails one or more of these conditions, for example by a broken chain.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which ruler is credited with ordering the first official written collection of hadith?
questions.explanation: The Umayyad caliph Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz (reigned 717–720 CE) feared hadith would be lost as scholars died, so he ordered scholars such as Ibn Shihab az-Zuhri to collect and write them down officially.

whyNot.B: Umar ibn al-Khattab, the second caliph, considered writing the hadith but decided against it in case people neglected the Qur'an.
whyNot.D: Harun ar-Rashid was a later Abbasid caliph; the official collection had begun before his time.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which of these hadith works is NOT one of the six major collections (al-Kutub as-Sittah)?
options: The Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal
questions.explanation: The six major collections are the Sahih of al-Bukhari, the Sahih of Muslim, and the Sunan of Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi, an-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah. Ahmad ibn Hanbal's Musnad is a very large and important collection, but it is not one of the six.

whyNot.B: Abu Dawud's Sunan is one of the six.
whyNot.C: At-Tirmidhi's Jami' (also called his Sunan) is one of the six.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: What does the term 'tawhid' mean?
options: Belief in the oneness of Allah
Belief in the Day of Judgement
questions.explanation: Tawhid is the belief that Allah is One, without partner, in His lordship, in His right to be worshipped, and in His names and attributes. It is the foundation of Islam.

whyNot.B: Belief in the Last Day is a separate article of faith.
whyNot.D: Purification before prayer is taharah.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: In Islam, associating partners with Allah in worship is called
questions.explanation: Shirk means joining partners with Allah, for example worshipping idols or praying to other beings. The Qur'an (4:48) says Allah does not forgive shirk if a person dies upon it, but forgives other sins as He wills.

whyNot.A: Kufr is disbelief in general, such as rejecting Allah or His messenger.
whyNot.C: Nifaq is hypocrisy: showing faith outwardly while hiding disbelief.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: What is the total number of obligatory (fard) rak'ahs a resident Muslim prays in a day across the five daily prayers?
questions.explanation: Add the fard rak'ahs: Subh (Fajr) 2 + Zuhr 4 + 'Asr 4 + Maghrib 3 + 'Isha' 4 = 17 rak'ahs.

whyNot.D: 15 comes from counting Maghrib as 1 rak'ah instead of 3.
whyNot.B: 20 assumes every prayer has 4 rak'ahs.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Alhaji Bello has ₦4,000,000 in savings, above the nisab, which he has held for one full lunar year. How much zakat must he pay on it at 2.5%?
questions.explanation: Zakat on money is 2.5% (one-fortieth) of wealth that has reached the nisab and been held for a lunar year. 2.5% of ₦4,000,000 = 4,000,000 × 2.5 ÷ 100 = ₦100,000.

whyNot.A: ₦400,000 is 10%, the rate on crops watered by rain, not on savings.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: A Muslim who cannot find water for wudu may purify himself for salat by tayammum. What is used for tayammum?
questions.explanation: When water is not available, or using it would cause harm, Allah permits tayammum with clean earth (Qur'an 5:6). The person strikes the earth with the palms and wipes the face and hands.

whyNot.D: Wiping with a cloth is not tayammum; the Qur'an names clean earth.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: The school of Islamic law followed by most Muslims in Nigeria was founded by
questions.explanation: The Maliki school, founded by Imam Malik ibn Anas of Madinah, spread across North and West Africa, and it is the school followed by most Muslims in Nigeria.

whyNot.B: The Hanafi school of Abu Hanifah is strongest in Turkey and South Asia.
whyNot.C: The Hanbali school is followed mainly in Saudi Arabia.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Scholars rule that hard drugs are forbidden because, like wine, they intoxicate the mind. This method of deriving a ruling is called
questions.explanation: Qiyas (analogical deduction) applies the ruling of a case in the Qur'an or Sunnah to a new case that shares the same cause ('illah). Wine is forbidden because it intoxicates; hard drugs also intoxicate, so they are forbidden too.

whyNot.C: Ijma' is the agreement of qualified scholars on a ruling, not reasoning by analogy.
whyNot.B: Taqlid is following a scholar's or school's opinion without examining the evidence oneself.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which of the following is one of the six articles of faith (arkan al-iman)?
questions.explanation: The six articles of faith are belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and divine decree (al-qadar). Zakat, fasting and Hajj are pillars of Islam (acts of worship), not articles of faith.

whyNot.B: Zakat is the third pillar of Islam, not an article of faith.
whyNot.C: Hajj is the fifth pillar of Islam, not an article of faith.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: According to Qur'an 2:234, how long is the waiting period ('iddah) of a woman whose husband has died (if she is not pregnant)?
questions.explanation: Qur'an 2:234 says widows shall wait four months and ten days. During this 'iddah the widow does not remarry; the period also shows respect for the late husband.

whyNot.C: Three menstrual cycles (quru') is the 'iddah of a divorced woman who menstruates (Qur'an 2:228).
whyNot.B: Three months is the 'iddah of a divorced woman who no longer menstruates (Qur'an 65:4).

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: A man dies and his only heirs are two sons and one daughter. After his debts and funeral costs are paid, ₦1,500,000 remains. Following Qur'an 4:11, how much does the daughter receive?
questions.explanation: Qur'an 4:11 gives a son twice the share of a daughter. Count shares: each son 2, the daughter 1, so 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 shares. One share = ₦1,500,000 ÷ 5 = ₦300,000, which is the daughter's portion; each son gets ₦600,000.

whyNot.D: ₦500,000 divides the estate equally among the three children, ignoring the 2 : 1 rule.
whyNot.C: ₦600,000 is each son's share, not the daughter's.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Prophet Muhammad (SAW) was born in Makkah in the 'Year of the Elephant'. This year is usually given as
questions.explanation: The Prophet was born in 570 CE, the year Abrahah's army came with an elephant to destroy the Ka'bah, so it is called the Year of the Elephant ('Am al-Fil).

whyNot.B: 610 CE is when he received the first revelation, at about 40 years of age.
whyNot.C: 622 CE is the year of the Hijrah to Madinah.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Who was the foster-mother (wet nurse) who cared for the young Muhammad (SAW) among the Banu Sa'd in the desert?
questions.explanation: As was the custom of the Makkan nobles, the infant Muhammad was given to a wet nurse from the desert. Halimah of the Banu Sa'd nursed and raised him for his early years.

whyNot.A: Aminah bint Wahb was his own mother, who died when he was about six.
whyNot.B: Khadijah was his first wife, whom he married at 25.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: During the Hijrah, Prophet Muhammad (SAW) and Abu Bakr hid for three days from the Quraysh in which cave?
questions.explanation: When they left Makkah in 622 CE, the Prophet and Abu Bakr hid in the Cave of Thawr, south of Makkah, for three days while the Quraysh searched for them, before setting out for Madinah.

whyNot.A: The Cave of Hira is where the first revelation came, not where they hid during the Hijrah.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: In which year of the Hijrah was the Battle of Badr fought?
questions.explanation: The Battle of Badr took place in Ramadan, 2 AH (624 CE). About 313 Muslims defeated a much larger Quraysh army, and Abu Jahl was among those killed.

whyNot.B: 3 AH is the year of the Battle of Uhud.
whyNot.C: 5 AH is the year of the Battle of the Trench (Khandaq).

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: What was the main cause of the Muslims' losses at the Battle of Uhud?
options: The Muslims ran out of water before the fighting began
The archers left their position on the hill against the Prophet's order
The Muslims were attacked at night without warning
The Prophet's army was led by an inexperienced general
questions.explanation: The Prophet (SAW) ordered about fifty archers to stay on the hill whatever happened. When the Muslims seemed to be winning, most archers left to collect booty. Khalid ibn al-Walid, then fighting for the Quraysh, attacked from behind and the Muslims suffered heavy losses, including Hamzah.

whyNot.A: Water was an issue at Badr, where the Muslims took control of the wells, not at Uhud.
whyNot.D: The Prophet himself led the Muslims at Uhud.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which Companion advised the Muslims to dig a trench to defend Madinah in 5 AH?
questions.explanation: When a large confederate army (al-Ahzab) marched on Madinah, Salman al-Farisi, who came from Persia, suggested a trench, a Persian method of defence. The trench stopped the enemy cavalry, and the siege failed.

whyNot.D: Hamzah had already been martyred at Uhud in 3 AH, two years before the Trench.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which of the following was a term of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah (6 AH)?
options: The Muslims would go back that year and return the next year to perform 'umrah
The Quraysh would accept Islam within ten years
The Quraysh would hand over the keys of the Ka'bah to the Muslims
The Muslims would pay a yearly tribute to the Quraysh
questions.explanation: At Hudaybiyyah the Quraysh and the Muslims agreed a ten-year truce. The Muslims would return to Madinah without performing 'umrah that year, and come back the following year to stay in Makkah for three days. The Qur'an (Surah al-Fath) called the treaty a clear victory.

whyNot.C: The Muslims took control of Makkah and the Ka'bah only at the conquest in 8 AH.
whyNot.B: There was no clause about the Quraysh becoming Muslims.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Caliph Abu Bakr's wars against tribes that refused to pay zakat or followed false prophets after the Prophet's death are known as
questions.explanation: After the Prophet's death in 11 AH, some tribes broke away, refused zakat, or followed false prophets such as Musaylimah. Abu Bakr fought them in the Ridda (apostasy) wars and reunited Arabia under Islam.

whyNot.D: The Battle of the Camel was fought in Ali's caliphate, in 36 AH.
whyNot.B: The Fijar wars were pre-Islamic wars fought when the Prophet was a young man.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which rightly guided caliph introduced the Islamic (Hijri) calendar, dated from the Hijrah?
questions.explanation: Umar ibn al-Khattab, the second caliph, saw the need for a common dating system for official letters. On the advice of the Companions he adopted the year of the Hijrah (622 CE) as year 1 of the Islamic calendar.

whyNot.A: Abu Bakr's short caliphate is remembered for the Ridda wars and the compilation of the Qur'an.
whyNot.C: Uthman is remembered for standardising the copies of the Qur'an.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: During the caliphate of Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Battle of Siffin was fought between Ali's forces and those of
questions.explanation: Mu'awiyah, the governor of Syria, demanded punishment of Uthman's killers before accepting Ali as caliph. Their armies met at Siffin in 37 AH (657 CE), and the fighting ended in arbitration.

whyNot.C: Abu Sufyan was Mu'awiyah's father; he had died before Ali became caliph.
whyNot.B: Amr ibn Hisham is Abu Jahl, who was killed at Badr in 2 AH.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Through which of the following did Islam first reach West Africa?
options: The return of freed slaves from Brazil
Trans-Saharan trade with North African merchants
questions.explanation: Arab and Berber traders crossing the Sahara to buy gold and other goods brought Islam to West African towns. Muslim scholars and teachers followed the trade routes, and some rulers accepted Islam.

whyNot.C: European missionaries spread Christianity, and arrived centuries after Islam.
whyNot.A: Returnees from Brazil came in the 19th century, long after Islam was established.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which ruler of the Mali Empire became famous for his pilgrimage to Makkah in 1324, during which he gave away so much gold in Cairo that its value fell?
questions.explanation: Mansa Musa (reigned about 1312–1337) travelled to Makkah in 1324 with a huge caravan carrying gold. His generosity in Cairo made Mali famous across the Muslim world.

whyNot.A: Sundiata Keita founded the Mali Empire, but the famous pilgrimage was made by Mansa Musa.
whyNot.D: Askia Muhammad was a ruler of Songhai who made his pilgrimage in 1496–1497.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Shehu Usman dan Fodio launched his jihad in Hausaland in the year
questions.explanation: After his Hijrah from Degel to Gudu in 1804, Usman dan Fodio's followers declared jihad against the rulers of Gobir that same year. The jihad led to the founding of the Sokoto Caliphate.

whyNot.C: 1754 is the year Usman dan Fodio was born.
whyNot.A: 1817 is the year he died in Sokoto.
whyNot.D: 1903 is the year the British conquered Sokoto.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Usman dan Fodio was born in 1754 in which Hausa kingdom?
questions.explanation: Usman dan Fodio was born at Maratta in Gobir into a Fulani family of scholars. He later preached in Gobir, and his conflict with its rulers led to the jihad of 1804.

whyNot.A: Kano was conquered by the jihadists, but it was not his birthplace.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Nana Asma'u, daughter of Usman dan Fodio, is best remembered for
options: translating the Qur'an into the English language
educating women through her poems and her network of women teachers
building the Djinguereber mosque in Timbuktu
leading the army that captured the Gobir capital, Alkalawa
questions.explanation: Nana Asma'u was a scholar and poet who wrote in Arabic, Fulfulde and Hausa. She trained women teachers ('yan taru) who travelled to teach rural women, making her a pioneer of women's education in northern Nigeria.

whyNot.C: The Djinguereber mosque was built in the 14th century in Mali's time, centuries before her.
whyNot.A: She wrote in Arabic, Fulfulde and Hausa, not English.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which of the following was a reform of Mai Idris Alooma of Kanem-Bornu?
options: He moved the capital of Bornu to Sokoto
He banned all trade across the Sahara
He set up Shari'ah courts with qadis and built brick mosques
He made Christianity the official religion of the court
questions.explanation: Mai Idris Alooma (late 16th century) made the pilgrimage to Makkah, appointed qadis to judge by the Shari'ah, replaced reed mosques with brick ones, and strengthened his army with firearms obtained through contact with the Turks.

whyNot.A: Sokoto was founded in the 19th century as the capital of the Sokoto Caliphate, not of Bornu.
whyNot.B: Idris Alooma encouraged trade across the Sahara, which also brought him firearms.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which Songhai ruler seized power in 1493, made the pilgrimage to Makkah, and promoted Islamic learning in Timbuktu?
questions.explanation: Askia Muhammad (Askia the Great) took power from the dynasty of Sunni Ali in 1493. A devout Muslim, he made the pilgrimage in 1496–1497, appointed qadis, and supported the scholars of Timbuktu.

whyNot.C: Sunni Ali was only nominally Muslim and treated the scholars of Timbuktu harshly.
whyNot.A: Mansa Musa ruled Mali, not Songhai, in the 14th century.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Who founded the town of Sokoto in 1809 and became the first Sultan of Sokoto?
questions.explanation: Muhammad Bello, son of Usman dan Fodio, founded Sokoto in 1809. After his father's death in 1817 he became Sultan (Amir al-Mu'minin) of the eastern part of the caliphate, ruling from Sokoto.

whyNot.D: Abdullahi dan Fodio, Usman's brother, governed the western part from Gwandu.
whyNot.A: Al-Kanemi was the leader in Bornu who resisted the jihadists.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Abu Ishaq as-Sahili, a poet and architect whom Mansa Musa brought back from his pilgrimage, is credited with building which mosque?
questions.explanation: On his return from Makkah, Mansa Musa brought scholars and the Andalusian architect as-Sahili, who built the Djinguereber (Great Mosque) of Timbuktu around 1327, using burnt-brick and mud techniques.

whyNot.D: The Gobarau mosque is in Katsina, in Hausaland, and was not built by as-Sahili.
whyNot.A: The Sankore mosque is in Timbuktu, not Gao, and is not the mosque credited to as-Sahili.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which scholar was the most influential teacher of the young Usman dan Fodio?
questions.explanation: Jibril ibn Umar, a scholar from Agades, taught Usman dan Fodio and strongly opposed un-Islamic practices. His ideas about reform deeply shaped the Shehu's later preaching.

whyNot.C: Al-Maghili lived in the late 15th century and advised rulers of Kano and Songhai, centuries before Usman.
whyNot.B: Ahmad Baba was a Timbuktu scholar of the 16th–17th centuries.

questions.subject: islamic-studies
questions.stem: Which angel brought the revelation of the Qur'an to Prophet Muhammad (SAW)?
